books.title: More Valuable Than Gold
books.art_why: The Amazon rainforest, miners, gold mining sites and modern equipment are real and photographable.

pages.text: The tangled trees of the Amazon rainforest are home to millions of species of animals and plants. The Amazon Rainforest Imagine walking through a beautiful forest with giant trees, vines, and large, colorful flowers. Strange sounds made by birds, monkeys, and other wild animals fill the air. Big, brightly colored snakes, frogs, and insects crawl along the branches. The temperature is high, but raindrops sprinkle through leaves overhead.
pages.brief: A dense Amazon rainforest scene with tangled giant trees, hanging vines, and large colorful flowers. Birds and monkeys move among the branches while brightly colored snakes, frogs, and insects crawl nearby. Raindrops sprinkle through the leaves overhead in the high temperature.

pages.text: It takes years for the rainforest to recover from the destruction caused by illegal mines, such as this one near the border of Brazil. Suddenly you come upon a bare area with no plants or animals and an enormous, deep hole gouged into the ground. The grinding of machines and the yells of people replace the wild forest sounds. Many workers hurry in and around the hole. They are mining for gold. This is South America’s Amazon rainforest. It’s home to many Indigenous societies and more kinds of plants and animals than any other place in the world. However, outside influences are destroying this rainforest.
pages.brief: A bare, damaged area in the Amazon rainforest with an enormous deep hole gouged into the ground. Many workers hurry in and around the pit, mining for gold. Machines grind and people yell, replacing the wild forest sounds. No plants or animals remain in the cleared patch near Brazil’s border.

pages.text: Threats to the Rainforest The Amazon River flows for about 4,000 miles (6,437 km) from the Andes Mountains to the Atlantic Ocean. In the river valley, constant warm temperatures and large amounts of rain allow for amazing biodiversity in the rainforest. The Amazon rainforest is so vast that it seems as though nothing could harm it. However, people destroy huge areas of the rainforest every year through deforestation. Deforestation happens for many reasons. Loggers cut down trees to make paper and wood products, such as furniture. Ranchers clear land for cattle. Farmers use land to grow soybeans, corn, and other crops. These satellite photos show the effects of logging in one section of the Amazon rainforest from 2000 to 2006.
pages.brief: A wide view of the Amazon River valley with warm rainforest and heavy rain supporting rich biodiversity. Beside it, satellite images compare one forest section, showing intact rainforest and areas where logging has cleared trees. Loggers cut trees for paper and wood, ranchers clear land for cattle, and farmers grow soybeans and corn.

pages.text: Tens of thousands of plant species, billions of insects, and many fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals live in the Amazon region. The forest’s destruction has wiped out thousands of plant and animal species. Scientists might have been able to study these extinct plants and animals to learn things that could help people. The Amazon rainforest is also home to hundreds of Indigenous communities, like the Yanomami and Munduruku (moon-doo-roo- KOO) peoples. Mining, logging, ranching, and farming operations overtake Indigenous lands and bring violence, disease, and destruction of Indigenous cultures and knowledge.
pages.brief: A rich Amazon rainforest filled with many plants, billions of insects, fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Indigenous communities such as the Yanomami and Munduruku live in the region. Around them, mining, logging, ranching, and farming operations overtake Indigenous lands, bringing violence, disease, and destruction of cultures and knowledge.

pages.text: Do You Know? Plants store large amounts of carbon, which they use to make energy. When humans burn the rainforest, large amounts of carbon dioxide are released into the air. Scientists think that in the future, the deforestation of the Amazon rainforest will produce more carbon dioxide than it removes. The deforestation of the Amazon rainforest adds to global climate change as well. Rainforest plants remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere for photosynthesis, the process by which they make their own food. With fewer plants, more carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere. Large amounts of carbon dioxide trap heat in Earth’s atmosphere and contribute to global warming. Though not the greatest causes of deforestation, gold prospecting and mining cause long-term damage. They also affect more than just the areas around the mines. The high price of gold fuels demand, which means the destruction will continue for years to come.
pages.brief: Rainforest plants remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere for photosynthesis, making their own food. A burning rainforest releases large amounts of carbon dioxide into the air. With fewer plants, more carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere and traps heat, adding to global warming. Gold prospecting and mining cause long-term damage beyond mine areas.

pages.text: Why Gold? Gold is very valuable and difficult to find in nature. Large amounts of it exist underground in the Amazon Valley. People mainly use gold to make jewelry. However, many computers, cell phones, and televisions contain gold wires. Gold on the outside of spacecraft keeps the Sun’s heat from damaging equipment. With so many uses for gold—and more expected—the price and global demand of this rare metal is often high. Gold Price per Ounce, 2000 to 2022 To meet the high demand, many companies based in countries like Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia offer miners more money than they can earn doing more environmentally- friendly jobs. Because deforestation contributes to high poverty levels, many families are forced to choose jobs like mining for gold.
pages.brief: Gold jewelry, gold wires inside computers, cell phones, and televisions, and gold on the outside of spacecraft show some uses of the valuable metal. A rising price line shows high global demand. To meet demand, companies offer miners more money than environmentally friendly jobs pay, and some families choose mining because poverty is high.

pages.text: Illegal miners in Peru search for gold in a protected part of the rainforest. Gold Mining in the Amazon The methods used in gold prospecting and mining are harmful to people as well as the rainforest. Many of the gold mines are small, illegal operations located in parts of the forest protected by governments. Many South American governments do not have enough money or officers to protect the land, which means these mines wipe out more and more of the forest every year.
pages.brief: Illegal miners in Peru search for gold in a protected part of the rainforest. Many gold mines are small illegal operations inside government-protected forest. South American governments lack enough money and officers to protect the land, so these mines wipe out more and more forest every year.

pages.text: To get the buried gold, prospectors cut down or burn all the trees. They then dig a deep pit with machines or blast out a pit with dynamite. The pit may be as deep as 50 feet (15 m). Miners blast away the walls of the pit with powerful water cannons. This process loosens the ore, which contains the gold, from the walls. The loosened, muddy mixture is sucked up into dump trucks that empty the mud into containers.
pages.brief: Gold prospectors cut down or burn trees, then dig or blast a deep pit as deep as fifty feet. Miners use powerful water cannons to blast the pit walls and loosen ore containing gold. The muddy mixture is sucked up into dump trucks that empty it into containers.

pages.text: Workers mix the mud with mercury, a toxic metal, sometimes using their bare hands or feet. The mercury separates the gold from the ore. Some smaller mines use copper pans or sheets to separate the gold and mercury mixture from the mud. Others use sluices, in which a filter captures the heavier gold and mercury mixture as the watery mud runs down. The mercury is removed from the gold, often by burning it away. The gold can then be sold.
pages.brief: Workers mix mud with toxic mercury, sometimes with bare hands or feet, to separate gold from ore. Smaller mines use copper pans or sheets; others use sluices where a filter captures the heavier gold and mercury mixture as watery mud runs down. The mercury is burned away from the gold, and the gold can be sold.

pages.text: This process contaminates the forest with mercury. In the soil, it poisons forest plants and farm crops. In rivers, it enters the bodies of fish. As larger fish eat smaller fish, the amount of mercury in the bodies of the larger fish increases until they become poisonous. When people or other animals drink contaminated water or eat contaminated plants or fish, they become poisoned by the large amounts of mercury. Because gold miners work so closely with mercury, they often become poisoned when they breathe in its fumes or touch it with their bare hands or feet. 3 As humans and other animals eat larger fish, the level of mercury in their bodies increases until it can become poisonous. Mercury poisoning can cause many health problems, including lung disease, kidney disease, shaking, blindness, and trouble walking and talking. People who have been poisoned may be in great pain and so sick that they can barely move. It can take years for people to recover from mercury poisoning, while others will never heal. 2 As larger fish eat smaller fish, the level of mercury in their bodies increases. 1 Small fish eat plants and other small animals contaminated with mercury.
pages.brief: The mercury contaminates soil, plants, farm crops, and rivers. Small fish eat contaminated plants and animals; larger fish eat smaller fish, building up poisonous mercury. People and other animals become poisoned by drinking contaminated water or eating contaminated plants or fish. Miners also breathe mercury fumes or touch it, risking lung and kidney disease, shaking, blindness, and trouble walking and talking.

pages.text: Illegal miners clear away the rainforest to make their camps. Protecting the Rainforest Many people are working to protect and preserve the rainforest. This is difficult work. Gold mining, logging, ranching, and other harmful activities are profitable and widespread throughout the Amazon region. Some governments in the Amazon region are spending more money to enforce laws and close down illegal mines. However, as long as poor people have few jobs and little money, they may want or need to mine gold. The best solution to the problem of rainforest destruction may be for governments to improve economic opportunities. For example, the government of Brazil has programs to improve the education and job skills of people who can’t otherwise afford schooling or training. This allows them to get other jobs besides those that harm the rainforest.
pages.brief: Illegal miners clear rainforest to make their camps. Many people work to protect and preserve the rainforest, though gold mining, logging, and ranching are profitable and widespread. Some governments spend more to enforce laws and close illegal mines. Brazil has programs to improve education and job skills so people can get jobs that do not harm the rainforest.

pages.text: Governments are not alone in protecting the rainforest. They have help from conservation organizations. These groups work with government agencies, businesses, and other organizations to study and conserve natural places. Continued efforts by both governments and conservation organizations are necessary to stop illegal mining and protect the rainforest. The destruction of the Amazon affects the entire world. Are the jewelry and other things we make from gold really worth damaging the health of the planet and its inhabitants? A farmer checks on a young tree as part of a reforestation project in Brazil.
pages.brief: Conservation organizations work with government agencies, businesses, and other groups to study and conserve natural places. A farmer checks a young tree in a reforestation project in Brazil. Continued efforts by governments and conservation groups are needed to stop illegal mining and protect the rainforest, because Amazon destruction affects the entire world.

books.title: Invasion of the Pythons
books.art_why: Real snakes, scientists, parks and wildlife work that exist today, so photographs are possible; no named famous person is the subject.

pages.text: Introduction Slogging through ankle-deep water in the Florida Everglades, the scientists approach their target. Suddenly, one of the team pounces and grabs the tail of a huge snake. Another researcher lunges and grabs the snake behind its head. Others quickly join the wrestling match between humans and this 16-foot (4.9 m), 150-pound (68 kg) Burmese python. The python finally tires, and they haul it back to the lab for study. The scientists win this time. A bigger battle is underway, though, because Burmese pythons aren’t even supposed to be in Florida. These large snakes are native to the jungles and marshy grasslands of India and other parts of South Asia. What are they doing in Florida?
pages.brief: Two scientists stand in ankle-deep water in the Florida Everglades gripping a huge Burmese python — one seizes its tail, another pins it behind the head, and teammates join the wrestling match. The 16-foot, 150-pound snake finally tires and is hauled away toward the lab.

pages.text: Who Invited That Guy? For millions of years, the movement of animals and plants was limited by natural barriers. Mountain ranges and deserts separated habitats, so species could not spread. Oceans were especially difficult to cross. That changed as transportation improved. By the 1800s, many humans moved to new lands, bringing familiar livestock and plant seeds with them. Sometimes animals—rats, lizards, dogs, and cats—crawled onto ships and were carried across the sea. Today people move farther and faster than ever before. Whether by human design or by accident, other species move as well. In their native lands, species usually have competition and predators to keep their numbers in check. If their new home lacks these challenges, a new species may multiply and take over, thereby becoming an invasive species. Kudzu vines from Japan, for example, have choked out other plants in the southeastern United States. On the island of Guam, the brown tree snake has wiped out much of the bird population. As other native species lose a familiar source of food or shelter, the entire ecosystem can suffer.
pages.brief: An 1800s sailing ship crosses open ocean, rats, lizards, dogs and cats crawling aboard while people carry livestock and plant seeds to new lands. Onshore in the southeast United States, dense kudzu vines smother other plants, and a brown tree snake perches on Guam.

pages.text: No one knows for sure how Burmese pythons got into the Everglades ecosystem. The first invaders may have escaped from Florida pet shops, or maybe some pet owners released their pythons when they grew too big to care for. Once the snakes got loose, they thrived in the heat and humidity, hiding in the tangled underbrush and gobbling up other animals. The invasion of the pythons was underway. Pythons as Pets Burmese pythons have become trendy pets among some snake fans. They are cheap to buy and are believed to be easy to control. Some owners can be careless about their pets, though. They may be unaware of how fast and how huge pythons grow. In a couple of years, a 2-foot (.6 m) snake can grow to 12 feet (3.7 m). Also, snakes are escape artists that will squeeze their way out of cages or aquariums that are not carefully locked. Now and then, large pet pythons have attacked and even killed people. In 2012, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service banned bringing new Burmese pythons into the United States. Owners must also insert a microchip into pet pythons to make them easier to trace.
pages.brief: A young Burmese python rests inside a glass aquarium, while a careless owner releases a grown snake into tangled Everglades underbrush. Nearby, a tiny microchip lies ready for insertion into a captive pet python so the snake can be traced.

pages.text: Threats by the Thousands The first Burmese python was reported in the Everglades in 1979. Another sixteen years passed before the next one was found. Since 2000, though, python reports have grown more and more common. When a nest of python eggs was discovered, it confirmed what wildlife biologists feared: Burmese pythons were breeding in the wild. Pythons reproduce rapidly. Females usually lay more than fifty eggs a year, and within three years of hatching, young pythons themselves are ready to breed. The result in the Everglades has been a population explosion as, year after year, more pythons lay eggs and more pythons survive. Python Removals in and Around Everglades National Park An increasing python population was probably only one factor that led to the dramatic rise in captures.
pages.brief: Wildlife biologists kneel in Everglades brush beside a discovered nest of python eggs, confirming the snakes are breeding in the wild. A female python lies coiled over more than fifty eggs hidden in the grass.

pages.text: Pythons hatch from their eggs ready to slither away and start eating and growing, reaching adult size in only four years. Burmese pythons average about 12 feet (3.7 m) in length, but the largest may stretch more than 20 feet (6.1 m) and top 200 pounds (90 kg). Creepy to some, beautiful to others, the way Burmese pythons kill is the stuff of nightmares. Pythons belong to a class of snakes called constrictors. These snakes track down live animals using their sense of smell and ability to sense heat. They then surprise their prey, latching on with a broad mouth lined with sharp teeth. Once the animal is caught, the python coils its muscular body around it and squeezes until its victim suffocates. Finally, the snake swallows its prey whole, stretching its jaws to gulp down animals as much as five times larger than its own head. Scientists have yet to get a true count of how many pythons live in the Everglades today. They estimate the python population to be anywhere between 5,000 and 100,000. In 2012, researchers captured the biggest Burmese python found so far in the Everglades. She was 17 feet 7 inches (5.4 m) long, and inside her were 87 eggs ready for laying.
pages.brief: Newly hatched Burmese pythons slither out of leathery eggs and spread into the grass. A big constrictor coils its muscular body around captured prey. A captured female python, 17 feet 7 inches long, lies stretched out with 87 eggs taken from inside her.

pages.text: An Everglades Nightmare The Everglades—nicknamed the River of Grass—is one of the most unusual ecosystems in North America. A region of wetlands in southern Florida, it consists mainly of marshes, swamps, and grasslands. Few hills and fewer buildings rise on the broad, flat landscape, but it is rich with plant and animal life and is an important home for many native insects, fish, mammals, and other animals. The American alligator is perhaps the most familiar Everglades native. This leathery reptile can grow up to 16 feet (4.9 m) long and is a fierce predator. Rarer is the Florida panther—only a few dozen of these big cats still roam in the wild. The Everglades is also home to many smaller mammals and is a paradise for birds, including the bald eagle, great egret, roseate spoonbill, and many other wading birds. With jaguars and pumas gone from Florida, the only big cat left there is the panther. Its population is tiny.
pages.brief: The flat Everglades wetlands stretch out as marsh, swamp and grassland under open sky. A leathery American alligator rests in the water, a rare Florida panther stalks through brush, and a bald eagle, great egret and roseate spoonbill stand among wading birds.

pages.text: Burmese pythons will gulp down any animal they can catch. In fact, they have been called “eating machines.” In the Everglades, researchers discovered a python that had killed and swallowed an 80-pound (36 kg) deer. In another case, they found a dead python with a 6-foot (1.8 m) alligator in its mouth. The two animals had killed each other in a life-or-death struggle. Worried that pythons might wipe out some of Florida’s native animals, one research team set out to discover whether this might be the case. In areas with large numbers of these snakes, the researchers studied the populations of small mammals, such as marsh rabbits, raccoons, bobcats, and opossums. They looked at animal counts along roadways from 1996–1997, before pythons became common, and then examined the same data for more recent years. What the team found was shocking: The populations of all these mammals had crashed. There were no signs of marsh rabbits or foxes at all. Yet where pythons were rare or absent, populations were unchanged. Many scientists think pythons are responsible—either they ate all these animals or wiped out the smaller animals that are food for bobcats, foxes, and other predators.
pages.brief: Researchers examine a dead python that had swallowed an 80-pound deer, and another python locked in a fatal struggle with a 6-foot alligator. Along Everglades roadways a team counts small mammals — marsh rabbits, raccoons, bobcats and opossums — where pythons are common.

pages.text: Vanishing Mammals Scientists compared mammal numbers in Everglades National Park before 2000 with numbers from 2003–2011. With the rise of pythons, native mammal numbers have crashed. Bobcat 87.5% decline Raccoon 99.3% decline Red fox 100% decline Opossum 98.9% decline Marsh rabbit 100% decline.
pages.brief: A bobcat, raccoon, red fox, opossum and marsh rabbit move through Everglades National Park habitat, the native mammals whose numbers crashed as pythons spread, while in places where the snakes are rare or absent the same animals remain unchanged.

pages.text: Threatened and Threatening Even as they threaten native animals that are endangered in the United States (eating the Florida panther’s prey, for instance, or simply eating wood storks), Burmese pythons are endangered in South Asia. Their numbers have been shrinking there because of the destruction of their habitat. Also, they are hunted for their skins and meat, as well as captured and sold as exotic pets. Pythons also eat birds in the Everglades. In one study, researchers found that birds make up 25 percent of a python’s diet. The feathers and bones of rare and endangered species, such as the wood stork, have been found in pythons’ bellies. How do scientists know what the pythons are eating? In most cases, they do a necropsy, slicing open dead pythons and studying the dead animals they find in their stomachs. The remains have mostly been of mammals, but birds that live in or near water are also at risk of being eaten.
pages.brief: A researcher performs a necropsy on a dead python, slicing it open to find feathers and bones of a rare wood stork inside its stomach. In South Asia, python habitat is cleared and the snakes are hunted for skins and meat or captured for the exotic pet trade.

pages.text: Part of why native animals may be so helpless against pythons is because these snakes are newcomers. Native species have evolved together, adapting to one another in order to coexist. For 16 million years, no snakes in Florida have been big enough to prey on many of these animals. The natives may not know how to protect themselves or their young from this invasive predator. What’s more, the ecosystem lacks any way to keep the invader in check. Burmese pythons live at the top of the Everglades food chain. Alligators will eat them if they can, but once a python gets big enough, it will even attack alligators. Burmese pythons live at the top of the Everglades food chain. Skip Snow, a biologist at Everglades National Park, pulls a bird from a python’s stomach.
pages.brief: Biologist Skip Snow pulls a bird from the stomach of a dead python at Everglades National Park. A large Burmese python sits at the top of the food chain, and in the marsh an alligator grips a python in its jaws.

pages.text: Fighting Back Finding pythons in the Everglades is tough. The landscape makes it easy for pythons to hide—and hard for humans to find them. Burmese pythons may hide in the grass and brush, and they can stay underwater for up to thirty minutes. Still, Florida workers and volunteers are taking action to try to bring pythons under control. At Everglades National Park, they track down and capture the snakes when possible— almost 2,000 in recent years. Hunters are also allowed to capture the snakes or kill them for their skins and meat. Unfortunately, hunters sometimes mistakenly kill small native snakes, thinking they are baby pythons. One way researchers track pythons is by using radio transmitters. They insert the device into a live snake and release it, and that snake might lead them to other pythons. A researcher inserts a radio tag into a live Burmese python.
pages.brief: Florida workers and volunteers push through tall grass and brush searching for hidden pythons, while a hunter carries off a captured snake. A researcher inserts a small radio transmitter tag into a live Burmese python before releasing it to lead the team to others.

pages.text: New laws have been put in place to prevent pet pythons from joining those in the wild. Still, most experts believe it is already too late to stop the python takeover of Florida. Wildlife biologists today fear that Burmese pythons may invade other parts of the country. They can swim to new territory and survive in most places where winters don’t get too cold. Many southern states could be at risk, from South Carolina all the way to California. Scientists continue to investigate the role that pythons play in the changing Everglades ecosystem. Until they learn more, they are careful about putting all the blame on pythons. Still, what we learn about these snake invaders in Florida may keep them from making their way across the country. A Burmese python curls up in the grass at Everglades National Park in Florida.
pages.brief: A Burmese python curls up in the grass at Everglades National Park in Florida. Elsewhere a python swims across open water toward new territory, where mild winters in southern states could let the snake survive and spread.

books.title: Malala the Brave
books.art_why: A biography of a named famous person.

pages.text: Malala the Brave.
pages.brief: A brave girl named Malala stands with quiet determination. She looks ahead with courage, ready to share her life. The scene is simple and focused, introducing a young heroine whose name promises bravery and resolve.

pages.text: Introduction Can you imagine living in a country where some children aren’t allowed to attend school? Where a child’s highest hope is to be able to get an education, and that hope is denied? This is the world in which a brave girl named Malala grew up. Malala’s Name Malala was named for a courageous poet and warrior woman who lived in Afghanistan long ago. She led Afghan fighters to victory in a battle against invading British soldiers in 1880.
pages.brief: A young girl imagines a country where some children cannot attend school. Nearby, a courageous Afghan poet and warrior woman from long ago leads Afghan fighters to victory against invading British soldiers in 1880. The two scenes connect Malala’s name to bravery and the hope for education.

pages.text: Malala stands with her parents and brothers, Khushal (left) and Atal. Malala’s World Malala Yousafzai (YOO-suf-zy) was born on July 12, 1997, in Mingora, a city in Pakistan’s Swat Valley. Her family includes two younger brothers. Malala’s father, Ziauddin (zee-OW-deen), is a champion of human rights, which are basic rights that everyone in the world should have. Malala’s father worked to make sure every child in Pakistan could receive an education. Since 1994, he has helped to open many schools in Pakistan’s Swat District that now teach over one thousand students. For many years, Malala attended one of the schools founded by her father. Malala’s father has always encouraged her to ask questions and think for herself since she was very young. He taught her to speak up for human rights, equality, and education.
pages.brief: Malala stands with her mother, father, and two younger brothers, Khushal and Atal. Her father, Ziauddin, champions human rights and has helped open many schools in Pakistan’s Swat District. The family is together in Mingora, a city in the Swat Valley, where Malala grew up.

pages.text: Malala’s mother, Tor Pekai, is a homemaker who follows Muslim traditions by living a private life out of view of others. Malala says that she admires her mother but knows that her own path in life is different. The Swat District is an area of northern Pakistan with high mountains and lush green valleys. Many people consider the region beautiful, and it used to attract tourists. However, not many people visit the area anymore because of the Taliban, a political group based in Pakistan and Afghanistan. The Taliban follow an extreme and fundamentalist version of the Islamic religion that is very different from the version followed by most Muslims. As part of their beliefs, the Taliban severely limit the rights of women. Most residents of areas controlled by the Taliban are forced to follow strict religious rules. For example, music, movies, and television are not allowed. The rules for women and girls are especially strict. Women and girls may not work outside the home, attend school, or wear makeup or bright clothing. They are not permitted to laugh out loud. After a certain age, girls cannot be outside the home without a male relative. The Taliban use violence, including acts of terrorism, to enforce their laws.
pages.brief: Malala’s mother, Tor Pekai, is shown at home, living a private life. Beyond the home, the Swat District has high mountains and lush green valleys. In the area, Taliban rules keep women and girls from school, work, bright clothing, and laughter.

pages.text: Malala’s family is deeply religious—but their religious practices didn’t align with the Taliban’s. When asked about her religion, Malala is quick to point out that the Islamic religion does not oppose education for girls. In her words, “Islam says that it is not only each child’s right to get [an] education, rather it is their duty and responsibility.” The Taliban started trying to take control of the Swat Valley in 2007. Pakistan’s government and army were unable to stop them. The Taliban attacked police officers and blew up religious and government buildings. Their many acts of violence included destroying girls’ schools in the area. By the end of 2008, the Taliban had blown up roughly 400 schools in Swat and over 1,500 schools in total. The Taliban announced that as of January 15, 2009, girls would no longer be allowed to attend school in the areas under their control.
pages.brief: Malala speaks about her faith, explaining that Islam does not oppose education for girls. In the Swat Valley, Taliban fighters attack police and government buildings and destroy girls’ schools. By the end of 2008, hundreds of schools are blown up, and girls are told they may no longer attend school.

pages.text: Throughout this period, Malala’s father kept his schools open, even though it was dangerous. Over half of Malala’s classmates were pulled out of school because their parents feared the Taliban. Malala stopped wearing her school uniform to avoid being targeted. Why Is Education Important? Education is much more than learning how to read and write. Education provides people with the tools they need to care for themselves and their families and to be active in their communities. Think about the following questions: • How can education affect the kind of job a person might have? • How might an education help people care for their families better? Consider things like food, medical care, educational opportunities for children, and other goods and services. • How might education and the prevention of child labor be connected? • How does education help make a community healthier? • How might education about certain issues affect the choices that people make when they vote? • How does education promote peace in communities and countries? • How might science education affect people’s attitudes about the environment? • How else does education make a difference in people’s lives?
pages.brief: Malala’s father keeps his schools open even though it is dangerous. Many classmates are pulled out by fearful parents. Malala walks without her school uniform to avoid being targeted. Around her, empty desks and worried families show why education matters for work, health, community, and peace.

pages.text: Malala’s Work Malala’s father encouraged his students to speak out against losing their right to an education. Malala and several friends gave an interview on a TV show in Pakistan in 2008. Malala then volunteered to appear on a talk show. She was nervous, but she knew she had to speak her mind. While on the talk show, she asked, “How dare the Taliban take away my basic right to education?” Malala’s courage in speaking out against the Taliban impressed many people. “One child, one teacher, one pen, and one book can change the world. Education is the only solution.” —Malala Malala started blogging on the Internet for the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) in 2009 at age eleven. She blogged about her dreams for her life and about what it was like to live under the rule of the Taliban. She used a pseudonym, or fake name, to hide her identity and keep from being targeted for her writing. After her blog was translated into English, people around the world read it. They were shocked about the situation in Swat and the Taliban’s efforts to prevent girls from attending school. Although Malala hoped to keep her identity private, her secret got out in December 2009.
pages.brief: Malala and several friends appear on a Pakistan TV show in 2008. Later, nervous but determined, Malala speaks on a talk show. At age eleven, she writes a BBC blog under a fake name, and people around the world read her words after translation. Her secret identity is revealed in December 2009.

pages.text: As Malala continued to speak out about education as a basic human right, her fame grew. She gave many interviews on television and in print. In 2010, the New York Times made a movie about her life. In 2011, Desmond Tutu, a world- famous activist and religious leader from South Africa, nominated Malala for the International Children’s Peace Prize. That same year, Pakistan’s prime minister awarded her Pakistan’s National Youth Peace Prize. In her own country and around the world, she was a voice of hope and empowerment. As Malala spoke out more and more, she and her father were both seen as threats to the Taliban’s goals. When she was fourteen, her family learned that the Taliban had called for her to die. Malala was afraid for her father’s safety since he was an anti-Taliban activist. However, neither she nor her family thought at first that she was in danger because she was a child.
pages.brief: Malala gives many television and print interviews as her fame grows. In 2011, Desmond Tutu nominates her for the International Children’s Peace Prize, and Pakistan’s prime minister awards her the National Youth Peace Prize. She and her father are seen as threats; the Taliban call for her to die when she is fourteen.

pages.text: The Attack Malala paid careful attention to her family’s safety as well as her own. She locked doors and avoided walking home from school. Instead, she took the bus. On October 9, 2012, she rode the bus home from school with several friends. A man got on the bus and asked which girl was Malala. Even though no one answered with words, her friends looked at her, so the man knew. He pulled out a gun and fired three shots, one of which struck Malala and injured her very badly. Two other girls were hit, too, though neither one had serious injuries.
pages.brief: On October 9, 2012, Malala rides the bus home from school with several friends. A man gets on and asks which girl is Malala. Her friends look at her without speaking. He pulls out a gun and fires three shots, badly injuring Malala and hitting two other girls.

pages.text: Malala nearly died after the attack. She was flown to a military hospital in a city a few hours away, where she received life-saving treatment. Malala was then transferred to a hospital in Birmingham, England. Many people made sure she received the best possible care. Malala was fortunate to recover from most of her wounds, although she will have some challenges for the rest of her life. The Taliban took credit for the attack. They said that other girls should pay attention to what happens when a girl speaks out. While Malala was in the hospital, she received cards, gifts, and flowers from thousands of people, including world leaders and movie stars. People around the world held candlelight gatherings to show their support. After she was far along in her recovery, Malala started attending school in Birmingham in March 2013. She and her family stayed in the United Kingdom, and she graduated from high school in 2017. Malala wasn’t happy to be away from the Swat Valley or her friends. In 2018, she visited Pakistan for the first time since the attack. “When someone takes away your pens, you realize quite how important education is.” —Malala.
pages.brief: Malala is flown to a military hospital, then to Birmingham, England, where many people care for her. Cards, gifts, and flowers arrive from thousands, including world leaders and movie stars, and candlelight gatherings show support. After recovering, she attends school in Birmingham in March 2013. In 2018 she visits Pakistan for the first time since the attack.

pages.text: Students, parents, and teachers in Karachi, Pakistan, show their support for Malala one month after she was attacked. MALALA TIME LINE 2011: Nominated for International Children’s Peace Prize; won Pakistan’s National Youth Peace Prize, which was renamed in her honor 2014: Became the youngest person ever awarded the Nobel Peace Prize 2008: Malala’s first public appearance, on a talk show in Peshawar 2009: Malala’s first BBC blog post is published; the Taliban order all girls’ schools closed 2012: Shot by Taliban; runner-up for 2012 TIME Person of the Year 1997: Born in Mingora, Pakistan.
pages.brief: Students, parents, and teachers gather in Karachi, Pakistan, one month after the attack to show support for Malala. They stand together in a public display of solidarity. Small scenes recall her birth in Mingora, her first public appearance, her BBC blog, the shooting, and the Nobel Peace Prize.

pages.text: Malala is introduced at the United Nations headquarters in New York City on July 12, 2013, before making her first speech following her attack. (Left) Malala’s book A Global Voice In July 2013, Malala gave a speech at the United Nations, less than one year after the attack. She called for children around the world to be permitted to get an education. Later that year, Malala received Europe’s top human rights award for her dedication to freedom of thought and human rights. She has met with President Obama, Queen Elizabeth II, and other world figures. Focus on Girls’ Education In 2012, United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon asked governments, organizations, businesses, religious leaders, and other people and groups around the globe to support education for girls. That same year, the United Nations and Pakistan established the Malala Fund for Girls’ Education. President Zardari of Pakistan donated the first $10 million.
pages.brief: At United Nations headquarters in New York City on July 12, 2013, Malala is introduced before giving her first speech since the attack. She calls for children around the world to be allowed an education. The scene also shows her book and the launch of the Malala Fund for Girls’ Education, with support from world leaders.

pages.text: In October 2014, Malala was chosen to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. At age seventeen, she was the youngest person ever given that honor. Malala said the award made her feel “more powerful and courageous.” She dedicated her award to “all those children who are voiceless,” saying, “My message to children around the world is [to] stand up for your rights.” The Taliban tried to silence Malala, but instead they made her voice carry even more loudly. She continues to support every child’s right to an education and refuses to be silenced by fear. Malala’s goal is to someday be Pakistan’s prime minister. Her father became a Special Advisor on Global Education for the United Nations. Malala and her father continue to work together, guided by their vision of a peaceful world and an education for every child. Malala meets U.S. President Barack Obama, First Lady Michelle Obama, and Malia Obama at the White House on October 11, 2013.
pages.brief: In October 2014, seventeen-year-old Malala receives the Nobel Peace Prize, the youngest person ever given that honor. She speaks with strength about children who are voiceless and urges children to stand up for their rights. She meets U.S. President Barack Obama, First Lady Michelle Obama, and Malia Obama at the White House on October 11, 2013.

books.title: Egypt
books.art_why: The book covers ancient Egypt and historical events from before photography existed.

pages.text: Egypt MEDITERRANEAN SEA Israel Alexandria Cairo Jordan Giza Pyramids Saudi Arabia Egypt Libya Gulf of Suez Luxor Aswan High Dam RED SEA Aswan EUROPE ASIA Sudan AFRICA Where Is It? The Arab Republic of Egypt is in the northeastern corner of the continent of Africa. A small part of the country, the Sinai (SEYE-neye) Peninsula, is located in Asia. The Sinai Peninsula shares its border with Israel and Palestine. To the north of Egypt is the Mediterranean (MEH-duh-tuh-RAY-nee-uhn) Sea, and to the east of much of the country is the Red Sea. The country has 2,450 kilometers (1,522 mi.) of coastline. Sudan is to the south of Egypt, and to the west is Libya.
pages.brief: A wide map drawing shows Egypt in the northeastern corner of Africa, with the Sinai Peninsula extending into Asia. The Mediterranean Sea lies to the north, the Red Sea to the east, Sudan to the south and Libya to the west. Coastline and bordering lands are visible around Egypt.

pages.text: Cairo (KEYE-roh), Egypt’s capital city, is located in the north. The Nile River flows through it on its way to the Mediterranean Sea. Cairo is one of the largest cities in Africa, with a population of more than twenty-one million people. Cairo sits on the same site as it did more than one thousand years ago. Muslim Arabs who conquered Egypt in 640 ce named it Al-Qahirah (el-KAH-hih-rah), which means “the victorious” in Arabic. Before that time, other ancient civilizations built towns on or near the site. Cairo is a place where ancient meets modern. Mosques and other buildings reflect Egypt’s long history. Many buildings date back to the times when Romans, Arabs, and Turks ruled Egypt. Near Cairo are the Pyramids of Giza, the monuments of ancient Egypt’s pharaohs (FEHR- ohz). Modern hotels line the Nile. The Pyramids of Giza are southwest of Cairo.
pages.brief: A view of Cairo beside the Nile River, where old mosques and historic buildings stand near modern hotels. The Pyramids of Giza rise southwest of the city. The river flows north toward the Mediterranean Sea, and the busy capital spreads across its banks as a place where ancient and modern Egypt meet.

pages.text: More than 106 million people live in Egypt. Many of Egypt’s cities and towns are located along the Nile, which runs through the eastern part of the country. Because the rest of the country is mainly desert, a large majority of Egyptians live near the Nile. People use ground water for cooking, washing, and drinking, and they use river water for irrigating crops. Many farmers grow cotton for Egypt’s large textile industry in the fertile land along the banks of the Nile. Farmers also grow wheat, rice, corn, beans, fruits, and vegetables. They dig canals that channel the river water to their crops for irrigation. In Egypt’s cities, many people work in service industries, and tourism is an important part of the country’s economy. In addition, people work in factories to produce textiles and process food. People Egyptian farmers use hoses to pump water into canals to irrigate their crops.
pages.brief: Egyptian farmers work fertile land along the Nile, using hoses to pump water into canals that carry river water to their crops. Fields of cotton, wheat, rice, corn, beans, fruits and vegetables stretch beside the river. Beyond the green banks, desert covers most of the country, while towns and cities cluster near the water.

pages.text: Most people in Egypt speak some form of Arabic. Most Egyptians are descended from people who originally lived in the Arabian Peninsula in Asia. Other Egyptians are of African descent, and many of these groups have their own languages as well. About 90 percent of Egyptians are Muslim, meaning they follow the religion of Islam. Nearly 10 percent are Christian. Christianity was the dominant religion in Egypt before Islam spread to the region around 640. Many Egyptians in cities wear western-style clothing, and many Egyptians also wear long-sleeved tunics called galabayas (gal-ah-BAY-ahs). Men often wear white, blue, or gray ones, while unmarried women usually wear bright colors. In addition, Muslim women typically wear a veil, called a hijab (hih-JAHB), that covers their heads. Muslims attend a lecture at a mosque in Cairo.
pages.brief: Inside a mosque in Cairo, Muslim Egyptians sit together for a lecture. Some worshippers wear long-sleeved galabayas, and Muslim women wear head coverings called hijabs. The gathering reflects Egypt’s mainly Muslim population, while the country also includes Christian Egyptians and people of Arab and African descent who speak Arabic and other languages.

pages.text: Egypt’s Landforms MEDITERRANEAN SEA Libyan Plateau Sinai Peninsula Cairo Qattara Depression Sinai Desert Mount Catherine Egypt Nile River Sahara Desert Gulf of Suez RED SEA Lake Nasser Land Most of Egypt is covered with deserts. The large Western Desert covers two-thirds of the country, the Eastern Desert lies next to the Red Sea, and the smaller Sinai Desert covers the Sinai Peninsula. All these deserts are part of the Sahara. Each desert has its own unique characteristics. The Western Desert looks like an endless sea of sand dunes with many sharp rocks. The Eastern Desert has wadis (WAH-deez), or dry beds of seasonal rivers that fill up with water only after a heavy rain. The Eastern Desert also includes rugged mountains in the east. The Sinai Desert has tall mountains and deep canyons. In all three deserts, green oases can be found.
pages.brief: A landform view of Egypt shows vast desert regions: the Western Desert with endless sand dunes and sharp rocks, the Eastern Desert with dry wadis and rugged mountains near the Red Sea, and the Sinai Desert with tall mountains and deep canyons. Green oases appear among the sands, and the Nile Valley cuts between the deserts.

pages.text: Lake Nasser Sinai Mountains Western Desert The fertile Nile River Valley is the border between the Western and Eastern Deserts. The Nile is one of the longest rivers in the world, flowing from south to north and ending at the Mediterranean Sea. Near its mouth, the river spreads out into the triangle-shaped Nile Delta. This well-irrigated land holds some of the most fertile soil in Egypt. The Nile Delta stretches about 160 kilometers (100 mi.) between Cairo and the Mediterranean Sea. In the south of Egypt, the Nile forms the world’s largest artificial lake, Lake Nasser. The lake was created in the 1960s when the Aswan Dam was built. Some historical sites were originally located on the land flooded to create Lake Nasser but were moved and reconstructed on safer ground nearby.
pages.brief: The Nile River flows from south to north through Egypt, spreading into the triangle-shaped Nile Delta before reaching the Mediterranean Sea. In the south, the Aswan Dam has created Lake Nasser, the world’s largest artificial lake. Fertile green land lines the river valley, while mountains and desert lie beyond, and relocated historical sites stand on safer ground nearby.

pages.text: Thousands of years ago, one of the world’s first civilizations developed along the banks of the Nile in Egypt. The seasonal flooding of the river provided rich land for the ancient Egyptians, and they were among the first people in the world to grow crops and use a plow. For about three thousand years, thirty different dynasties of pharaohs ruled ancient Egypt. Some ancient Egyptians believed the pharaohs were living gods, and they built huge stone monuments and tombs for them. The ancient Egyptians were also polytheistic, which means they believed in many gods. The pharaohs led the building of elaborate stone temples to honor different Egyptian gods. Between about 2700 and 1000 bce, Egypt was one of the greatest civilizations in the world. Hatshepsut The temple of Hatshepsut (haht-SHEP-soot) is located across the Nile from the present-day city of Luxor, near the site of the ancient Egyptian city of Thebes. Hatshepsut is one of the few known female Egyptian pharaohs. She reigned from around 1473 to 1458 bce. Ancient images show her wearing a false beard and traditional male clothing. History.
pages.brief: Along the Nile, ancient Egyptian farmers work rich land left by seasonal floods. Nearby, workers build stone temples and tombs for pharaohs, including the temple of Hatshepsut across the Nile from present-day Luxor. Hatshepsut is shown in traditional male clothing and a false beard, one of the few known female pharaohs.

pages.text: Over the centuries, several outside forces have conquered or occupied Egypt. In 332 bce, the emperor Alexander the Great invaded Egypt and made it part of the Greek Empire. Egypt was under Greek rule for about three hundred years. Alexander founded the city of Alexandria, which still sits on the northern coast and is the country’s main seaport. After centuries of Roman and Persian control, in 640 ce, a Muslim army from the Arabian Peninsula conquered Egypt. Muslim dynasties, including the Fatimids, Mamluks, and Ottomans, ruled Egypt until the 1700s. In 1798, France attempted to invade Egypt, motivating the British to become involved in Egypt’s government—the British did not want France to gain control of Egypt. The Ottoman Empire regained control of Egypt through the next century, but British and French influence remained. During World War I (1914–1918), Britain made Egypt a British protectorate, or a country that is protected and controlled by another country. In 1922 Egypt won its independence from the British.
pages.brief: A historical scene shows outside forces arriving in Egypt over the centuries. Alexander the Great’s Greek rule begins, Alexandria is founded as a seaport, and later a Muslim army from the Arabian Peninsula conquers Egypt. Muslim dynasties rule, then French and British influence grows, until Egypt wins independence from Britain in 1922.

pages.text: Landmarks Every year, millions of people visit Egypt to see its ancient landmarks. One of the most famous landmarks is the Valley of the Kings in southern Egypt. Some of Egypt’s most famous pharaohs were buried here in more than sixty tombs, along with countless treasures. Tomb robbers stole many of these treasures long ago. However, the tomb of Tutankhamun (toot-an-KAH-muhn) still had its treasures when it was discovered in 1922. Many of these amazing treasures are displayed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. The temples at Abu Simbel, along the banks of Lake Nasser, are another popular tourist site. Two of the temples were built by Ramses II, pharaoh of Egypt from 1279 to 1213 bce. Four giant stone statues of Ramses II sit at the entrance to the Great Temple, which was carved out of a cliff. Inside this temple, three hallways extend into the cliff and include more statues and painted scenes. The hallways lead to a shrine at the temple’s center dedicated to some of the Egyptian gods. temple at Abu Simbel.
pages.brief: At Abu Simbel beside Lake Nasser, four giant stone statues of Ramses II guard the entrance to the Great Temple carved into a cliff. Inside, hallways with more statues and painted scenes lead toward a shrine for Egyptian gods. Elsewhere, the Valley of the Kings holds tombs, and Tutankhamun’s treasures are displayed in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.

pages.text: Camels are particularly well suited to Egypt’s desert conditions because they can survive on very little water. Animals People in Egypt’s rural areas raise many animals, such as sheep, goats, donkeys, and water buffalo. Some people also raise and use camels for work. Some wild animals live in the harsh conditions of the deserts. One desert animal is the fennec, a small fox with large ears. The fennec spends most of its day underground in a burrow and comes out at night to find food. Many snakes, lizards, and scorpions also live in the deserts. The ibex (EYE-beks), a sturdy wild goat, is another animal that can survive in the deserts’ difficult conditions. The Nile and its valley are also home to many kinds of animals. Hundreds of different types of fish swim in the Nile’s waters, and crocodiles can be found in the southern part of the river.
pages.brief: A desert scene shows a camel used for work in the sand, while a fennec fox with large ears peeks from its burrow. Sheep, goats, donkeys and water buffalo are kept in rural areas. Snakes, lizards, scorpions and the sturdy ibex survive the harsh desert, and fish and crocodiles live in the Nile.

pages.text: Riding in a felucca, or small sailing boat, on the Nile is a popular tourist activity in Egypt. Conclusion Egypt is an amazing country filled with history. Both animals and people live in its rugged deserts. Cutting a path through the desert, the Nile River provides life-giving water and fertile land for crops. Throughout history, the various civilizations that found a home in Egypt shaped its people and culture and produced knowledge that benefited the world. Egypt’s many historical sites hold secrets and treasures that should be important to everyone.
pages.brief: A felucca, a small sailing boat, glides on the Nile with tourists aboard. The river cuts through the desert, bringing life-giving water and fertile land for crops. Around it, Egypt’s rugged deserts hold animals and people, while the country’s long history and many civilizations have shaped its culture and produced knowledge that benefited the world.

pages.brief: A summary view of Egypt shows the capital city Cairo, where Arabic is the primary language. Egyptians of Islamic and Christian faiths live in a country of over 106 million people across 995,450 square kilometers. Egyptian pound currency is part of daily life.

books.title: The Last Great Race
books.art_why: The book is about a real annual race and real Alaskan places, dogs, and mushers, not a named famous person, so photos fit.

pages.text: Introduction It is hard to imagine anyone wanting to travel almost 2,000 kilometers (1,242 mi) across the Alaskan wilderness in the dead of winter. It is even harder to imagine someone doing it behind a sled pulled by a team of dogs. Yet every year since 1973, dozens of people have participated in what is known as “The Last Great Race on Earth.” The race, better known as the Iditarod, starts in Anchorage, Alaska, on the first Saturday in March. It is without a doubt one of the most grueling sporting events ever held.
pages.brief: A musher stands behind a sled pulled by a team of dogs in the Alaskan wilderness in deep winter. The team travels across snow, heading into remote country. The scene suggests the start of a long, grueling race from Anchorage, Alaska, on the first Saturday in March.

pages.text: The Inspiration The early Iditarod Trail was the trail of the Indigenous Athabaskan peoples. It has been in use for hundreds of years, but it was not mapped and marked by Americans until 1908. That was the year gold was discovered in what became the town of Nome. In the past, the Iditarod was mainly used as a mail and supply route during the winter. Supplies were carried using a Native Alaskan practice that involved teams of sled dogs. Mushers, or sled drivers, led the teams across the snowy terrain. Over time, the Iditarod Trail grew until it became a large route system, connecting trails from Nome to Anchorage.
pages.brief: Athabaskan people and later mushers use the early Iditarod Trail as a winter mail and supply route. Dog teams pull sleds loaded with supplies across snowy terrain. In the background, the town of Nome and the discovery of gold are suggested. The trail connects routes from Nome to Anchorage.

pages.text: However, as technology and modes of transportation improved, the Iditarod Trail was used less and less. That meant there was less need for Alaskan sled dogs. Several people living in Alaska began to consider ways to preserve the skill of dogsledding. They wanted to help save the Alaskan sled dogs. Do You Know? Some people mistakenly give the serum run of 1925 credit for being the inspiration behind the Iditarod. The serum run happened after a terrible disease called diphtheria struck the town of Nome, Alaska. The disease could only be treated with an injection of serum. A fierce storm prevented transport of the serum from Anchorage to rural Nome by other means. So, dogsledding teams rushed the serum to the town, saving many lives. Although the events were amazing, they were not the origin of the Iditarod.
pages.brief: A dogsled team races through a fierce storm to carry serum to Nome, Alaska, during the 1925 diphtheria outbreak. The team pushes across snowy ground while wind and snow swirl around the dogs and musher. The scene shows the urgent serum run that saved lives but was not the origin of the Iditarod.

pages.text: History The practice of dogsledding was created from a mix of Native and Russian skills. It was the main mode of transport in rural Alaska for centuries. But by 1967, dogs were being replaced by snowmobiles, cars, and trucks. Two Alaskans, Dorothy Page and Joe Redington Sr., wanted to do something that would help save this 6,000-year- old tradition. Dorothy, an Alaska history buff, and Joe, a dog breeder and musher, decided to hold a sled- dog race along the Iditarod Trail, a route that saw more and more use during the Alaskan gold rush. The trail got its name from Native Alaskans, who called the surrounding hunting area Haiditarod, or “The Distant Place.” The route of the first race was about 90 kilometers (56 mi) and took only two days to complete. Alaskan museum named after Dorothy Page.
pages.brief: Dorothy Page and Joe Redington Sr. stand together with a sled-dog team, planning a race along the Iditarod Trail. The trail crosses land once used during the Alaskan gold rush. Nearby, a museum named after Dorothy Page is shown. The first race followed a route of about 90 kilometers and took two days.

pages.text: In order to attract mushers, Joe and Dorothy raised $25,000 in prize money. This was enough money to get 58 mushers to enter. But the next year, the race was canceled because the mild winter led to a lack of snow and a lack of interest. Another race was held in 1969, but organizers could only raise enough money for a $1,000 prize, and only 12 mushers entered. Joe Redington Sr. But the lack of interest did not discourage Joe Redington Sr. He was determined to make the race longer and more challenging. In 1973, he extended the route to around 1,800 kilometers (1,100 mi). It now stretched from Anchorage to Nome and was the longest sled-dog race in the world. Joe managed to increase the prize money to about $50,000. In 1973, 35 mushers entered the first official Iditarod. It took the winner 20 days to complete the race, and the last-place finisher reached Nome 12 days later.
pages.brief: Joe Redington Sr. stands beside a long line of mushers and dog teams entered in the first official Iditarod. The route stretches from Anchorage to Nome across Alaska. The scene shows the race extended to about 1,800 kilometers with a large prize, as 35 mushers set out and the winner finishes after 20 days.

pages.text: The Route The trail taken by the mushers carrying serum in 1925 covers only about half of today’s northern Iditarod race trail. The current trail uses two routes, the northern and the southern, which split off for about 500 kilometers (300 mi) in the middle of the race. On even-numbered years, mushers take the northern route, and on odd- numbered years, they take the southern route. The official opening of the race is a bustling ceremony in Anchorage. The dogs make a ceremonial run from Anchorage to Eagle River. Then the dogs are trucked to the official start in Wasilla. This way, the dogs are not competing on the dangerous city streets of Anchorage, and they do not have to cross the treacherous Cook Inlet. The busy start in Anchorage.
pages.brief: A busy ceremonial start fills the streets of Anchorage, Alaska, with dog teams, mushers, and spectators. The dogs run from Anchorage to Eagle River, then are trucked to Wasilla for the official start. The scene shows the race opening while avoiding dangerous city streets and the treacherous Cook Inlet.

pages.text: The Iditarod Trail.
pages.brief: A wide view of the Iditarod Trail as a long route through the Alaskan wilderness. The path stretches away from the viewer, winding across open land. No racers, dogs, or buildings appear. The scene focuses only on the trail itself, quiet and open.

pages.text: Legendary musher Susan Butcher, who set a record four wins in five years, and her sled dogs. Not every team starts at the same time. Instead, teams take off at two-minute intervals to prevent teams from running into each other. The differences in time are erased at the required 24-hour stop, where officials hold the teams back for a few extra minutes. Since the race takes over a week to complete, there are 26 checkpoints along the route where mushers and dogs can rest. Before the race begins, mushers send dog food and other supplies to the checkpoints so they will not have to carry them on the trail. The average distance between checkpoints is 74 kilometers (46 mi)—longer than the entire 1967 race—and the greatest distance between checkpoints is 150 kilometers (93 mi).
pages.brief: Legendary musher Susan Butcher runs behind her sled dogs on the Iditarod Trail. The team moves across the snow, with Susan guiding the huskies. In the scene, teams start at two-minute intervals and rest at checkpoints, where mushers have sent dog food and supplies ahead of time.

pages.text: Off they go! The dogs can keep a steady speed of about 19 kilometers per hour (12 mph) for about 4 to 6 hours before they get tired. This is usually long enough to get from one checkpoint to the next. But the dogs also rest on the trail, so the mushers don’t always stop at every checkpoint. In order to keep the teams on course through the trackless wilderness, the trail is marked with orange stakes and reflective tape. Additional markers are set up in the mountains and along the coast. Each year, volunteers set out about 12,000 stakes. Getting lost could cost a musher their life, so it is important that the trail be well marked.
pages.brief: A dog team runs at a steady pace along the snow-covered Iditarod Trail. Volunteers set out orange stakes and reflective tape to mark the route through the wilderness. The dogs pull the sled while the musher guides them, and extra markers stand in the mountains and along the coast.

pages.text: The Iditarod Trail is filled with some of the most beautiful scenery in the world. It crosses the Alaska Mountain Range at a gap known as Rainy Pass, though during the Iditarod, it is more likely to be a snowy pass. The trail also follows the Yukon River Valley and travels along the coast of the Bering Sea before reaching Nome. Along the way, it passes through thick forests and over frozen tundra. The teams must cross frozen streams and rivers, which can be deadly if the ice is too thin. Wild animals such as moose have been known to attack and kill dogs. And racers can encounter fierce storms with arctic winds and driving snow.
pages.brief: A dog team travels through stunning Alaskan scenery, crossing the Alaska Mountain Range at Rainy Pass. The trail passes thick forests, frozen tundra, the Yukon River Valley, and the Bering Sea coast. A moose stands near the route, and dark storm clouds with arctic wind and driving snow gather over frozen streams.

pages.text: The trail ends in the small city of Nome. During the winter, the sun rises for only a few hours a day, and the race is a welcome celebration for the residents. Citizens of Nome line the streets to watch the finishers come in. While 55 to 75 mushers usually start, every year several drop out because of sickness, injury, or simple exhaustion. Today, winners of the Iditarod usually complete the race in 10 to 12 days. A record time of 8 days, 18 hours, and 46 minutes was set in 2011 by Inupiat Jewish racer John Baker. There can be a full week between the times when the first and last mushers cross the finish line. Do You Know? During the early days of dogsledding, a red lantern was hung outside a check- point to help the musher find shelter. The lantern remained lit until the musher arrived. Today, a red lantern is hung over the finish line of the Iditarod. The lantern is lit at the start of the race, and the last musher to cross the line puts it out.
pages.brief: Crowds line the snowy streets of Nome, Alaska, to watch Iditarod finishers arrive. The winter sun sits low after only a few hours of daylight. A red lantern hangs over the finish line. Inupiat Jewish racer John Baker is shown finishing in a record time of 8 days, 18 hours, and 46 minutes.

pages.text: The Mushers Mushers come from all walks of life. They include professional athletes, tradespeople, authors, doctors, teachers, and lawyers. Since 1974, people of all genders have competed in the Iditarod. Two women have won the race. One of them, Susan Butcher, has won four times. While many are Alaskans, mushers come from all around the world. They come from many of the 50 states and from countries such as Canada, Russia, Norway, Japan, New Zealand, Great Britain, and Italy. To enter the Iditarod, a musher must be at least 18 years old. They must have competed in a previous Iditarod or two qualifying races of at least 805 kilometers (500 mi) in the previous two years. Sled-dog racing is a solo sport, and all mushers compete in the Iditarod alone. They have no crews waiting at the checkpoints to help them feed and care for their dogs. Most mushers will feed their dogs and make straw beds for them even before they feed themselves. Do You Know? Since 1986, the Iditabike Race has been held alongside the Iditarod Trail. In this 322-kilometer (200-mi) race, a hearty group of mountain bikers rides over the snow and ice, braving sub-zero temperatures and strong winds.
pages.brief: Mushers from many walks of life gather with their dog teams, including teachers, doctors, lawyers, and athletes. Susan Butcher stands among them as a four-time winner. A musher kneels to feed dogs and make straw beds before caring for themselves. Nearby, mountain bikers ride over snow and ice in the Iditabike Race.

pages.text: Unfortunately, the costs of competing in the race have risen over the years. Feeding and caring for the dogs, and sled equipment, are all expensive. This has led to difficulties for Indigenous Alaskan mushers who live in smaller rural communities to enter. In 2018, less than 10 out of the 67 mushers in the competition were Indigenous Alaskan. Still, mushers like Ketil Reitan and Peter Kaiser are trying to keep the activity alive. So what would cause someone to brave temperatures as low as −51° Celsius (−60° F), strong winds, blowing snow, wild animals, and treacherous ice, all on very little sleep? The winner’s prize of $50,000 or more may be an incentive, but most do it for the challenge, for the love of the sport, and the love of their dogs. Most participants are thrilled simply to finish the race.
pages.brief: An Indigenous Alaskan musher in a rural community tends a sled-dog team, facing the high costs of food, care, and equipment. Mushers Ketil Reitan and Peter Kaiser are shown keeping the activity alive. In freezing temperatures, strong winds, blowing snow, and treacherous ice, a musher presses on with little sleep for the love of the sport and the dogs.

pages.text: The Dogs The Iditarod is really about the dogs. The dogs who run the race, called huskies, have been specially bred to pull sleds the way collies have been bred to herd sheep. The sturdy, tough huskies can pull a sled carrying supplies and the musher, a total weight of 136 to 182 kilograms (300–400 lbs). This may seem like a lot, but huskies love to pull. Huskies have also been bred to withstand extreme cold. They have two layers of fur. The outer layer, made of thick hairs, protects the dog from wind and water. The inner layer is a lot like a sheep’s wool. It serves to insulate the body from cold temperatures and keep body heat from escaping. Some people even use husky hair to make warm hats and gloves.
pages.brief: A sturdy husky stands in the cold, showing its thick double coat of fur. The outer layer protects against wind and water, while the inner layer insulates body heat. The dog is built to pull a sled carrying supplies and a musher. Some people use husky hair to make warm hats and gloves.

pages.text: The dogs do not lose heat by sweating through their skin as humans do. Instead, they pant, and they sweat through their feet. These adaptations allow huskies to run comfortably at temperatures below −51° Celsius (−60° F). Do You Know? Often, sled dogs on the Iditarod wear “booties” on their feet. The booties keep the dogs’ paws dry and prevent cuts from the sharp ice and rocks on the trail. A dog team can go through as many as 1,000 booties during an Iditarod. This can get pretty expensive, since the booties cost about fifty cents each.
pages.brief: A husky runs with booties on its feet, keeping its paws dry and protected from sharp ice and rocks. The dog pants to release heat and sweats through its feet. The scene shows how huskies stay comfortable running in temperatures below -51° Celsius, while a team can wear through many booties.

pages.text: Huskies have also been bred to work as a team. This is important, since the whole team must work together to pull the sled. An Iditarod team can have as many as 16 dogs. Usually, an experienced lead dog runs at the front of the team and helps set the pace. Huskies are extremely friendly dogs, and, like most dogs, they love to please their owners.
pages.brief: A team of up to 16 huskies pulls a sled together, with an experienced lead dog running at the front. The lead dog helps set the pace while the other dogs work as a team. The huskies appear friendly and eager to please their owner, showing how they are bred to pull together.

pages.text: Care of the huskies before, during, and after the race is of utmost importance to the mushers and to the officials who run the Iditarod. Veterinarians wait at each checkpoint to examine the dogs as they come in. Dogs suffering from frostbite, exhaustion, or injury are pulled from the race. In fact, most mushers drop off one or more dogs that become tired or don’t want to run anymore. There are three mandatory stops during the race to let the dogs rest. The first one, taken at the musher’s choice of checkpoint, is 24 hours long. The other two are 8 hours long and are made at specific checkpoints. Mushers who mistreat their dogs are disqualified.
pages.brief: A veterinarian at a checkpoint examines a husky as the dog team rests in the snow. The vet checks for frostbite, exhaustion, or injury; dogs that are unwell are pulled from the race. A musher makes a long mandatory stop to let the dogs rest, showing that care for the huskies is of utmost importance.

pages.text: The dogs eat a lot during the race to keep their energy high. One dog can consume up to 10,000 calories per day. The dogs’ diets are rich in fat and protein from meat, pure fat, and dry dog food. They also need a lot of water, which the mushers warm up so that the dogs will not lose heat. The dogs typically eat three meals a day during rests, and they also get lots of snacks on the trail. Food Consumed per Meal Food Type Quantity Dry dog food.4 kilograms (12 oz) Fat.25 kilograms (8 oz) Like any athletic team, the dogs go through rigid training before the race. Sled dogs are trained to pull from the time they are puppies. Between September and February before the Iditarod, teams make practice runs of up to 2,253 kilometers (1,400 mi). They also compete in smaller races of 322 kilometers (200 mi) or more. In the end, the best-trained team is usually the winner.
pages.brief: A musher prepares food for a hungry husky team during a rest on the trail. The dogs eat meals rich in fat and protein, with warm water and snacks, and one dog can consume up to 10,000 calories a day. In training, the team makes long practice runs and competes in smaller races before the Iditarod.

pages.text: The Iditarod keeps alive the practice of dogsledding. Conclusion The Iditarod, also known as the “Last Great Race,” is a grueling competition between sled-dog teams. They race across the Alaskan wilderness for 10 to 12 days for a more than $50,000 prize. Mushers come from around the world to compete. Journalists, TV networks, and newspaper reporters from across the globe come to cover the race. But it is not the money or the fame that attracts the mushers. The mushers do not really race their teams against one another; they race against the hardships of the wilderness and against themselves. Any musher will tell you that the true heroes of the Iditarod are the huskies who run almost 2,000 kilometers (1,243 mi) over some of the harshest, most beautiful land on Earth.
pages.brief: A dog team races across the Alaskan wilderness under a vast sky, with journalists and TV cameras covering the event. The huskies pull the sled for 10 to 12 days over harsh, beautiful land. The scene emphasizes that the true heroes are the dogs, who run almost 2,000 kilometers and keep the practice of dogsledding alive.

pages.text: Explore More On the Internet A. In the address window, type www.google.com. B. Type Iditarod into the search window and click on “Google Search.” C. Read the colored links. Click on one that looks interesting. D. When you want to explore more links, click on the back arrow at the top left. E. You can also look up other Iditarod-related subjects, such as Susan Butcher, huskies, or dog training. At the Library Ask your librarian to help you find books on the Iditarod. You can also look up books on dogsledding, huskies, and life in Alaska. Many adventure stories and other fiction books have been written about this rugged state. And some of the most amazing adventures are true.
pages.brief: A young reader sits at a computer, exploring more about the Iditarod online. Nearby, a librarian helps find books on dogsledding, huskies, and life in Alaska. Shelves hold adventure stories and true tales about the rugged state. The scene shows two ways to explore more: using the internet and asking a librarian for books.

books.title: Comic Cons
books.art_why: Contemporary real-world conventions and named attendees can be photographed.

pages.text: Robin, the Joker, and Batman spend quality time together at the 2014 New York Comic Con. Welcome to Comic Con Packed with thousands of other fans in an auditorium, you wait for the stars to arrive. It’s warm inside your Chewbacca costume, and you’re impatient. Suddenly the audience is on its feet, cheering. You jump up to see the Iron Man himself, Robert Downey Jr., walk out onstage. The Avengers panel has begun. This is the world of comic cons: colorful, crowded, and built for fans of pop culture. If you collect comic books, watch movies, or play video games, there’s something for you at a comic con. These fan conventions, called cons for short, happen all over the country.
pages.brief: At the 2014 New York Comic Con, Robin, the Joker and Batman stand together among thousands of fans. In a warm auditorium, a fan in a Chewbacca costume waits as the audience rises and cheers for Robert Downey Jr. walking onstage as Iron Man for The Avengers panel.

pages.text: Origin Story Shel Dorf, a comic book artist, was one of the first people to start comic book conventions. Dorf organized small gatherings of comic fans in Detroit in the 1960s. He went on to found the convention now known as Comic-Con International (CCI): San Diego in 1970. The first San Diego convention attracted about 100 fans; it now hosts over 130,000 people every year. Hundreds of other comic cons have sprung up across the country— and the world. Today there are comic cons on every continent except Antarctica. Tickets for these events sell out months in advance. Some fans camp at ticket booths for days to be sure they get in. Legendary writer, editor, and publisher Stan Lee often appeared at comic cons. Lee helped create many of Marvel Comics’ most popular superheroes, including the Fantastic Four, the Incredible Hulk, Thor, Spider-Man, and the X-Men. He died in 2018.
pages.brief: Shel Dorf, a comic-book artist, stands with about 100 fans at the first San Diego comic convention in 1970. In another scene, Stan Lee appears at a comic con, while fans camp at ticket booths for events that now draw over 130,000 people.

pages.text: College students browse comic books at a 2015 book fair. The Rise of an Art Form What has caused this explosive growth? First, comic books have become more popular in recent years. Comic books had many readers during the “Golden Age” of the 1930s and 1940s. They became much less popular for several decades afterward. During that time, many people thought of comics as kid stuff. But in the late 1980s and early 1990s, comic book series such as The Sandman and Watchmen broke new ground and were praised by critics as serious works of art. Since then, interest in comic books has soared, and writers and artists continue to explore new topics and styles.
pages.brief: College students browse comic books at a 2015 book fair. The comics include 1930s and 1940s Golden Age stories and serious late-1980s and early-1990s works like The Sandman and Watchmen, praised by critics after comics were once thought of as kid stuff.

pages.text: A modern comic might tell a traditional superhero story, a story about war, or a story about family drama. Comic books known as graphic novels are popular with young adults. Graphic memoirs, another kind of comic book, often deal with serious themes. For example, Art Spiegelman won a Pulitzer Prize—a highly respected achievement—for his graphic memoir Maus. His work was based on interviews with his father, a Holocaust survivor. As topics for comic books have expanded, so have audiences. Fans of every color, age, and gender can find something to relate to in comic books. As a result, comic cons are booming.
