Second, the enormous success of recent Hollywood movies based on comic books has brought many people to comic cons. Movies such as The Dark Knight (2008), Wonder Woman (2017), and Black Panther (2018) attracted many new fans. Movies are now a big part of comic cons. Famous actors, writers, and directors from comic-book movies often appear on panels and draw huge crowds. Spider-Man first came to the big screen with a blockbuster film in 2002.
pages.brief: Modern comic books show stories about superheroes, war and family drama, with graphic novels and Art Spiegelman’s Pulitzer-winning graphic memoir Maus. Nearby, fans of different colors, ages and genders gather as famous actors, writers and directors from comic-book movies such as The Dark Knight, Wonder Woman and Black Panther appear on panels.

pages.text: Artists draw manga-style illustrations during the 2017 Libya Comic Convention in Tripoli. Movies are only the beginning, though. Comic cons around the world also celebrate video games, novels, and television shows. The audience has become so large that some cons focus on just one art form. For example, many fans attend cons for anime and manga (animated films and comic books from Japan). There are cons for fans and collectors of classic comics. There are cons for fans of sci-fi and fantasy fiction. There are even cons for fans of steampunk, horror, and humor, among many others.
pages.brief: At the 2017 Libya Comic Convention in Tripoli, artists draw manga-style illustrations. Around them, the convention celebrates more than movies: video games, novels and television shows, plus separate cons for anime and manga, classic comics, sci-fi and fantasy, steampunk, horror and humor.

pages.text: Big Cons and Small Comic cons happen in cities all over the world. Outside the huge conventions in San Diego and New York, the crowds are smaller but just as enthusiastic. Check online or in your local newspaper to find out if there’s a comic con coming to a town near you. You might be surprised at what you’ll find: local fans mix with big-name cartoonists and movie stars at many smaller cons. If you go, you just might see the star of your favorite show or your favorite writer. You are also likely to meet local artists and make new friends. A brother and sister attend the 2019 Edinburgh Comic Con on their respective dragons, Night Fury and Light Fury.
pages.brief: A brother and sister attend the 2019 Edinburgh Comic Con, each riding a dragon—Night Fury and Light Fury. Around them, local fans mix with big-name cartoonists and movie stars at a smaller convention, in a city setting where fans check online or in a local newspaper for events.

pages.text: Captain America and Loki battle it out at the 2016 MCM Comic Con in London. Cosplay Many fans display their own creativity at comic cons. Some do this through cosplay. In cosplay, fans dress up in costumes as characters from comic books, anime, manga, and other fantasy genres. Cosplay is serious business for fans worldwide. Costumes can be bought, custom- built, or handmade. Many cosplayers make realistic props that go with their characters. Some cosplayers act like their favorite characters while they are in costume. Costumes can be simple or incredibly detailed. Figuring out how to make or build a costume is a big part of the fun for many fans. Cosplay is a major part of comic cons, with hundreds of costumed fans in the audience. Many conventions also hold cosplay contests, where cosplayers can pose for photos and act in skits based on their characters.
pages.brief: Captain America and Loki battle at the 2016 MCM Comic Con in London. Nearby, cosplayers in costumes from comic books, anime, manga and fantasy genres pose for photos, carry realistic props and act like their favorite characters, with costumes bought, custom-built or handmade for contests and skits.

pages.text: Celebrity Appearances At comic cons, fans can also meet creators personally. Stars often take part in panels where they speak about the experience of making comic books, films, and shows. Audience members can sometimes ask questions during panels, have their photos taken with celebrities, and get autographs. These personal meetings become treasured memories for many fans. Isaac Hempstead-Wright and Elle Fanning appear at CCI: San Diego to promote their animated film The Boxtrolls.
pages.brief: Isaac Hempstead-Wright and Elle Fanning appear at CCI: San Diego to promote their animated film The Boxtrolls. On a panel, stars speak about making comics, films and shows; audience members ask questions, take photos with celebrities and get autographs that become treasured memories.

pages.text: Attendees flow through the giant exhibit hall at the New York Comic Con in New York City. The Exhibit Hall The center of most comic cons is the exhibit hall. Fans can buy and trade comic books here, along with action figures, toys, and other merchandise. Experienced collectors can find rare editions of comic books. New collectors can get a head start on their collections. There is often an author signing area in the exhibit hall where fans can meet artists and writers. Even if you’re not looking to buy anything, there is always a lot to see in the exhibit hall. Cosplayers wander by in colorful costumes; movies and movie trailers are shown regularly. Celebrity sightings are always possible, and there is an endless supply of colorful merchandise to browse through.
pages.brief: Attendees flow through the giant exhibit hall at the New York Comic Con in New York City. Fans buy and trade comic books, action figures, toys and merchandise, browse rare editions, meet artists and writers at a signing area, and watch as cosplayers wander by in colorful costumes.

pages.text: Growing Pains and Issues The popularity of comic cons has not come without some controversy, though. Some comic book fans feel that the bigger cons have become too large. They think that the focus has moved away from comic books. Many comic cons could, in fact, be described as pop culture conventions rather than comic book conventions. The audience for comic books and comic cons has changed as well. While comic con attendees used to be mostly male, about forty percent of recent CCI: San Diego attendees are female. More than half of the people attending recent cons are under twenty-nine. The increased diversity of the comic con audience brings larger crowds and is a welcome develop- ment for most fans. Comic cons can also be a place to discuss larger controversies. With the recent comeback of the comic book form, authors have taken on serious topics like race, gender, politics, and war. These comics are not to everyone’s liking. Some comics can even become the subjects of “banned book” campaigns, where a library is asked to take a book off the shelves. Spider-Man and Batman comics, for example, have been challenged in some places because of adult themes. Readers, teachers, and librarians often discuss censorship on panels at comic cons.
pages.brief: At a comic con panel, readers, teachers and librarians discuss censorship. Around them, attendees reflect a changing audience: about forty percent of recent CCI: San Diego attendees are female, and more than half are under twenty-nine. Some fans feel bigger cons are too large and focus less on comic books than on pop culture.

pages.text: Stars from the film Black Panther attend a comic con panel in 2017. One result of these talks has been the rise of the labels “graphic novel” and “graphic memoir” to describe comics that are meant for adults. Some comics are still aimed at children, but comics as a whole are no longer “kids only.” Some comics are fictional and some aren’t; some are educational and some are meant for entertainment. Some deal with adult themes, while others provide an escape into fantasy worlds. Since comics are diverse, should all comics be shelved together in libraries and schools? What role do comics have in our society? These questions are frequent topics at comic con panels.
pages.brief: Stars from the film Black Panther attend a comic con panel in 2017. On the panel, speakers discuss how comics are no longer kids only: some are fictional, some educational, some for entertainment, and some deal with adult themes, raising questions about how libraries and schools should shelve them.

pages.text: Pushing the Boundaries Keeping up with the variety of comic books can be challenging, but overall, it’s an exciting time for comic cons. The huge range of the comics available today has resulted in bigger and wider audiences for comics and conventions. Fans of every age, color, and gender can find themselves represented in a comic somewhere. Heroes might look like Superman, a young girl from Botswana, or a reporter on the ground in Bosnia. There is no limit to what can happen in a comic book or who can be its heroes. In the end, this is what draws people to comic cons. The cons (and the stories that inspire them) create worlds where ordinary people can be transformed into heroes. Many people return to that experience over and over. A young girl shows off her pink Star Wars stormtrooper costume at CCI: San Diego.
pages.brief: A young girl shows off her pink Star Wars stormtrooper costume at CCI: San Diego. Around her, fans of every age, color and gender gather, drawn to conventions where stories can transform ordinary people into heroes as varied as Superman, a young girl from Botswana or a reporter in Bosnia.

books.title: Catching Air
books.art_why: Real people doing real wind sports today — hang gliding, skydiving, parasailing — which a camera can photograph; only the old Icarus tale and Lilienthal are historical, so the book stays photo.

pages.text: Catch≤ng A≤r.
pages.brief: A wide open sky, bright and clear, stretching high above the ground and out over a coastline — plenty of open space where a person could soar and swoop, catching air on the wind.

pages.text: Air and Flight Look, up in the sky! Is it a huge bird? Is it Superman? No, it’s a regular person flying high, or “catching air,” while hang gliding, skydiving, or parasailing. Maybe you’d like to try one of these wind-powered sports and soar and swoop through the wide-open skies. All you need is a sense of adventure, the right equipment, and an understanding of how wind works.
pages.brief: A person soaring high in the sky, arms out, catching air while hang gliding, skydiving or parasailing. The wide-open sky stretches away as the flyer swoops through it — a regular person, not a bird, not Superman.

pages.text: First, let’s look at air. You can’t exactly see air, which is a collection of gases, and you can’t really feel it unless it is moving. But air has weight and temperature, and takes up space (volume). Air moves around. When air heats up, it becomes lighter and rises. Air becomes wind when cooler, heavier air rushes in to replace the warmer, lighter air that is rising. A light wind can move leaves; a heavy wind can move the whole tree! Hot-air balloons rise because the heated air inside the balloon is a higher temperature than the cooler air outside.
pages.brief: Leaves on a tree pushed by a light breeze while a heavier wind bends the whole tree. Nearby, a hot-air balloon rises, its heated air lighter than the cooler air outside, lifting the balloon and taking up space in the sky.

pages.text: Wind-sport enthusiasts pay attention to their natural surroundings. They know areas of land heat up faster than areas of water. They need moving air, so they like tall slopes and cliffs. As warm air rises from land, a cooler wind from the sea rushes in to replace it. When this wind strikes the face of a cliff, it is deflected upward. This strong updraft of air creates lift —and a great ride! Often, wind-sporters look to birds for flying advice. Hawks or seagulls circling lazily overhead are riding a rising column of air called a thermal. Smart wind-sporters will also try to catch thermals for rides. wind wind Wind-sporters catch updrafts to give them a boost into the sky.
pages.brief: A cliff above the sea, wind rushing in from the water and deflecting upward along the rock face. A hawk and a seagull circle lazily in a rising column of warm air, while a wind-sporter on the slope watches them for flying advice.

pages.text: Hang Gliding The hot summer sun sits high in the mid- afternoon sky. A gentle breeze blows in from the sea. A woman with a triangular-shaped, winged contraption on her shoulders runs down a slope and leaps from the cliffs rising about 915 meters (3,000 ft) above the shore. Yikes! What is she doing? The wing fills with air and billows out, and up she goes! The pilot has stretched out flat and is hanging from a cocoon-like harness attached to the wing. To climb up or dive down, she pushes or pulls back on a long metal control bar. To turn left or right, she leans. The edge of the wing tips down, and the glider banks and turns gracefully through the air.
pages.brief: A woman with a triangular winged glider on her shoulders runs down a slope and leaps from cliffs about 915 metres above the shore. The wing fills with air and billows out, and she hangs flat in her cocoon harness, leaning to bank and turn.

pages.text: She is hang gliding! And she may sail in the sky for hours if conditions are good—and if she understands a few principles of aerodynamics (air-oh-die-NAM-iks), or, the study of how objects move through the air. The special shape of the wing produces lift as the glider moves through the air. The curved top surface of a wing is a longer distance than the straight underside of a wing. Air moving over the longer, curved top has to move faster than the air moving under the wing. As the air moving over the top of the wing speeds up, the air molecules spread out—which decreases the air pressure. The greater air pressure underneath the wing creates lift and causes the wing to rise.
pages.brief: The hang glider sails through the sky for hours. Air moves over the longer curved top of the wing faster than beneath it, spreading out and lowering the pressure above, while the greater pressure underneath creates lift and makes the wing rise.

pages.text: How to Hang Glide To take off, the pilot runs down a steep slope to gain speed, create airflow over the wing, and create lift for the glider. He’s off! Hanging from the harness, or a special chair seat, the pilot steers along the winds. He catches and rides one updraft, then another. But this isn’t a place to relax and daydream. The pilot has to pay attention as he turns, circles, climbs, and dives. When the pilot pulls the control bar back, the glider gains speed but loses altitude, or height. (For every 1.22 meters, or about 4 feet, that the glider moves forward, it also drops about 30 centimeters, or 1 foot.) When he pushes the control bar forward, the wing edge tips up and the glider rises, but it loses speed. The natural downward force of Earth’s gravity will pull the hang glider down if it stalls, or stops moving forward. To stay up in the air and keep riding along the wind, the pilot keeps the glider moving forward. The glider’s harness keeps the pilot’s body straight to cut wind resistance.
pages.brief: A pilot runs down a steep slope to gain speed and lift off, hanging from his harness. He steers along the winds, catching one updraft then another, turning, circling, climbing and diving, pulling the control bar back to speed up and drop.

pages.text: What It Takes Equipment: Harness, helmet, goggles, parachute, glider, and flotation gear if near water. Clothing: Wear a heavy jacket, jeans, and gloves. It can get very cold at higher altitudes. (Air temperature falls by about 2.2 degrees Celsius, or 4 degrees Fahrenheit, about every 300 meters, or 1,000 feet, up.) Size: Harnesses are designed to fit a person who is 1.5 to 2 meters (5 to 6½ ft) tall and weighs 40 to 113 kilograms (90 to 250 lbs). Skills: The ability to carry an 18-plus kilogram (40 lb) weight on your shoulders while jogging. But balance and endurance are more important than strength or speed. Good reflexes and an ability to make fast decisions are a must. Requirements: Age 16 or older and able to pass a three- to six-month training course. Cost: $5,000 to $6,500 to train and to purchase your hang-gliding equipment. glider helmet goggles harness.
pages.brief: A hang glider pilot dressed for cold air in a heavy jacket, jeans and gloves, wearing a helmet and goggles. Beside him are his parachute, flotation gear and glider, its harness built to hold a pilot straight and cut wind resistance.

pages.text: The Story of Icarus People have been fascinated by the dream of flight for thousands of years. A Greek myth tells of the inventor Daedalus (DEH-duh-lus) and his son, Icarus, who were imprisoned on an island. Their only way out: to fly. Daedalus watched birds. Then he fashioned wings for himself and his son from feathers held together by wax. They escaped! But Icarus ignored his father’s cautious warning and flew too high in the sky. The heat of the sun melted the wax, and Icarus fell to the sea and drowned. Icarus is a good story but not good science. People could never flap their winged arms fast enough to generate sufficient power to overcome the pull of gravity.
pages.brief: Daedalus and his son Icarus, imprisoned on an island, strap on wings made of feathers held together with wax. They escape into the sky, but Icarus ignores his father's warning, flies too high, and the sun melts the wax, dropping him into the sea.

pages.text: Do You Know? In the 1800s, German inventor Otto Lilienthal discovered that a properly engineered wing would help a person stay aloft for hours at a time. The Lilienthal glider from around 1895 is designed like a bird’s wing, with a curved upper surface. The Wright Brothers used information from Lilienthal’s experiments to invent the first airplane. • The longest hang glider ride lasted 36 hours. • Hang gliders typically travel 160 to 320 kilometers (100 to 200 miles). The farthest flight on record is just more than 700 kilometers (435 miles), which was set July 17, 2001, in Zapata, Texas, by Austrian Manfred Ruhmer. • Flight heights can range from as low as 1.5 meters (5 ft) above the ground to more than 4.8 kilometers (3 miles) high!
pages.brief: German inventor Otto Lilienthal in the 1800s, hanging beneath a glider built like a bird's wing with a curved upper surface, staying aloft for hours. His experiments gave the Wright Brothers the information they used to invent the first airplane.

pages.text: Skydiving A small plane buzzes overhead. At an altitude of 3,048 meters (10,000 ft), the passenger door opens. A person crouching in the doorframe leaps out, arms and legs spread wide. Within 10 seconds, the skydiver is free-falling at 193 kph (120 mph). That’s twice as fast as a car zooming by on a highway. Finally, at about 762 meters (2,500 ft) above the ground, he pulls the ripcord. Out comes the small drogue chute that pulls out the canopy, or larger chute. It fills with air, and the skydiver is jerked upward. He continues to fall, but now at a leisurely 16 to 20 kph (10–20 mph). For the next 3 minutes, he enjoys the view and the ride before landing on his feet in a clearing.
pages.brief: A small plane high overhead opens its passenger door and a skydiver crouches in the frame, then leaps with arms and legs spread wide. He free-falls, pulls the ripcord, the canopy fills with air, and he glides down to land on his feet in a clearing.

pages.text: How a Parachute Works Gravity pulls the free-falling skydiver down toward Earth at speeds of 193 kph (120 mph) or more. When the parachute opens, it fills with air and slows the skydiver’s speed. Air trapped in the canopy (the “umbrella” part) presses up against the chute, providing resistance that slows the fall. The skydiver glides to Earth. Buttons Away! What you need: Four-holed button. Four 15-inch-long strands of thread. Scissors. Plastic bag. Tape. What you do: 1. Cut a 20-centimeter (8-in) square from the plastic bag. 2. Tape one end of each strand of thread to a corner of the plastic. 3. Thread each strand through a different hole in the large button. 4. Tie the threads together. 5. Gently hold or pinch the top side of the plastic in its center, and let the button dangle. 6. Drop your homemade parachute from a high spot, such as off the side of a deck. 7. Watch the button glide to the ground.
pages.brief: A skydiver hangs beneath a full parachute canopy, air trapped inside pressing up against the fabric and slowing his fall to Earth. Beside him, a homemade parachute of plastic, thread and a four-holed button dangles and glides down.

pages.text: A diamond formation Skilled skydivers can free-fall in formations. To decrease their free fall speed, they hold their arms and legs outstretched in the “spread-eagle” position and join hands. Multiple bodies provide more wind resistance, so the divers can float for a longer time. To increase free fall speed, skydivers learn to fall in a standing, or vertical, position. Now that you know how to skydive, what’s next? Experienced skydivers, or sport parachutists, compete in such events as landing accuracy, free fall speed, and freestyle. They put on shows and do stunts in the air, such as passing a baton to each other or creating group formations in the sky.
pages.brief: Skilled skydivers join hands in a diamond formation, arms and legs outstretched in the spread-eagle position so more bodies catch the wind. Others fall in a standing vertical position to go faster, practising stunts and passing a baton in the sky.

pages.text: What It Takes Equipment: Jumpsuit, helmet, goggles, main parachute, reserve parachute, harness with attached backpack that holds both. An automatic activation device opens the reserve chute if something goes wrong. Skills: Have enough strength to carry about 16 kilograms (35 lbs) of equipment and control the toggle switches that steer the chute. Be able to deal with the shock of the chute opening, as well as extreme changes in temperature. Size: Harnesses are designed to fit a person who is 1.5 to 2 meters (5 to 6½ ft) tall and weighs 40 to 113 kilograms (90 to 250 lbs). Requirements: Age 16 or older and in good shape. Pass eight training levels, including many jumps with instructors. A student must make 20 solo jumps and pass a written test. Cost: $3,000 to $6,000 for training and equipment. helmet goggles harness jumpsuit parachute.
pages.brief: A skydiver's gear laid out: jumpsuit, helmet, goggles, main parachute, reserve parachute and a harness with a backpack holding both, plus an automatic activation device. The skydiver stands ready, carrying about 16 kilograms and holding the toggle switches.

pages.text: BASE Jumping If skydiving from a plane doesn’t get your pulse racing, how about parachuting from a tall Building, Antenna tower, bridge Span, or cliff high above Earth? Welcome to the sport of BASE jumping. Most BASE jumps are made from around 305 meters (1,000 ft) high, which is considerably less than the height at which skydivers open their parachutes. BASE jumpers have just 20–30 seconds in the air to open their chutes and land in a small safety zone. Crazy? Maybe. But only expert skydivers with a minimum of 200 jumps can attempt such daredevil feats, and many places that could be used for BASE jumping have made it illegal because of the danger.
pages.brief: A BASE jumper leaping from a tall structure — a building, an antenna tower, a bridge span or a cliff about 305 metres high. With only 20 to 30 seconds in the air, the jumper opens the chute and aims for a small safety zone below.

pages.text: • Expert skydivers can land on a tiny target that is about the size of a tennis ball. • The highest and fastest skydive on record occurred in 2012, when BASE jumper Felix Baumgartner jumped from a capsule attached to a high- altitude balloon floating at about 39 kilometers, or 128,000 feet. That’s over 24 miles high! During his free fall descent of 4 minutes and 22 seconds, Felix reached speeds of over 1,340 kph, or 833 mph. He was the first person to break the sound barrier without using an airplane or other vehicle!
pages.brief: Felix Baumgartner in 2012 stepping from a capsule hanging beneath a high-altitude balloon about 39 kilometres above Earth, then free-falling for 4 minutes 22 seconds at over 1,340 kph. Far below, an expert skydiver lands on a tiny target.

pages.text: Parasailing A 10-year-old girl standing on shore straps a harness over her life jacket. She adjusts her helmet and gives the driver of the speedboat the “thumbs-up” signal. The motor roars, the boat scoots forward, and the towrope connecting the girl to the boat tightens. She takes a few steps and begins to glide on the water. Is she water-skiing without skis? No, she is parasailing! As the boat zooms into the bay, the colorful parachute dragging behind her fills with air. The girl rises like a human kite, 61 meters (200 ft) into the sky. The boat moving forward provides thrust, the power to take off. The air rushing into the parachute provides lift. As long as the towrope stays tight, the flyer sits back and enjoys the ride —and the admiration of all those watching from the ground.
pages.brief: A 10-year-old girl on the shore straps a harness over her life jacket, adjusts her helmet and gives the speedboat driver a thumbs-up. The boat roars off, the towrope tightens, and the colourful parachute fills with air, lifting her 61 metres like a human kite.

pages.text: When towing a parasailor, the speedboat cruises between 24 and 48 kph (15–30 mph). It needs to go fast enough to create lift but not so fast that a wave will make it lose control. When turning, or if a strong gust of wind blows from behind, the boat needs to speed up. Slack in the towrope will cause the parasail to fall. Parasailing is not recommended when the wind is blowing stronger than 24 kph (15 mph). The height a flyer reaches depends on the speed of the boat and length of the towrope. On average, recreational parasailors reach the height of a 20-story building; maximum height is 183 meters (600 ft) over oceans and 91 meters (300 ft) over large lakes and bays. Some special- attraction parasail rides can go as high as 305 meters (1,000 ft).
pages.brief: A speedboat towing a parasailor across the water at 15 to 30 mph, going fast enough to make lift but not so fast it loses control. The flyer rises high above the bay, towrope stretched tight, up to the height of a 20-storey building.

pages.text: Unlike hang gliding and skydiving, para- sailing has no minimum age requirement. There is no special training for the parasailor, though the boat driver needs to have experience. There are many ways to parasail. Strap on a harness or sit in a specially designed chair. Ride alone or with a friend. Parasailing is usually done on oceans, lakes, and bays. Flyers take off from the shore from a barge in the water or from a boat equipped with a winch. Rides from parasailing companies typically last around 10 minutes and can cost $50 or more. A basic parasail, plus accessories, can cost $1,000 and up. Parasailing History.
pages.brief: A parasailor in a harness riding alone above a bay, while another flies with a friend in a specially designed chair. They lift off from a barge and from a boat fitted with a winch, the parachute high over the water on a short ride.

pages.text: Paragliding Paragliding combines elements of three wind sports: parasailing, hang gliding, and parachuting. Paragliders wear a wing-shaped parachute, and some attach a frame harness with a motor that looks like a big fan. They may take off from a tall cliff or snowy mountainside. Often, paragliders compete to see who can cover the greatest distance or make the best time along a specific airborne course. They may take photos of reference points along the way to prove they passed a designated spot.
pages.brief: A paraglider beneath a wing-shaped parachute launches from a tall cliff beside a snowy mountainside, a frame harness with a motor like a big fan on his back. He races a course for distance and time, photographing reference points along the way.

books.title: The Transcontinental Railroad
books.art_why: Historical 1860s railroad construction and landscapes make drawn reconstruction the right fit.

pages.text: Introduction Before the 1860s, a trip from New York City to San Francisco, California, could take six months. Over the long months of traveling, people had to carry all their food or hunt and gather it from the land. The trails west went through the lands of Indigenous peoples who had already had many negative dealings with outsiders and learned not to trust them. Still, thousands of settlers made the journey to California every year. The West Coast offered rich farmland, wonderful weather, and gold. At the time, the fastest way to travel was by railroad. Railroads crossed the eastern United States as far west as Chicago, Illinois, and Omaha, Nebraska. Building a direct railroad across the United States would allow settlers to get to California much more quickly. It would also allow settlers in the West to reach the East Coast to order goods, send and receive mail, and visit loved ones.
pages.brief: A long overland trail stretches west from New York City toward California, with settlers carrying or gathering food during a journey that could last six months. Indigenous people stand near the trail, wary after past dealings with outsiders. In the distance are rich farmland, warm weather, and gold, while eastern railroads reach Chicago and Omaha.

pages.text: Who Will Build the Railroad? People had wanted a transcontinental railroad, a railroad that crossed the entire North American continent, for years. But no one had built one. Building a railroad of that size was too expensive for any one person or company to pay for. Engineers had no calculators, no computers, and no airplanes to chart the land. Also, the Northern and Southern states were fighting each other in the Civil War, making agreement over a railroad impossible. In July of 1862, Congress passed the Pacific Railroad Act, declaring that a transcontinental railroad must be built. The government broke treaties with Indigenous peoples to give both companies land on either side of the proposed tracks. The companies sold the land to help pay for the railroad. They also hired immigrants and underpaid Black people to cut costs.
pages.brief: Engineers study rough land with simple tools while Northern and Southern soldiers fight in the Civil War background. In Congress, lawmakers pass the Pacific Railroad Act in July 1862. Railroad companies sell land on both sides of a proposed track and hire immigrant and Black laborers at low pay.

pages.text: Pitting the companies against each other made sure that the railroad would be built quickly. Whoever built the most track would get the most money. The railroad work continued even though many workers died from accidents or natural disasters. The Central Pacific started work in January 1863 just outside Sacramento, California.
pages.brief: Two railroad companies race to lay the most track, since more track means more money. Workers face accidents and natural disasters as construction continues. Just outside Sacramento, California, Central Pacific workers begin clearing ground and preparing the line in January 1863.

pages.text: Who Will Win the Race? The Civil War and financial trouble kept the Union Pacific Railroad from starting construction for two years. The war was taking up all the iron, gunpowder, and workers that the railroad needed for building track. But work got underway soon after the war ended in 1865. By 1866, it looked as if the Union Pacific would easily win the race. Preparing to lay track was a complicated process. First, surveying crews studied the land, putting stakes in the ground to mark exactly where the track would go. Second, a crew of graders went out. They removed any vegetation, filled in any low spots, and dug to make a flat, smooth track. Across the flat land of the plains, the graders often had little to do.
pages.brief: Surveying crews place stakes across the land, marking where track will go. Graders remove vegetation, fill low spots, and dig a flat, smooth path. On the flat plains they have little to do. After the Civil War ends in 1865, Union Pacific construction gets underway, and by 1866 it seems likely to win.

pages.text: Laying the track required several groups of workers. First, a team of workers laid down wooden timbers called ties across the track. Next, other workers dragged the heavy iron rails into place. Then, another group pounded in iron spikes and bolts that held the rails to the ties. Finally, a last group carried in sand and gravel, called ballast, to fill in around the new tracks. Using this system, the Union Pacific Railroad could lay 2 to 3 miles (3–5 km) of track in a single day. Right behind all these crews, the very first train to cross the plains rolled down the new track. The train carried all the wood, rails, iron spikes, tools, and ballast the crews needed. It also carried sleeping cars, a kitchen and food storage, repair shops, and goods, such as clothing. It was like a rolling town that built itself as it went.
pages.brief: Rail workers lay wooden ties, drag heavy iron rails into place, pound spikes and bolts, then fill around the track with ballast. A train follows close behind, carrying rails, tools, food, sleeping cars, repair shops, and clothing. It is like a rolling town that builds the railroad as it moves.

pages.text: The citizens of this working town were mostly immigrants from Ireland, Germany, and the Netherlands; Civil War veterans; and formerly enslaved Black people. They built the railroad across the plains with incredible speed, quickly reaching the Rocky Mountains. The Sioux, Arapaho, and Cheyenne tribes were devastated by the railroad. The American bison, also known as buffalo, which the Indigenous people depended on for their existence, could not travel across the tracks. Settlers killed thousands of bison, until they were almost gone. Without bison, the Indigenous peoples of the plains could not survive. Tribes lost many people from the disease, hunger, and conflict that came with the massacre of the bison. Settlers hunted bison nearly to extinction.
pages.brief: Railroad workers from Ireland, Germany, and the Netherlands, Civil War veterans, and formerly enslaved Black people lay track across the plains toward the Rocky Mountains. Nearby, bison are blocked by the rails while settlers hunt them. Sioux, Arapaho, and Cheyenne families face hunger, disease, and loss.

pages.text: The railroad also brought a flood of settlers to the plains. The railroad companies sold the land of the Sioux, Arapaho, and Cheyenne to the settlers. They began farming and building their homes there. The trains also brought litter, noise, air pollution, and prairie fires caused by sparks from the wood- or coal-burning engines. Indigenous people raided some trains to try to halt the railroad. As the Union Pacific advanced across the West, Indigenous people fought against the illegal seizing of their land. They stole supplies and livestock, and even killed some workers. The Union Pacific demanded that the army protect the workers and the railroad. Soon, the U.S. government sent soldiers onto the plains, where they engaged in many battles with Indigenous people.
pages.brief: Settlers farm and build homes on land sold by railroad companies. A train leaves litter, noise, smoke, and sparks that start prairie fires. Indigenous people raid the train and take supplies and livestock. U.S. soldiers arrive on the plains and fight many battles with Indigenous people.

pages.text: Who Will Conquer the Mountains? The work on the Central Pacific was going more slowly. Right away, the company had to cut a track into the steep and snowy Sierra Nevada. Because trains at the time could not climb steep hills or go around sharp corners, the workers somehow had to make the jagged mountains into a smooth, gently rising trail. The workers cut away the solid granite mountainsides and filled in gorges and ravines with rocks and soil, wheelbarrow by wheelbarrow. It was slow, painful work, and very few people wanted to do it. Almost all the white men hired by the Central Pacific Railroad quit within a week.
pages.brief: A steep, snowy Sierra Nevada mountainside blocks the Central Pacific. Workers cut away solid granite and fill a gorge with rocks and soil carried in wheelbarrows, trying to make a smooth, gently rising trail. The slow, painful work causes several white laborers to set down their tools and leave.

pages.text: Central Pacific reluctantly hired some Chinese workers to see if they would do better. Chinese workers faced racism and discrimination. Yet, Chinese workers often lasted a long time on the job because of their cleanliness and healthy habits. By 1868, Chinese workers made up most of the Central Pacific’s workforce. To get the railroad over the Sierra Nevada, the Chinese workers had to cut fifteen tunnels through solid rock. They used only hand drills, sledgehammers, and loose gunpowder. Through the winter, a total of forty-four snowstorms buried the mountains. The workers built tunnels, sleeping areas, and workspaces under an average of 18 feet (5.5 m) of snow. All their supplies had to be brought up the side of the mountain by ox wagon or by hand.
pages.brief: Chinese workers cut fifteen tunnels through solid rock in the snowy Sierra Nevada using hand drills, sledgehammers, and loose gunpowder. After many winter snowstorms bury the mountains, they build tunnels, sleeping areas, and workspaces under deep snow. Supplies arrive by ox wagon or are carried up the mountain by hand.

pages.text: The most famous accomplishment of the Chinese workers was to cut a track into the side of an enormous cliff they called Cape Horn. People who wrote about the project later described workers in woven reed baskets big enough to hold two people. They were lowered in the baskets from the top of the cliff. The workers drilled holes into the sides of the cliff, stuffed the holes with black powder, and lit a fuse. The workers at the top hauled up the baskets as fast as they could, hoping to pull everyone out of the way before the cliff was blown apart. But with these accomplishments came tragedy. Accidents crushed some workers, and the cold weather froze many to death. Avalanches buried entire groups of people alive—some were not found until spring. The Central Pacific Railroad did not keep track of how many Chinese laborers were killed while building the transcontinental railroad. Some accounts estimate around 1,200 died. Finally, in 1867, the track broke through the mountains, and the Central Pacific moved onto the deserts of Utah. Chinese workers played an important part in building the transcontinental railroad.
pages.brief: At Cape Horn, Chinese workers hang in woven reed baskets from a cliff, drilling holes and setting black powder while workers above haul them up fast. Snow and rock show the dangers of accidents, cold, and avalanches. In the distance, the track breaks through the mountains toward the Utah desert.

pages.text: Where Will They Meet? The Union Pacific had a much easier time crossing the Rocky Mountains than the Central Pacific had crossing the Sierra Nevada. They took a gentle route called the South Pass, and they also moved quickly onto the deserts of Utah. On May 10, 1869, workers, railroad owners, journalists, and politicians gathered at Promontory Point, Utah, for the completion of the transcontinental railroad. The race was over—the Union Pacific had laid 1,086 miles (1,748 km) of track, and the Central Pacific had laid 689 miles (1,109 km), though the Central Pacific got extra money for building through the Sierra Nevada. To celebrate the completion of the first railroad to cross the United States, the heads of the two companies would drive the last four spikes into the track. Special spikes were made of gold and silver. Leland Stanford, the head of the Central Pacific, and Thomas Durant, head of the Union Pacific, each swung a sledgehammer and missed! The crowd cheered anyway. The transcontinental railroad was complete.
pages.brief: At Promontory Point, Utah, workers, railroad owners, journalists, and politicians gather on May 10, 1869, for the completion ceremony. Leland Stanford and Thomas Durant swing sledgehammers at the last gold and silver spikes and both miss. The crowd cheers anyway as the transcontinental railroad is finished.

pages.text: The Route of the Transcontinental Railroad KEY Central Pacific Railroad Union Pacific Railroad Promontory Point Wyoming Central Pacific Railroad Nebraska Omaha Utah Nevada Union Pacific Railroad Sacramento Colorado California Conclusion After all the years of labor and danger, California was only a few days’ travel away from New York. Railroads stretched to Salt Lake City, Oregon Territory, and the Southwest. More towns sprang up along the tracks now that goods and mail could travel easily. The railroad companies made millions of dollars from the sale of Indigenous land, while the laborers never got any further payment. Yet, for the first time, a transcontinental railroad connected the country from east to west.
pages.brief: A wide view of North America shows the completed railroad spanning east to west, with trains traveling between New York and California and lines reaching Salt Lake City, Oregon Territory, and the Southwest. Towns grow along the tracks. Railroad company owners count millions from Indigenous land sales while laborers remain unpaid.

books.title: The Amazing Amazon
books.art_why: The Amazon rainforest and its animals exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Chapter 1: There Is a Place There is a place where monkeys swing and howl, jaguars leap from tree to tree, and insects create huge colonies underground. In this place, bananas, pineapples, coconuts, and chocolate grow in abundance. In this place, tiny frogs live in flowers and climb trees, and pink-colored dolphins swim in the river. Storms come often to this place, and the air is sweet. Some sunlight filters through the vines and leaves of the tall trees, but it is mostly dark here on the ground. It is hot, humid, and surprisingly still. Rainwater trickles down through the foliage from leaf to leaf. You hear a slow sound: drip, drip, drip. Your skin is sweaty, an insect lands on your neck, and an ant quietly walks across your sandal. Suddenly a little brown monkey swings to a nearby branch, a bright yellow eyelash viper slithers up a tree, and a bright green Amazon parrot flutters past. Welcome to the Amazon basin, a tropical rainforest. Rainforests Rainforests are located all over the planet. Tropical rainforests are close to the equator, between 23.5° N latitude and 23.5° S latitude.
pages.brief: A hot, humid tropical rainforest in the Amazon basin. A little brown monkey swings to a nearby branch while a bright green parrot flutters past. A yellow eyelash viper slithers up a tree. Tiny frogs sit among flowers and climb trees. Pink river dolphins swim in the river. Tall trees filter sunlight, and rainwater drips from leaf to leaf.

pages.text: Subtropical rainforests occur outside the tropics. Both types of rainforests share characteristics, but subtropical rainforests have fewer species of trees, plants, and animals than tropical rainforests. Rainforests live up to their name: they are forests where it rains almost every day. In fact, a typical tropical rainforest receives between 150 and 400 centimeters (59–157 in) of rain each year. They are also warm. Their temperature averages between 25° and 35° Celsius (77°F–95°F). Rainforests are green year-round. The humidity is between 77 and 88 percent. Their rainy, hot, and humid climate is perfect for tall trees, vines, ferns, and other plants. The really thick parts of rainforests are what we call jungles. Amazing Amazon.
pages.brief: A warm tropical rainforest with tall trees, vines, and ferns grows thick and green year-round. Rain falls almost every day, making the air hot and humid. Dense jungle undergrowth fills the lower forest. The wet climate supports many plants, and the thick green forest stretches in a band around the planet.

pages.text: Tropical rainforests cover a small part (about 6 percent) of Earth’s surface. But more than half (50 percent) of the world’s plant and animal species are found in them—that’s close to thirty million species of plants and animals! Most of the world’s rainforests are in Africa, Southeast Asia, and South America. The Amazon The Amazon rainforest lies in South America. Most of its 5.5 million square kilometers (1.4 billion acres) are in Brazil, but parts of the rainforest are also in Peru, Venezuela, Ecuador, Colombia, Guyana, Bolivia, Suriname, and French Guiana. It is the largest tropical rainforest in the world, with more different types of insects, plants, and animals than any other place on Earth. Scientists discover new species of insects and plants there every year. The Amazon River flows through the heart of this rainforest. Flowing at a rate of up to 7 kilometers per hour (4.3 mph), the water is brown from all the silt it carries. It is like a huge sea of fresh water. It has more than one thousand tributaries. Catfish, piranhas, and dolphins all live in the Amazon River.
pages.brief: A vast tropical rainforest covers the Amazon basin in South America. The wide Amazon River flows through the heart of it, carrying brown silt. Catfish, piranhas, and dolphins swim in the river. Tall trees and dense green plants fill the forest, which lies mostly in Brazil and also in several neighboring countries.

pages.text: This book will take you on a tour of the Amazon rainforest, traveling from the tallest trees to the rainforest floor. Along the way, you will meet an eagle, monkey, jaguar, and ant. You will even hear what these Amazon natives would say—if they could talk. So just how big is the Amazon River? • The Amazon River can be more than 48 kilometers (30 mi) across at its widest point during the rainy season. • It flows almost 6,437 kilometers (4,000 mi) to the Atlantic Ocean. • Within its mouth is an island the size of Switzerland. • It is home to more than forty thousand plant species. • The river’s arapaima fish can grow to be 3 meters (10 ft) long and weigh 180 kilograms (400 lb)! • Its volume is greater than the next eight largest rivers combined! The Amazon is the world’s widest and largest river. Amazing Amazon.
pages.brief: An eagle, a monkey, a jaguar, and an ant appear along a tour of the Amazon rainforest. Nearby, the wide Amazon River flows toward the Atlantic Ocean, carrying brown water. A long arapaima fish swims below. The river is the world’s widest and largest, with an island in its mouth and many tributaries.

pages.text: From the Amazon Yearbook Sloths are slow-moving animals. They seem to just hang out (upside down!) in the trees. Sloths sleep up to twenty hours a day. When they’re awake, they hardly move, which allows algae to grow on their fur. But, hey, it helps them blend into the forest. Sammy “Slowpoke” Sloth Sammy was voted: Most Likely to Survive, but Least Likely to Succeed The tapir is a large, hoofed animal that is related to the horse and the rhinoceros. Tapirs often weigh well over 136 kilograms (300 lb), and they like to swim in the river, bathe in the mud, and they are nocturnal, preferring to look for food when it is dark. Tamara the Tapir Tamara was voted: Best Personality At approximately 1.2 meters (4 ft) long and standing 60 centimeters (2 ft) at the shoulder, the capybara is the world’s largest rodent. (But Katie doesn’t like to be Katie Capybara.
pages.brief: A slow-moving sloth hangs upside down in a tall rainforest tree, its fur tinged with algae. A large tapir stands near mud and water, ready to swim or bathe. A capybara, the world’s largest rodent, rests beside the river with slightly webbed feet. These Amazon animals look out from the forest.

pages.text: Capybaras’ slightly webbed feet help them swim. Katie was voted: Most Likely to Win a Rat Race The poison arrow frog has super-bright colors and designs. This ostentatious patterning warns other animals that its skin is poisonous. Some native people in the Amazon rainforest have used the frog’s poison for centuries when they go hunting. Paulo the Poison Arrow Frog Paulo was voted: Most Dangerous Amphibian Chapter 2: Layers of the Rainforest To better understand the rainforest, scientists have “divided” it into four layers, or sections. You can think of it like a four- story building, with the highest trees making up the top floor, called the emergent layer, and the next-highest trees making up the canopy layer. Below them is the understory layer. At the bottom is the rainforest floor. Rainforest Layers Amazing Amazon.
pages.brief: The rainforest is shown as four layers like a four-story building. Tall emergent trees rise at the top, with the canopy below, then the dark understory, and the rainforest floor at the bottom. A bright poison arrow frog with vivid colors and patterns sits in the lower forest, warning others with its poisonous skin.

pages.text: High Risers The tallest trees of the rainforest are the emergents. They are like big umbrellas that rise as much as 60.9 meters (200 ft) above the thick forest. Emergents are exposed to sun, wind, rain, and lightning. Big roots support these giant trees. Because rainforest soil is shallow, tree roots often grow above the ground. The kapok tree is deciduous, meaning it sheds its leaves during the dry season, and has tall roots that extend out like wooden walls. These roots are so big that your whole class could hide behind just one of them! Not many animals live in the emergent layer; however, some birds, bats, monkeys, and butterflies do visit to eat leaves and fruit. One huge bird, the harpy eagle, actually lives up there, high above the Amazon. Harpy eagle Spotlight Interview: The Harpy Eagle Interviewer: Hello there, Harpy. Is it true that you are the largest eagle in the Americas? Harpy: I think so. In your people terms, I am about one meter tall, which is more than three feet high.
pages.brief: High in an emergent kapok tree, a huge harpy eagle perches with broad wings and big talons. A rainforest interviewer looks up at the eagle. Sun, wind, rain, and lightning beat on the exposed treetop. Thick roots spread above the shallow soil like wooden walls.

pages.text: Interviewer: It looks as if you have some big wings as well. Harpy: Oh, these things? I was born with these. If I stretch them out like this, they are longer than most people. You see? My wingspan is two meters across—about six and a half feet. Flying fast really helps me find food. Interviewer: What is your favorite food? Harpy: Oh, I like pizza delivered to my door. Just kidding—there’s no pizza here in the rainforest! I hunt sloths, monkeys, and fellow birds. Monkeys are probably the tastiest. Interviewer: Is that what your big talons are for? Harpy: Yep. Since they are thirteen centimeters long—that’s about five inches—these meat hooks can scoop unsuspecting animals right off tree branches. Interviewer: Do you ever fear revenge, like a monkey uprising? Harpy: No, I’m the top bird around here. I build my stick nests 27 to 43 meters, or about 90 to 140 feet, up in the tallest trees. I choose trees with widely spaced branches so I have a clear flight path in and out of my nest. That way I can see what’s around. Monkeys don’t normally go up that high. Hey, there’s a monkey now! I’ll see you later! Amazing Amazon.
pages.brief: The harpy eagle stretches its two-meter wingspan in the tall trees and shows its long talons. A rainforest interviewer stands nearby, asking about food and hunting. The eagle describes hunting sloths, monkeys, and birds. Its stick nest sits high in a tree with widely spaced branches, giving a clear flight path.

pages.text: Crazy Canopy The rainforest’s real action is in the canopy layer. This primary layer is where most of the rainforest plants and animals live. It is like a thick roof woven out of tree branches, plants, and vines that covers the two remaining layers. About 80 percent of the sunlight in the rainforest is absorbed by the trees in this layer, so very little gets to the lower layers. Many trees in the canopy are covered with climbing vines and epiphytes. Epiphytes are plants that grow on top of other plants and receive most of their moisture and nutrients from the air. Most of the rainforest’s flowers, fruit, and seeds are found in this layer. With so much good canopy food, it makes sense that animals hang out here. Many animals rarely come down to the ground, preferring to eat, sleep, hunt, and give birth high up in the trees. Many of them fly, jump, glide, and hop to get from tree to tree. Sloths, toucans, and parrots are just some of the canopy’s residents, but the hardest ones to ignore are probably the howler monkeys. Their name befits their behavior, as these monkeys (the largest of the New World monkeys) howl and scream to keep other animals out of their territories.
pages.brief: Thick canopy branches, vines, and epiphytes form a green roof over the rainforest. Flowers, fruit, and seeds grow high in the trees. A sloth hangs from a branch, a toucan and parrot perch nearby, and howler monkeys howl and scream to guard their territory. Most sunlight is absorbed by the leaves above.

pages.text: Spotlight Interview: The Howler Monkey Interviewer: Wow, that was one loud and distinctive howl! Excuse me, but could you please stop screaming for one moment? I would like to ask you a few questions! Howler: Okay, but hurry up. If I don’t scream like this regularly, other monkeys may come into our territory to claim our food. Interviewer: Do you always stay up here in the canopy? Howler: This is our home, my man. On the ground, there are some really big animals—it’s Amazing Amazon.
pages.brief: High in the canopy, a loud howler monkey screams while a rainforest interviewer covers his ears. The monkey grips a branch with its hands and feet. It explains that it must howl to keep other monkeys from claiming its food. Below the canopy, the jungle floor holds big animals.

pages.text: When it comes to safety, we don’t monkey around. We’re herbivores, so up here we can eat fruit, leaves, and flowers, and we can live in safety. Interviewer: Does your long tail help you? It looks prehensile. Howler: Yeah, if by prehensile you mean “grab onto.” My tail helps me climb, but my hands and feet are very useful for climbing, too. Interviewer: You sure use big words for a monkey. Hey, stop the howling! If you can be heard from five kilometers, or three miles, away, just think how loud it is for me. What makes you so loud anyway? Howler: I have a special bone in my windpipe. My throat is like a hollow sound box. See the big swelling under my chin? Here, touch it. Interviewer: Oww! That’s not funny—you have sharp teeth! Okay, Mr. Monkey, you can go back to howling now. The Darker Story The understory is the third level of the rainforest; it is below the canopy and above the ground. The ferns, plants, and young trees that grow in this layer rarely reach much more than 3.6 meters (12 ft) in height. It is dark in the understory because very little light shines through the thick canopy. Understory.
pages.brief: In the canopy, the howler monkey hangs by its long prehensile tail and uses its hands and feet to climb. It shows a swelling under its chin and a special bone in its windpipe. The rainforest interviewer reaches out and then pulls back after the monkey shows sharp teeth.

pages.text: The flowers these plants produce are brightly colored and emit strong scents to attract pollinators such as birds and insects. The understory is not nearly as busy as the canopy, but many animals do live here. About 220 species of poison arrow frogs hide in the foliage. Venomous and nonvenomous snakes wrap around trees like vines. Birds peck and pull insects from the wood. Large cats such as cougars and jaguars leap between branches. Spotlight Interview: The Jaguar Interviewer: Hey, put me down! And don’t bite. Bad cat, bad big cat! Jaguar: Sorry, I thought you were a monkey. Lucky for you that you’re not as tasty. Hey, what do you think you’re doing here anyway? Interviewer: I came to interview you, the Jaguar Amazing Amazon.
pages.brief: In the dark understory, a jaguar leaps between branches and catches a rainforest interviewer by the back. Wide leaves catch small rays of light, and brightly colored flowers attract birds and insects. Poison arrow frogs hide in the foliage, snakes wrap around trees, and birds peck insects from the wood.

pages.text: Americas. Mr. Jaguar, are you really 2.6 meters (8.5 ft) long? Jaguar: That’s what they say. I weigh 136 kilograms (300 lb), too. Not many animals mess with me. By the way, you can just call me Jag. Interviewer: Okay, Jag, what do you do for exercise? Jag: I get bored with just one sport. That’s why I cross-train: I run, swim, climb, fish, and hunt. Interviewer: What do you hunt? Jag: Lots of things. My spots, called rosettes, camouflage me so my prey won’t see me coming until it’s too late. Sometimes I climb up in the canopy to eat sloths and monkeys. On the ground, I hunt peccaries, tapirs, and yummy capybaras. On lazy days, I lie near the river and catch fish with my claws. When I’m really hungry or want a challenge, I kill anacondas and caimans. Let’s face it, I’m one big carnivore. Interviewer: Wow, I don’t want to be in your powerful jaws ever again! If you’ll excuse me, I need to go now. Chapter 3: Keeping It Clean If you walked around the rainforest floor, you might be surprised. It is not just one thick jungle. Sure, you would see roots, ferns, herbs, and baby.
pages.brief: A powerful jaguar stands in the rainforest, its rosette spots camouflaging it. The rainforest interviewer asks about its length and hunting. The jaguar runs, swims, climbs, fishes, and hunts peccaries, tapirs, capybaras, anacondas, and caimans. It lies near the river, ready to catch fish with its claws.

pages.text: But most of the green would be high above you. Earthworms, termites, fungi, and bacteria eat up the fallen fruit, leaves, and branches, recycling it back into nutritious soil. Plants decay quickly on the rainforest floor. When a big tree falls, the insects quickly munch it down into small pieces. A leaf that falls from a tree decomposes in a mere six weeks in the rainforest, whereas in other ecosystems it could take up to a year. Also on the ground are big animals such as giant anteaters, deer, tapirs, peccaries, and capybaras, but they are far outnumbered by the smaller spiders, beetles, and ants. Ant highways crisscross the rainforest floor. One kind of ant, the famous leaf-cutter ant, even parades around with leaves and flower petals in its mouth, creating trails that stretch more than 30 meters (98 ft) across. Trivia Question In the Amazon rainforest, are there more mammals, birds, insects, or reptiles? Answer: Insects! (There are more than two hundred types of mosquito alone. There are well over one thousand different kinds of butterflies. And just think of all the ants!) Amazing Amazon.
pages.brief: On the dark rainforest floor, earthworms, termites, fungi, and bacteria break down fallen fruit, leaves, and branches into rich soil. Giant anteaters, deer, tapirs, peccaries, and capybaras stand among roots and ferns. Leaf-cutter ants parade with leaves and flower petals, making long trails across the ground. Spiders, beetles, and ants are everywhere.

pages.text: Spotlight Interview: The Leaf-Cutter Ant Interviewer: Hey down there! Yeah, you—the one carrying the big leaf over your head! I’d like to ask you a few questions. Do you have a moment? Ms. Ant: Sure, but I do need to hurry back to the fungus garden. We’re low on food. Interviewer: Did you really just climb up a tree and cut off that leaf? Ms. Ant: That’s correct. And now I’m carrying it back to our underground colony, where smaller ants will chew it up into little spongy bits. Interviewer: So you don’t eat the actual leaf? Leaf-cutter ants.
pages.brief: A leaf-cutter ant carries a big leaf over its head along a trail on the rainforest floor. A rainforest interviewer kneels down to ask questions. The ant explains that it climbed a tree to cut the leaf and is hurrying it back to an underground colony, where smaller ants will chew it into spongy bits.

pages.text: Ms. Ant: No, even though we are herbivores, we use the leaves as a substrate for the cultivation of a special type of fungus. Then we eat the fungus. Want to try some? Interviewer: No, thank you—I, uh, just had lunch. So tell me, what is it like underground? Ms. Ant: We have deep nests with hundreds of chambers. We have a stratified society, meaning different ants perform different jobs in different places within the colony. In the middle rooms, smaller ants tend to our fungus gardens, and our only queen is in a different room laying up to thirty thousand eggs in one day. That’s why there are almost five million of us here! Now if you’ll excuse me, I need to sniff my way home. And please watch your feet—if you step on our trail, it might alter the scent and I might get lost! Bromeliads are cone- shaped plants that grow on trees. Their cones catch a lot of rainwater and form little swimming pools high above the ground. Tiny frogs, salamanders, and crabs live in these pools. Mosquitoes and dragonflies lay eggs in them. Amazing Amazon.
pages.brief: Inside a deep underground nest, many chambers hold fungus gardens tended by smaller ants. The leaf-cutter ant explains that the queen lays up to thirty thousand eggs in one day. High above the ground, a cone-shaped bromeliad catches rainwater, forming a little pool where tiny frogs, salamanders, crabs, mosquitoes, and dragonflies live.

pages.text: Chapter 4: Who, Me? Yes, you. Do you eat bananas? Do you like chocolate? Have you ridden a bicycle with rubber tires? Well, guess what! Bananas, chocolate, and rubber all grow in the Amazon rainforest. Many more things come from the Amazon, too, such as pain and cancer medicines, woods for furniture, pineapples and other fruits, and fresh air. The Amazon is a rich, living treasure. Insects buzz by that do not even have names yet. Trees grow, fall, and decompose into rich soil. Rainstorms fill up frogs’ swimming pools. And perhaps most importantly, plants of the rainforest take carbon dioxide from the air and replace it with oxygen. Rainforests contribute approximately 24 percent of the oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere. Humans and other animals need oxygen in order to live. The Amazon rainforest is a real place. Even if it is far away from you, the Amazon lives at this very moment. As you read these words, a jaguar slinks through the understory, a leaf-cutter ant marches back to a fungus garden, and the scream of a howler monkey echoes throughout the forest. Can you hear it? The Amazon rainforest is home to many living things.
pages.brief: A rich, living Amazon rainforest shows bananas, chocolate, and rubber trees. Insects buzz, trees grow and fall into rich soil, and rainstorms fill frogs’ swimming pools. A jaguar slinks through the understory while a leaf-cutter ant marches to a fungus garden. A howler monkey’s scream echoes through the forest, and plants release oxygen.

pages.text: Explore More Did you like learning about the Amazon rainforest? Well, there is much more to see. If you do some research, you’re bound to find some very interesting animals! 1. At the Library Tell your librarian that you are interested in books about the Amazon rainforest. 2. On the Web In the address window, type: www.google.com Then type: Amazon rainforest. Click on “Google Search.” Read the colored links. Click on one that looks interesting. When you want to explore other links, click the “back” arrow on the top left. Or try a new search: Amazon River Amazing Amazon.
pages.brief: A child sits at a library table with books about the Amazon rainforest and a computer showing a search screen. The child reads about rainforest animals and follows links to explore more. A librarian stands nearby, ready to help find more books and information about the Amazon River and rainforest.

pages.text: 3. Try This! Where do you live? Do you live in the rainforest? What about in a desert, tundra, or pine forest? Do you live on the coast, up in the mountains, or out on the plains? You must live somewhere, right? If you live in a town or city, sometimes it can be hard to tell what kind of region you live in. But there are clues all around. What kinds of trees and bushes grow nearby? What kinds of birds fly overhead? What is the weather like? Look around and investigate. If you are not sure, ask your teacher, librarian, parent, or friend. Once you figure it out, make a report. Draw a picture like the one on page 9, but make it for your area. What kind of insects, plants, and animals are native to your home? You could find this information by walking around outside. You could also ask other people. Or you could read a book or search the Web. You’ll probably be surprised by the cool things you learn about your neighbors!
pages.brief: A child looks around a town or city neighborhood, noticing trees, bushes, birds overhead, and the weather. The child investigates what kind of region they live in, then draws a picture and makes a report about local insects, plants, and animals. A teacher, librarian, parent, or friend helps answer questions.

pages.text: John Adams (left), from the United States, extends an offering to George III (right) of England in 1785. A Historic Meeting John Adams, one of America’s Founding Fathers, traveled to England in 1785 to meet with King George III. Adams stood before the king, who looked at Adams skeptically. The United States had declared its independence from Great Britain just nine years earlier, and relations between the two nations were rocky. Adams humbly offered the United States’ hand in friendship. He spoke of honor and affection between the two nations and expressed good wishes for the king’s health and happiness. The king smiled, replying that he accepted Adams’s offer, and the brief meeting ended. Great Britain, the country King George III ruled and loved, had suffered due to the loss of the American colonies. He was determined, and vowed to lead his nation to greatness again.
pages.brief: John Adams stands on the left, humbly extending his hand toward King George III on the right in 1785. The king looks at Adams skeptically, and the two men meet in a historic diplomatic encounter between the United States and England.

pages.text: The Making of a King Princess Augusta of Wales gave birth to George on June 4, 1738. His royal family included his grandfather, King George II, and his father, Frederick, Prince of Wales. The king and Frederick did not get along. Their political opinions differed, which created family tension. Young George grew up in that stressful environment. A sensitive and emotional boy, George struggled with his education, even though his parents provided excellent teachers. It wasn’t until the age of eleven that he learned to read. One year later, his father died of a lung ailment, leaving George the heir to the British throne. The future king turned to his teacher, Lord Bute, for support. He would soon need it. Portraits show young Prince George (left) and Lord Bute (right). Lord Bute taught the king about the government and the world.
pages.brief: Portraits show young Prince George on the left and his teacher Lord Bute on the right. George appears as a sensitive, emotional boy, and Lord Bute stands as the supportive teacher who instructed him about government and the world.

pages.text: North American British Territories in 1763 This map shows Great Britain’s territory in North America before the French and Indian War (purple) and the areas they gained after the war (red). In the mid-1700s, Great Britain was a powerful ruler in different places around the world. Its colonies in India and North America provided markets where British merchants sold goods. The British monarchy led the way for the nation. However, the British Parliament often clashed with the king. In 1760, George II died, and at the age of just twenty-two, George became King George III. At that time, Great Britain was in the middle of fighting for control of land in the Seven Years’ War against France and other countries in Europe. Battles also took place in North America, where the war was called the French and Indian War. When Great Britain won the war, it gained many French territories and grew larger than ever before.
pages.brief: A map of North America shows Great Britain's territory before and after the French and Indian War, using different colored regions to show land held earlier and land gained after the war. The map places the colonies within the wider struggle between Britain and France.

pages.text: Two Officials Clash The victories in the Seven Years’ War thrilled King George III, but the British public did not give him much credit. Instead, William Pitt, war minister to King George, earned the praise. William Pitt was an enemy of Lord Bute, the king’s mentor. Pitt and Bute argued at the end of the war. Pitt wanted to expand the war into Spain, but Bute and the king did not. The conflict became so heated that Pitt resigned his post in the king’s ministry. The king appointed Bute prime minister, the leading position in the king’s ministry. Bute formally ended the Seven Years’ War with a treaty signed in 1763. He resigned shortly after that. William Pitt was the driving force behind Britain’s victory. Even so, Lord Bute opposed him and urged George III to do the same.
pages.brief: William Pitt and Lord Bute face each other in a heated argument at the end of the Seven Years' War, while King George III stands nearby. Pitt, the war minister, wants to expand the war into Spain, but Bute and the king oppose him.

pages.text: King George selected Sophia Charlotte as his wife without having met her. She arrived in England, met the king, and married him the next day. A Royal Family George III may have lost his closest political advisor, but he had gained a partner for life. In 1761, the king married a German princess named Sophia Charlotte. Their long, successful marriage lasted more than fifty years, and they had fifteen children together. Happy at home, George was determined to be a great leader. He worked hard to learn more about the British Parliament and how it could be improved. The king remained keenly aware of global affairs as well. A Simple Man Despite his royal rank, King George enjoyed the simpler things in life. He loved agriculture and spent many days inspecting his kingdom’s farms. His favorite activities included horseback riding, music, attending the theater, and playing cards.
pages.brief: King George III meets Sophia Charlotte, a German princess, as she arrives in England; they marry the next day. In another scene, the king enjoys a simple country life, inspecting farms, riding horses, listening to music, attending the theater, and playing cards.

pages.text: The Colonies The greatest challenge King George III faced was the American Revolution. The war began with a series of parliamentary acts that outraged the American colonists. Great Britain levied taxes on goods the colonists used: the Sugar Act taxed molasses; the Stamp Act taxed all printed paper; and the Townshend Acts taxed paint, glass, and tea. The colonists opposed the taxes and issued boycotts of British goods. Then, on the night of December 16, 1773, a group of colonists dressed as Native Americans boarded a British ship docked in Boston Harbor. The ship carried crates of tea, and the colonists dumped the crates into the water. King George responded to the Boston Tea Party with a challenge: “The colonies must either triumph or submit.” The Boston Tea Party rallied the colonists who felt oppressed by British taxes.
pages.brief: American colonists dressed as Native Americans board a British ship docked in Boston Harbor at night and dump crates of tea into the water. King George III reacts with a stern challenge, while colonists rally against British taxes on molasses, printed paper, paint, glass, and tea.

pages.text: America Fights Back The American Revolution began in 1775, when soldiers fired shots at the Battles of Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts. King George realized he needed more troops to lead Great Britain to victory, so he hired the services of about thirty thousand German soldiers, called Hessians. Teamed with the Hessians, the king’s army defeated the colonists in some early battles. However, when General George Washington led a surprise attack in late 1776, the British were pushed back. In 1778, a decisive event occurred: the French joined the American side. Supported by their allies, the Americans won the war in 1781. King George, sensing he might be blamed for the defeat, claimed, “I am innocent of the evils that have occurred.” Upon declaring independence from Britain in 1776, some colonists tore down a statue of King George in New York City.
pages.brief: Soldiers fire shots at the Battles of Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts, beginning the American Revolution. German Hessian soldiers fight alongside the British king's army, and General George Washington leads a surprise attack; colonists tear down a statue of King George in New York City.

pages.text: At times, King George III’s illness resulted in violent outbursts, and he was restrained. Illness and Revolution In the late 1780s, after the loss of the colonies, people around King George III began to notice his failing health. He seemed nervous. He said strange things and talked to imaginary people. He could be violent, too, shouting and pushing people. These were just the emotional symptoms —he weakened physically as well. Deeply alarmed, the king’s family and ministers asked doctors to help. They conducted treatments common during that era. They had the king drink medicine, and they opened his veins and bled him. They also began a course of strict discipline, punishing the king harshly if he acted strangely. This treatment appeared to help, and soon the king began working again.
pages.brief: King George III suffers from violent outbursts and is restrained by attendants as his health fails. Doctors treat him by having him drink medicine, opening his veins to bleed him, and enforcing strict discipline; the king appears nervous, shouts, pushes people, and speaks to imaginary figures.

pages.text: The political cartoon “The Rival Gardeners” expresses how both George III and Napoleon had their own gardens (lands) to attend to. A revolution in Ireland also commanded the king’s attention around that time. The conflict centered on religion. Ireland was a Catholic nation, and Great Britain’s Parliament had passed laws limiting the rights of Catholics living there. After the British army stifled a rebellion, Great Britain’s Parliament merged with Ireland’s in 1800, creating the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. The king’s challenges were not over, though, and the early 1800s saw Great Britain at war with France once again. After the French Revolution of 1789, a young general named Napoleon Bonaparte rose to power in France. Napoleon wanted to conquer lands in Europe, including Great Britain. England had to defend itself. The Napoleonic Wars ended in 1815 with Great Britain and its allies again defeating Britain’s old rival.
pages.brief: A political cartoon shows King George III and Napoleon Bonaparte as rival gardeners tending their own gardens of land. In another scene, British soldiers stifle an Irish rebellion, while Parliament merges with Ireland's to create the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.

pages.text: A New King George In 1809, Great Britain celebrated George III’s fiftieth year on the throne. Despite his reign’s rough beginnings, the king had reached new heights of popularity, and most subjects believed that George III had led his country well for half a century. Thousands of his subjects cheered him. The following year, the king suffered a terrible tragedy. His youngest daughter died suddenly of tuberculosis at the age of twenty-seven. The king was shocked and heartbroken. Soon the symptoms of his earlier illness returned. He went into a steep physical and mental decline. In 1811, it became clear that the king could no longer perform his duties. The British Parliament named his eldest son, George, as regent, or temporary ruler. When George III finally passed away in January 1820, young George ascended to the throne just as his father had done decades earlier. George IV served as king from 1820 to 1830.
pages.brief: Thousands of subjects cheer King George III as he celebrates fifty years on the throne. Later, the king is heartbroken when his youngest daughter dies of tuberculosis, and his illness returns; his eldest son, George, becomes regent while the king declines.

pages.text: A Complex Portrait King George’s legacy offers a picture of a complicated yet strong leader. Some people think of George III as the king who let the American colonies win their independence. Others think of him as the ruler who went insane. Many historians, however, have begun to rethink their opinions of him. Some historians believe symptoms of his mental illness are linked to physical disease. As a leader, George III always put his country first. He rallied and led his nation to victories in the Seven Years’ War and the Napoleonic Wars. He also fought hard to keep the British colonies in America. The king’s personal life has also been given more consideration, and history has shown that George was a hard worker, a loyal husband, and a loving father. King George reigned for sixty years—longer than any monarch before him.
pages.brief: A formal painted portrait of King George III presents him as a complicated yet strong leader, dressed in royal eighteenth-century clothing. The image invites reflection on his long reign, his victories in the Seven Years' War and Napoleonic Wars, his struggle to keep the American colonies, and his devotion to family.

pages.text: The Life of George III 1738: George is born on June 4 1751: Frederick, Prince of Wales and George’s father, dies 1756: Seven Years’ War begins 1760: King George II, George’s grandfather, dies, and George becomes king 1763: Seven Years’ War ends 1775: First shots of the American Revolution 1781: The British surrender to the American colonists at Yorktown 1788: George III shows signs of a serious mental illness; resumes duties a year later, appearing to be cured 1798: Britain stops the Irish Rebellion 1809: The king celebrates fifty years on the throne 1815: The British defeat Napoleon 1820: Thousands attend George III’s funeral.
pages.brief: A sequence of historical portraits and scenes traces George III's life from his birth in 1738 to his funeral in 1820, including his father's death, the Seven Years' War, becoming king, the American Revolution, his illness, and fifty years on the throne.
