books.title: Hungry Right Here?
books.art_why: The book describes present-day American children, families, food banks, schools, and volunteers, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: Hungry Right Here?
pages.brief: A quiet American neighborhood with a few houses, a sidewalk, and a distant school under a plain sky; no people are visible, and the scene feels ordinary and close to home. The street is calm, with no signs of wealth or struggle, inviting viewers to look closely at an everyday place.

pages.text: The Invisible Epidemic It’s the last day of school! Everyone is excited about the long summer break—everyone except a boy named Aaron. His stomach rumbles. The only food he’s had today is the school lunch, and he knows the cupboards at home are empty. His mom works two jobs, but by the end of the month they always run out of money for food. He sighs, thinking of the long summer ahead.
pages.brief: Aaron, a boy, sits among excited classmates on the last day of school, his stomach rumbling. He pictures empty cupboards at home, his mother working two jobs, and a long summer ahead with little food.

pages.text: Like Aaron, millions of American children go hungry every day. Maybe you are one of them. According to the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), 35.2 million Americans lived in “food-insecure” homes in 2019. This means they did not always have enough food for everyone living there. Of these Americans, 10.7 million were children. That’s about one in seven children in the United States. Hunger brings pain and stress. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has found that children who don’t get enough to eat have more health problems and miss more school than those who do. When kids are hungry at school, they have a harder time learning. Hunger also has long-term effects. Too little food can slow children’s physical and mental development. The United States grows lots of food. The government has programs to help people who can’t afford food. Yet there is an epidemic of hunger in the United States. Why? All-you-can-eat buffets suggest a land of plenty. But is it for everyone?
pages.brief: One hungry child in a school cafeteria cannot concentrate while classmates eat; in the distance, an all-you-can-eat buffet glows with plenty. The scene contrasts American food abundance with children who lack enough food at home and suffer health and learning problems.

pages.text: Why People Can’t Afford Food When families don’t have enough money, they often have to make tough choices. Sometimes that choice is to either pay the bills or eat. Millions of Americans work full time and sometimes still go hungry—women in particular. USDA numbers show that more than 60 percent of adults receiving food assistance are women. According to the U.S. Census, more than 80 percent of single parents caring for children are women. These women are twice as likely to live in poverty as single men caring for children. When mothers are living in poverty, their children often are, too. A mother uses government assistance to buy fresh food.
pages.brief: A mother stands at a grocery checkout, holding a wallet and choosing carefully between paying bills and buying food. She uses government assistance for fresh food; nearby, other single mothers shop with children, showing how poverty often passes from mothers to children.

pages.text: During the Great Depression, the government gave out surplus food to help feed hungry Americans. How Food Assistance Works Federal food assistance began in 1933 as a way for the government to help farmers. The USDA bought farmers’ extra crops and gave them to those in need. In 1939, the government began giving actual stamps that people used to buy that extra food. By 1964, the program allowed people to buy any type of food, not just extra from farmers. In 2008, the Food Stamp Program was renamed the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) to reflect the program’s new focus on nutrition.
pages.brief: In a Great Depression food line, government workers give surplus crops to hungry Americans. Nearby, farmers’ extra produce is gathered. A later scene shows people using paper food stamps at a small grocery counter, then shopping for any type of food in a modern store.

pages.text: Who Receives SNAP Benefits? 23% elderly people or people with disabilities 44% children 33% other adults In 2018, nearly two-thirds of SNAP recipients were children, elderly people, or people with disabilities. In 2019, SNAP helped more than thirty-five million Americans. The average monthly food stamp benefit is less than $5 a day. Another federal program helps pregnant women and children under the age of five. It provides specific nutritious foods such as milk, baby formula, and baby food. For more than thirty million children, the National School Lunch Program (NSLP) also provides free or reduced-cost lunches at public schools, regardless of income.
pages.brief: Elderly people, people with disabilities, children, and other adults stand together as people who receive food assistance. A pregnant woman holds milk, baby formula, and baby food; schoolchildren receive free or reduced-cost lunches in a public school cafeteria.

pages.text: The Politics of Hunger The government offers a safety net to many hungry Americans. Yet the amount of money budgeted for federal food programs varies from year to year. Who draws up the budget? Congress, our national lawmakers in Washington, D.C. In some years, Congress cuts billions in spending for SNAP; in other years, it increases spending for school lunch programs. People disagree about how much the federal government should spend on these food programs. They disagree about who the government should help feed and how the government should determine who gets that help. Because of other rising costs, such as childcare, housing, and education, many families today struggle to pay their bills. To help with that struggle, some people think more Americans should receive food assistance. A five-year-old holds a sign to help protest a 2013 House farm bill. The bill would have cut SNAP by $20.5 billion. Actual cuts in November 2013 affected more than forty-seven million Americans.
pages.brief: A five-year-old holds a sign at a protest near government buildings in Washington, D.C., surrounded by adults and children. Elsewhere, families face rising costs for childcare, housing, and education, while lawmakers debate how much the federal government should spend on food programs.

pages.text: Filling the Gap When government funding is not enough to meet the needs of hungry Americans, local food programs help fill the gap. Food banks in every state collect food from growers, restaurants, and grocery stores. They give the food to charities, such as food pantries or soup kitchens, that serve the public. Food banks often provide canned or boxed foods because storing fresh fruits and vegetables is difficult. For people with lower incomes, the need for these fresh foods can sometimes be filled by community gardens. Here, people plant, care for, and harvest food to use at home or share with the community. Many community gardens grow vegetables for their local food banks. Food Deserts High-poverty areas are often “food deserts”—places not served by large grocery stores. Some are in inner cities where stores have closed. Others are in rural areas with small populations. People in these areas often can’t afford to travel ten or fifteen miles to buy groceries, so they buy basic food at small, local stores. Prices are generally higher, and small stores often don’t carry nutritious foods like quality meat or fresh produce. Food deserts can make life particularly difficult for communities of underrepresented people that lack access to supermarket chain stores.
pages.brief: Volunteers sort canned and boxed foods at a food bank, then food pantries and soup kitchens serve the public. In a community garden, people plant, care for, and harvest vegetables for home and donation. A small local store in a high-poverty food desert offers higher prices and little fresh produce.

pages.text: Feeding America, the largest organization helping American families, has more than two hundred food banks and sixty thousand food pantries that feed about twelve million kids each year. However, charities provide less than 6 percent of the food assistance in the United States. As costs rise, wages stay the same, and federal food programs are cut, these organizations are finding that they cannot meet the needs of hungry people. They often run out of food and have to turn families away. Do You Know? The nonprofit organization AmpleHarvest.org connects more than 7,500 food charities with gardens that want to donate produce.
pages.brief: A large food-bank warehouse holds shelves of food while volunteers pack boxes and families wait for help. Some shelves run low, and staff turn families away. Nearby, a garden charity connects gardeners who want to donate extra produce to food charities that serve hungry people.

pages.text: Kids Can Make a Difference Many kids help fight hunger in America. Students in New Hampshire held a “hunger banquet” for their parents. The “cost” to attend the banquet was canned food for the food pantry. A sixth-grade class in Massachusetts made an award-winning video about hunger to educate people in their community. Other students have raised money for food banks through bake sales, art sales, car washes, walk-a-thons, and read-a-thons. Sam Adamo played his cello at a local farmer’s market and collected $700 for his local food bank in Rhode Island. Carson Pazdan created a cookbook for and by kids. The cookbook sales raised more than $20,000 for the Northern Illinois Food Bank. Macy Stewart collected 844 pounds (383 kg) of food by handing out bags in her school and asking classmates to fill them for St. Mary’s Food Bank in Surprise, Arizona. When seven-year-old William Winslow realized that kids in his part of North Carolina would not have food over spring break, he asked a local grocery store to let him stand outside and talk to people. He told them about BackPack Buddies, a program that sends meals home on weekends for students in need.
pages.brief: Children and teens fight hunger in many ways: students host a canned-food banquet for parents, a sixth-grade class makes a video, and kids run bake sales, art sales, car washes, walk-a-thons, and read-a-thons. Sam plays cello at a farmer’s market; Carson makes a cookbook; Macy hands out bags; William stands outside a grocery store.

pages.text: William collected 8,100 pounds (3,674 kg) of food for BackPack Buddies in 2016. In only one weekend, William collected 1,400 pounds (635 kg) of food and $305 in cash donations. Now in fourth grade, he still holds a fundraiser each year. In 2016, he organized 171 volunteers to collect donations at ten grocery stores. Donations provided eleven thousand meals to children in his area. In 2017, he hopes to expand throughout the state of North Carolina. William says, “I’m just an involved, regular kid. Any kid can make a difference if they want to. It’s just whether they want to or not.” Higher Wages, Less Hunger Raising the minimum wage is one way to fight hunger. Several states have raised their minimum wage to $10 to $15 per hour, which lowered their hunger rates.
pages.brief: William Winslow, a fourth-grade boy, stands outside a grocery store with volunteers, collecting food donations and cash; boxes of food pile up around them. He speaks with shoppers. In a separate scene, a minimum-wage worker counts higher pay at a register, showing one way to reduce hunger.

pages.text: Map the Meal Gap Food Insecurity Rates Use this map to compare rates of hunger within your state. Next, compare your state and region with others. Where is the percentage of food insecurity highest? Lowest? How Can People Help? People with a family garden can donate extra vegetables to a local food pantry—or plant an extra patch to donate! Kids can also donate part of their allowance and encourage others to do the same. Kids in Virginia came up with a plan to allow kids to donate a dime to the food bank each time they bought lunch. Create a plan at your school to support food banks.
pages.brief: A colorful map of the United States shows regions in different tones while people compare their state and region. Nearby, a family garden grows extra vegetables for a food pantry; schoolchildren drop dimes into a food-bank collection at lunch; and a school group plans support for food banks.

pages.text: Volunteers prepare meals at the Central Kitchen in Washington, D.C. Find out what the local food bank and charities need and at what time of year the need is greatest. Share what you find with friends, family, and neighbors. Write letters to Congress and to your state and local governments. Encourage your leaders to support programs that help make sure no child goes hungry. We have what it takes to make sure that children like Aaron never go hungry again. We just need the will to make it happen. Calling for Help If you or someone you know is hungry and needs help, call 1-866-3-HUNGRY or 1-877-8-HAMBRE (for Spanish). The National Hunger Hotline connects callers with emergency food providers, government assistance programs, and various social services.
pages.brief: Volunteers prepare meals at Central Kitchen in Washington, D.C. Families and neighbors share information, write letters to Congress and local governments, and call a hunger hotline for emergency food, government assistance, and social services. Friends and community members gather to support programs that help ensure no child goes hungry.

books.title: The Balloon Brothers
books.art_why: The book centers on named historical inventors, the Montgolfier brothers, so a cartoon retelling fits.

pages.text: The Balloon Brothers.
pages.brief: Two brothers stand side by side in front of a large balloon, presented as the central subjects of the opening page. The balloon is rounded and plain, and the brothers face forward together with calm expressions, alone against a simple background.

pages.text: Witnessing the Birth of a New Age An excited crowd of 130,000 gathered outside the Palace of Versailles (vair-SYE), just outside Paris, France, on the afternoon of September 19, 1783. They had come to see the flight of a large hot-air balloon built by two brothers. This was the moment of truth for Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier (mon-GOLF-yay). The king and queen of France watched from the palace courtyard. The beautiful silk-and-paper balloon was decorated with gold designs on a blue background. There was tension in the air. Three animals waited in the wicker basket suspended beneath the balloon. The unusual passengers were a sheep, a rooster, and a duck. These animals had been chosen as part of a scientific experiment. No one was sure what would happen to people who went up in a balloon. Since ducks often fly in the air, the brothers thought the duck would be fine. The rooster was included because it was also a bird, but one that didn’t fly very high. The sheep was thought to be similar to a person since it was a mammal that lived on the ground. The brothers were anxious to learn if these animals could go up in a balloon and come down unharmed.
pages.brief: An excited crowd of 130,000 fills the area outside the Palace of Versailles on a September afternoon. The king and queen watch from the palace courtyard. A large silk-and-paper balloon decorated with gold designs on a blue background waits above a wicker basket holding a sheep, a rooster, and a duck.

pages.text: The Montgolfiers filled their balloon with hot, smoky air from a fire burning in a pit. Shortly after 1:00 pm, the balloon was released. As the crowd looked on in wonder, it rose to a height of about 460 meters (1,500 ft.). Eight minutes later, it settled back to Earth 3.2 kilometers (2 mi.) away. The animals were just fine. People had long dreamed of being able to fly. That day had finally dawned. The way was now clear for people to fly into the clouds. And the Montgolfiers deserved much of the credit.
pages.brief: The Montgolfiers’ hot, smoky balloon rises from a fire pit before a watching crowd shortly after one o’clock. It climbs about 460 meters into the sky, then settles back to Earth 3.2 kilometers away. The sheep, rooster, and duck are shown safe in the basket after landing.

pages.text: Two Brothers with Big Ideas The Montgolfier brothers were part of a large family from a small town in southern France. Their father, Pierre Montgolfier, was a successful paper manufacturer. His factories were the official suppliers of stationery to the court of King Louis XVI. Joseph and Étienne took over the family business in the 1770s. Their successful business left them plenty of free time to pursue other interests. In his early forties, Joseph became intrigued with the possibility of flight. Since the 1600s, scientists had been exploring the possibility of making a lighter-than-air craft that would fly because of the principle of buoyancy. No one had yet figured out how to build such a vehicle, however. Buoyancy was first understood by the ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes (ark-uh-MEE- deez). It involves the density of an object—its weight for a given volume—compared with that of a fluid around it. ( Fluid in this sense can mean either a liquid or a gas.) If the density of an object is less than that of the fluid surrounding it, the object will experience an upward force. A cork floats because its density is less than that of water. A balloon filled with hot air rises because the.
pages.brief: Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier stand inside the family paper factory in a small town in southern France. Their father, Pierre, supervises stacks of stationery made for the court of King Louis XVI. Joseph looks thoughtful, pondering flight, buoyancy, and the ideas of the ancient Greek mathematician Archimedes.

pages.text: An object with a density greater than the fluid in which it is immersed will sink. Joseph suspected that a light gas contained within a lightweight enclosure might make flight possible. He read about such a gas that several past researchers had reported from their experiments. Scientists had known about this mysterious gas for many years. In 1766, English chemist Henry Cavendish identified the gas as an element. He gave it the name “ inflammable air” because it was highly explosive. French chemist Antoine Lavoisier (la-VWAH-zee-ay) renamed it “hydrogen.” Joseph filled small paper spheres with hydrogen and released them, but his experiments were disappointing. The spheres rose just a few meters before coming back down. Hydrogen atoms are so small that they passed right through the paper into the surrounding air. Elements and Atoms Elements are the chemical building blocks of the universe. Every element is made up of atoms. They are the smallest particles of substances that still have the properties of that substance. Oxygen and hydrogen are both elements. One oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms can combine to form one molecule of water.
pages.brief: Joseph Montgolfier stands outdoors releasing several small paper spheres filled with hydrogen. The spheres lift only a few meters before drifting back down. Nearby, simple visual symbols for oxygen and hydrogen atoms show the elements and atoms, with one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms forming a water molecule.

pages.text: Joseph looked for another way to build a flying machine. One day, he noticed that shirts drying over a smoky fire puffed upward. Like most people, he had often seen smoke rising from chimneys. This, he concluded, was the answer: smoke! In early 1783, the Montgolfiers began burning different materials to find ones that produced a lot of smoke. They found that a mixture of damp straw and chopped-up wool worked best. It also smelled terrible. But the smoke did indeed give buoyancy to any sort of light container. The brothers concluded that smoke must contain something unknown with a lifting property. They named this marvelous substance “Montgolfier gas.” Of course, there was no such substance. The lifting effect was caused by the hot air itself. When air gets heated, the molecules within it move around faster. This causes the air to expand and become less dense. When contained within a balloon, the lighter air makes the balloon rise. Joseph-Michel Montgolfier Jacques-Étienne Montgolfier.
pages.brief: Joseph Montgolfier watches shirts drying above a smoky fire as the cloth puffs upward. Later he and Étienne burn damp straw and chopped wool producing thick terrible-smelling smoke. The brothers stand beside the fire convinced the smoke contains a lifting substance they call Montgolfier gas.

pages.text: Constructing “Smoke-Powered” Balloons Without understanding the real science behind hot-air balloons, Joseph and Étienne continued to build and test new balloons. The brothers experimented by using different materials for the envelope, including silk, paper, and linen. As their work moved forward, they also made their balloons larger. The balloons rose ever higher into the air. The brothers’ experiments began to attract attention. A crowd filled the town square of a village in southern France on June 4, 1783, for the test of a large balloon made of cloth lined with paper. The crowd watched in amazement as the unoccupied balloon soared some 2,000 meters (6,560 ft.) into the sky. After a ten-minute flight, the balloon landed about 2 kilometers (1.2 mi.) away. Successful test flights such as this one launched a balloon craze in France. From “Ascending Machines” to Balloons The balloons that got the French people so excited were not called that until after the Montgolfiers made history. Earlier, they were called “ascending machines”—or later, “aerostats.” The name “balloon” was taken from the French word ballon, meaning “a large ball used in games.”
pages.brief: A crowd fills the town square of a village in southern France on June 4, 1783. The people watch in amazement as a large unoccupied balloon made of cloth lined with paper soars into the sky. After a ten-minute flight, the balloon lands about two kilometers away.

pages.text: A Balloon Rivalry The Montgolfier brothers asked the French Academy of Sciences to officially recognize their work. The academy withheld approval, however. It decided to wait in case someone else invented a better balloon. The Montgolfiers’ chief rival was a physicist named Jacques Charles (ZHOCK SHARL), who proposed building a hydrogen balloon. The Montgolfiers had long since given up on using hydrogen in favor of their hot-air balloons, but Charles saw great possibilities in this approach.
pages.brief: The Montgolfier brothers stand before members of the French Academy of Sciences, waiting for official recognition. The academy members hold back approval. Across the room, the physicist Jacques Charles studies a hydrogen balloon, signaling a rivalry between his approach and the Montgolfiers’ hot-air balloons.

pages.text: In July 1783, with the academy’s approval, Charles began work on his balloon. He was assisted by two brothers, Nicolas-Louis and Anne-Jean Robert (roh-BEAR), both professional engineers. The three constructed a small test balloon made of silk and coated with rubber to keep the hydrogen from escaping. In the meantime, King Louis invited the Montgolfier brothers to Paris. He wanted them to build a dazzling balloon that would display his glory to all of France. As the court favorites, the brothers now received government funding for their work. The two teams each wanted to be the first to launch a balloon with human passengers. The race was on. A Better Gas for Balloons: Helium Hydrogen is the lightest element—only one-fourteenth the weight of air. At first glance, it seems like the perfect gas for balloons. However, hydrogen is dangerous to work with because it catches fire and explodes easily. A much better gas for balloons is helium, the second-lightest element. Helium does not catch fire or explode. It is therefore completely safe for use in lighter-than-air flight. Helium was not discovered until the 1880s, so it was not available to balloon makers in the 1700s.
pages.brief: Jacques Charles and the engineer brothers Nicolas-Louis and Anne-Jean Robert work on a small silk balloon coated with rubber. In another part of Paris, King Louis invites the Montgolfier brothers to build a dazzling balloon for France. Both teams prepare for a race to launch the first human passengers.

pages.text: Soaring into the Blue On August 27, 1783, a large crowd gathered at a grassy area in Paris where the Eiffel Tower now stands. They had come to witness the launch of the Charles balloon. Among the onlookers was a famous American, Benjamin Franklin, who was serving as U.S. ambassador to France. The balloon was relatively small—about 4 meters (13 ft.) in diameter—with alternating red and white stripes. The Scientific Method The Montgolfier brothers and Jacques Charles aimed to answer a question: Is it possible to construct a lighter-than-air device that will enable people to fly? To answer that question, they followed a procedure known as the “scientific method.” The scientific method has several steps: • Do background research. • Test your hypothesis with observations or experiments. • Analyze your data and draw a conclusion. • Communicate your results.
pages.brief: A large crowd gathers on a grassy area in Paris where the Eiffel Tower now stands. Benjamin Franklin, the American ambassador to France, stands among the onlookers. A small balloon with alternating red and white stripes is shown ready for launch, about four meters in diameter.

pages.text: In the late afternoon, the unpiloted balloon was released. It rose quickly and flew northeast for less than an hour, landing about 15 kilometers (9 mi.) away in a small village. Terrified villagers attacked this strange monster from the heavens with their pitchforks. Now it was the Montgolfiers’ turn to wow Paris. On September 19, they launched their test balloon with its animal passengers at Versailles. When the animals landed safely, the time for a human trial was finally at hand. Since the flight would be very dangerous, the king felt it should be done by a pair of prisoners who had been sentenced to death. However, a science teacher and a soldier volunteered. Their historic flight took place on November 21, this time from the outskirts of Paris. The balloon towered 23 meters (75 ft.) high. It was covered with various golden designs in honor of the king and royal family. With the science teacher and the soldier aboard, the balloon rose into the air. Twenty-five minutes later, it landed about 8 kilometers (5 mi.) away, settling between a pair of windmills outside the city. The two men were hailed as heroes.
pages.brief: Villagers with pitchforks attack a strange balloon that lands in their village. Later a huge decorated balloon rises from the outskirts of Paris with a science teacher and a soldier aboard. It floats for twenty-five minutes and settles between two windmills outside the city as the men are hailed as heroes.

pages.text: Benjamin Franklin observed the historic flight. Asked by another spectator what this balloon was good for, he reportedly answered, “What good is a newborn baby?” On December 1, just ten days after the Montgolfiers’ triumph, Jacques Charles and Nicolas-Louis Robert made the first human ascent in a hydrogen balloon. Taking off from the Tuileries (TWEE-luh-reez) Garden in Paris, they flew for more than two hours. They came down in a town about 36 kilometers (22 mi.) away. In the following years, the Montgolfiers launched several more balloons. The brothers were honored by the French Academy of Sciences, and their father, Pierre, was made a nobleman by King Louis.
pages.brief: Benjamin Franklin stands among spectators after the Montgolfier flight and speaks to another onlooker. Ten days later Jacques Charles and Nicolas-Louis Robert lift off in a hydrogen balloon from the Tuileries Garden in Paris. The balloon carries them for more than two hours before landing in a town about thirty-six kilometers away.

pages.text: The Legacy of Lighter-Than-Air Flight The passion for ballooning soon spread throughout Europe. It was not long, however, before the risks involved became clear. In June 1785, two men were killed while attempting to fly across the English Channel in a balloon. Despite the risks, pioneers continued to develop balloon designs long after the balloon craze of the late 1700s had ended. In the 1800s, lighter-than-air vehicles were given rudders and motorized propellers. By the 1930s, huge airships were flying passengers back and forth across the Atlantic Ocean. The golden age of airships ended abruptly when the German airship Hindenburg caught fire and crashed while landing in New Jersey in 1937. Today, airships are mostly used for advertising. They can often be seen flying above open-air stadiums during large sporting events. Gas balloons are mostly used for gathering weather data, while hot-air balloons are mostly used for recreation. Many areas hold festivals each year in which hundreds of colorful hot-air balloons fill the sky. These events can make it appear as though balloon mania never ended.
pages.brief: A colorful hot-air balloon festival fills the sky with many balloons. In the background, a huge 1930s airship flies over the Atlantic, while a modern airship floats above an open-air stadium. A weather balloon rises with instruments, and hundreds of festival balloons drift overhead.

books.title: Canada
books.art_why: Modern Canada, its people, wildlife, cities and celebrations can all be photographed.

pages.text: Canada Where Is It? Canada is the northernmost country in mainland North America and the second-largest country on Earth. Large countries usually have many neighbors, but Canada has only one—the United States. The border between them is about 8,893 kilometers (5,525 mi.) long, making it the longest border in the world between two countries. Canada’s national motto is “From sea to sea” because the country stretches from the Pacific Ocean in the west all the way to the Atlantic Ocean in the east and the Arctic Ocean to the north.
pages.brief: Canada’s vast northern landmass sits in North America, with the Pacific Ocean to the west, the Atlantic to the east and the Arctic to the north. Along its long southern edge it meets only the United States, stretching from sea to sea.

pages.text: Canada’s 202,080-kilometer (125,566 mi.) coastline encircles not only the vast mainland but over 52,000 islands as well. It is by far the world’s longest national coastline. Stretched out, it could circle the globe five times. Canada consists of ten provinces and three territories, each with its own democratically elected legislature. Canadians also elect representatives to send to their Parliament in Ottawa, the country’s capital. There is a lot to see in Ottawa, and a good place to start is the observation deck of the 92-meter (302 ft.) Peace Tower. From there, visitors can see people boating on the Ottawa River or hiking in the city’s many parks. In the winter they can also see people ice-skating to work on the world’s largest skating area, the Rideau Canal. The city also boasts 267 other outdoor rinks. From the tower, they can view the stately Parliament buildings, museums, hotels, and theaters along with signs and advertisements in Arabic, Spanish, and Chinese. Ottawans skate on the 7.8-kilometer (4.8 mi.) Rideau Canal with the Peace Tower in the background.
pages.brief: From the Peace Tower observation deck in Ottawa, visitors look out over the Ottawa River, city parks, Parliament buildings, museums, hotels and theaters. Below, people boat on the river, hike in parks, and in winter skate along the frozen Rideau Canal.

pages.text: People With one in every five people born in other countries, Canada is diverse. Most Canadians, however, do not think of themselves as a “melting pot,” in which different cultures blend together. Instead, many think of Canada as a “mosaic,” in which immigrants retain their culture and strengthen the nation through diversity. Some of the first European settlers in the land we now call Canada were from France and England. Before Canada became a country, these people settled separate colonies that were often at war with each other. They had different languages and religions, but eventually the groups learned to get along. Because of this, Canada has two official languages: French and English. France and Britain helped build the nation of Canada on the ancestral lands of Indigenous peoples who had been living in the area for thousands of years. Today, less than five percent of Canadians are Indigenous peoples, with most belonging to three groups: First Nations, the Inuit, and the Métis (may-TEE). First Nations people and Métis live throughout the country, and the Inuit continue to live in the far north. Life in Indigenous communities has changed over the years, but many who live in them continue to.
pages.brief: A diverse group of Canadians of many backgrounds appears together, reflecting French, English, First Nations, Inuit and Métis heritage. Families and communities represent immigrant cultures from around the world, while Indigenous people maintain traditional languages, history and culture across the country.

pages.text: For example, they teach about their history and learn to speak Indigenous languages. Inuit children play at school. Through the years, many immigrants came from Germany and other European countries, as well as China, India, the Americas, and the Middle East. While richly diverse, this vast country is sparsely populated. Probably due to better farmland and access to waterways, most of its population—90 percent, by some estimates—lives within 160 kilometers (100 mi.) of the country’s southern border. Many urban Canadians work in service industries such as tourism, transportation, or banking. Away from the cities, some people work to extract Canada’s many resources such as oil, copper, and gold. Others farm the land or cut timber from the vast forests that blanket the country. Resources and manufactured goods are sold as far away as China, but most are traded across the border with the United States.
pages.brief: Inuit children play at school in the north. Elsewhere, Canadians work in tourism, transportation and banking, or extract oil, copper and gold; others farm and cut timber. Many people live near the southern border, and goods are traded with the United States and China.

pages.text: Regions of Canada Land Canada holds majestic mountains, vast plains, lakes, and endless forests. Parts of the north have ice and snow all year. Geographers divide the country into seven landform regions. In the east is the Appalachian region, with rolling forested hills dotted by farms. Waterways define another region, the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence lowlands. It is the smallest region but an important one, known as “Canada’s heartland.” About half of all Canadians live in large cities in this region.
pages.brief: Forested Appalachian hills dotted with farms lie in the east, while the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence lowlands form Canada’s small heartland. There, large cities hold about half of all Canadians. Elsewhere lie majestic mountains, vast plains, lakes, endless forests, and northern ice and snow.

pages.text: The forested Canadian Shield is a huge region that wraps around Hudson Bay. Long ago, glaciers scraped the area clean of soil and exposed the rocky surface. When the glaciers melted, thousands of lakes formed. Within this wet region lies a cold, marshy area known as the Hudson Bay lowlands. Tourists camp, hike, and canoe in parks in the Cordillera region. The interior plains are grasslands in the south and forests in the north. Today the grasslands are used for raising livestock and growing grains. In the far west is the Cordillera region with great mountain chains. The highest are the Rocky Mountains, with snow-covered peaks reaching 3,954 meters (13,000 ft.). In between the mountains are fertile valleys where farmers grow fruit and other crops. To the north of all these regions and their forests lies the Arctic tundra, where freezing temperatures prevent any trees from growing. Niagara Falls In the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence lowlands, water plunges down 57 meters (188 ft.) at Niagara Falls. The part of the falls in Canada—Horseshoe Falls—is 670 meters (2,200 ft.) long.
pages.brief: The rocky Canadian Shield wraps around Hudson Bay, dotted with lakes and edged by cold marshes. Tourists camp, hike and canoe in Cordillera parks. Interior plains support livestock and grain; Rocky Mountain peaks rise above fertile fruit valleys. Treeless Arctic tundra lies far north, and Niagara Falls plunges into the Great Lakes lowlands.

pages.text: Animals In the Arctic, a land of ice and snow, animals tend to be white in color. Their camouflage helps them survive. Polar bears have black skin, but their fur looks snow white. Harp seal pups are hard to see because they, too, are white. The arctic fox has a white coat in winter but sheds it for a brown one when the snow melts. Beluga whales are white, as are birds such as the tundra swan. In the forests south of the Arctic, moose, beaver, black bears, and wolves all blend in with the colors of the forest floor. The small animals of the grassy plains, such as ground squirrels and pocket gophers, dig underground tunnels to live in and raise their young. The best way to survive in the mountains is to be sure-footed. In the Rocky Mountains, goats and bighorn sheep have hooves that are great for running, jumping, and rock climbing.
pages.brief: White polar bears, harp seal pups, arctic foxes, beluga whales and tundra swans blend into Arctic snow and ice. In southern forests, moose, beaver, black bears and wolves match the forest floor. Ground squirrels and pocket gophers dig tunnels on the plains, while mountain goats and bighorn sheep climb rocky slopes.

pages.text: All around Canada are animals that survive the cold winter and lack of food by migrating. Many birds migrate, but so do some fish, whales, turtles, grazing animals, and even dragonflies. Huge herds of grazing caribou move hundreds of miles from one part of Canada to another. Other animals go farther south, leaving Canada for a warmer climate. The champions for long-distance migration are the small but swift arctic terns. They fly from their breeding grounds in the Arctic all the way to Antarctica, a forty-day journey of some 35,500 kilometers (22,060 mi.). Then, six months later, they fly all the way back again. Canadian Wildlife Rocky Mountain goat Canadians share their huge homeland with countless species of birds, fish, mammals, and plants. The country works to protect the land, air, and water for people as well as the wildlife that lives there. arctic tern caribou humpback whale.
pages.brief: Caribou herds travel hundreds of miles across Canada, while birds, fish, whales, turtles and dragonflies migrate too. Arctic terns fly from the Arctic to Antarctica and back, a journey of about 35,500 kilometers. A Rocky Mountain goat, arctic tern, caribou and humpback whale represent Canadian wildlife protected along with land, air and water.

pages.text: History For many thousands of years, what is now Canada was home to self-governing First Nations people and the Inuit. The first Europeans to arrive were the Icelandic Vikings who sailed from Greenland more than one thousand years ago. Survival was difficult, and they eventually left. In 1497, British explorer John Cabot arrived in what today is eastern Canada and claimed land for England. Later, French explorers also claimed lands. The French and English found two resources that helped make money back in Europe: codfish and fur. More traders came and colonies developed. The foreign nations formed alliances with the First Nations people and a network to sell beaver pelts. During the 1400s to 1700s, France and England were often at war, as were their colonies. Canadian lands were handed from winner to winner until Great Britain eventually maintained control. As the colonies grew, they displaced First Nations people and took over their lands. The growing colonies began to desire more independence. In 1867, Britain made the colonies a dominion, with its democratic government’s capital in Ottawa. In 1931, Canada became fully independent when it became part of the British Commonwealth of Nations.
pages.brief: First Nations people and Inuit live across the land for thousands of years. Viking sailors arrive from Greenland; John Cabot claims eastern land for England; French explorers follow. Codfish and beaver fur draw traders and colonies. France and England fight, Britain takes control, colonies displace Indigenous peoples, and in 1867 Canada becomes a dominion.

pages.text: Canada Day Calgary Stampede Quebec Winter Carnival Celebrations Canada Day, the nation’s birthday, is on July 1. People celebrate with parades, barbecues, and fireworks. The largest celebration is held in Ottawa. The Calgary Stampede celebrates Canada’s Old West with bull riding, barrel racing, steer wrestling, bronc riding—even chuck wagon racing. Called “The greatest outdoor show on Earth,” it attracts about a million visitors. Canadians have winter festivals, too, with dogsled races, skiing, and ice-skating. The Quebec Winter Carnival is the largest such festival in the world. There you can enjoy the snow-sculpture contest, visit an ice castle, and even stay in a hotel made of ice and snow that is built every winter and melts away every summer.
pages.brief: Canada Day parades, barbecues and fireworks fill Ottawa on July 1. The Calgary Stampede shows bronc riding, bull riding, barrel racing, steer wrestling and chuck wagon racing. At the Quebec Winter Carnival, visitors see snow sculptures, an ice castle and a hotel built of ice and snow that melts each summer.

pages.text: Conclusion Canada, one of the largest countries on Earth, includes regions of towering mountains, rolling plains, dense forests, frozen tundra, and endless rocky shores. Each region has its own plants, animals, resources, and people. The people who live there may speak French, English, or one of many other languages, but they are all Canadian and proud of their cultural mosaic. Ice hockey originated in Canada and is the country’s national sport (left). People gather for a public event in Ottawa (top). Children from Nunavik, an Inuit village, go to hockey practice (bottom).
pages.brief: Towering mountains, rolling plains, dense forests, frozen tundra and rocky shores show Canada’s varied regions. People speak French, English and many other languages as one cultural mosaic. Children from Nunavik, an Inuit village, go to hockey practice, while people gather for a public event in Ottawa. Ice hockey, Canada’s national sport, began there.

pages.brief: Canada’s landmass fills a broad northern landscape, with Ottawa as its capital city. The country’s population is 38 million people, its land area is 9,984,670 square kilometers, English and French are official languages, and the Canadian dollar is used.

books.title: Jackie Robinson
books.art_why: A named historical person is best shown as a cartoon biography.

pages.text: Introduction The Ebbets Field stands were full on April 15, 1947. Brooklyn Dodger Jackie Robinson picked up his baseball bat. The crowd watched as the only African American in Major League Baseball (MLB) walked to the plate. Insults rang out from the other team’s dugout. The Dodgers’ general manager, Branch Rickey, had warned him this would happen. The words hurt, but Robinson had promised not to respond. He would play ball and let his bat do the talking. Many people took note of the great courage Jackie Robinson showed that day. His courage would make him a baseball legend and a champion for equal rights.
pages.brief: Show Jackie Robinson in a Brooklyn Dodgers uniform at Ebbets Field, holding his baseball bat and walking toward the plate as a full crowd watches. Opposing players shout insults from their dugout; Robinson stays calm and determined, remembering Branch Rickey’s warning and his promise not to respond.

pages.text: The Early Years Jack Roosevelt Robinson was born on January 31, 1919, the youngest of five children in a poor Georgia family. The Robinson family moved to California when Jackie was a boy. There, he became known as a talented athlete in not one but several sports.
pages.brief: Show young Jack Roosevelt Robinson as the youngest of five children in a poor Georgia family. Then show the Robinson family moving to California, where Jackie as a boy becomes known as a talented athlete in several sports, with him trying different sports.

pages.text: Jackie Robinson attended the University of California at Los Angeles (UCLA). He was a star on the school’s football, track, basketball, and baseball teams. Robinson was the first student in the school’s history to win special awards in four sports in a single year. In spite of this success, Robinson did not graduate from UCLA. The Robinsons had little money. He left school in 1941 to help support his family.
pages.brief: Show Jackie Robinson at UCLA as a star on the football, track, basketball, and baseball teams. Include him winning special awards in four sports in a single year. Then show him leaving school in 1941 because the Robinsons had little money and he wanted to help support his family.

pages.text: Taking a Stand Robinson played semiprofessional football after college. Then, in December 1941, the United States entered World War II. Like many young men at the time, Robinson was called up to serve in the U.S. Army. Robinson served at Fort Hood, Texas. One day in 1944, he and a group of soldiers got on an army bus. The bus was segregated —white soldiers sat in the front and black soldiers in the back. Yet Robinson knew he was no less a soldier than the white men. He refused an order to move to the back of the bus. For this, he was arrested. The army wanted to punish Robinson, but many people defended him. He was a good soldier who had only stood up for what was right. In the end, he was found not guilty.
pages.brief: Show Jackie Robinson in a U.S. Army uniform at Fort Hood, Texas, boarding an army bus with other soldiers. White soldiers sit in front and black soldiers in back; Robinson refuses an order to move to the back. Show him arrested, then defended by many people and found not guilty.

pages.text: You’re Hired! After his time in the army, Robinson worked at a Texas college coaching basketball. In 1945, he received a letter from the Kansas City Monarchs, a professional baseball team. They offered Robinson a contract to play with them for four hundred dollars a month. The Monarchs were part of the Negro Leagues. At that time, baseball was segregated. White and black athletes played in separate leagues. Robinson signed on to play for the Monarchs, thinking it might be a way to someday get into the all-white major leagues.
pages.brief: Show Jackie Robinson coaching basketball at a Texas college after his army service. Then show him receiving a letter from the Kansas City Monarchs in 1945, offering a contract for four hundred dollars a month. Show him signing with the Negro Leagues team and hoping it may lead to the all-white major leagues.

pages.text: Robinson showed everyone he was a skilled player. He caught the eye of Branch Rickey, general manager of the Brooklyn Dodgers. Rickey felt that there should not be separate baseball leagues based on race. Instead, as he put it, professional baseball should be “color-blind.” He wanted the Dodgers to sign a player from the Negro Leagues, a first attempt to integrate major league baseball. Rickey knew that this player would not only have to be a great athlete. He would also have to show strong character in the face of abuse. In 1945, Rickey met with Robinson. Rickey offered to hire him on one condition: Robinson could not respond to any prejudice against him because of his race.
pages.brief: Show Jackie Robinson as a skilled player catching the eye of Branch Rickey, general manager of the Brooklyn Dodgers. Show Rickey meeting Robinson in 1945 and offering to hire him on one condition: Robinson cannot respond to prejudice because of his race. Rickey wants professional baseball to be color-blind.

pages.text: A Team of Two A Team of Two Robinson was at first very surprised. How could this man expect him to not fight back against prejudice? Rickey explained that the best way to fight back would be to play well. Robinson would show just how good he was.
pages.brief: Show Jackie Robinson looking very surprised as Branch Rickey explains his idea. Robinson wonders how he can be expected not to fight back against prejudice. Rickey tells him the best way to fight back is to play well, so Robinson can show just how good he is.

pages.text: Number 42 Takes the Field On October 23, 1945, Jackie Robinson signed on to play for the Dodgers’ minor league team. Spring training for the team was held in Florida. There, Robinson had a taste of what he would face as MLB’s first African American player. He could not stay in the same hotels as the rest of the team. Other minor league teams refused to play because of Robinson. Opposing pitchers threw the ball at him. Even some of his teammates didn’t want to play with him. Punishing Pitches Punishing Pitches.
pages.brief: Show Jackie Robinson signing with the Dodgers’ minor league team on October 23, 1945. In Florida spring training, show the abuse he faces: separate hotels from teammates, other minor league teams refusing to play, opposing pitchers throwing at him, and some teammates not wanting to play with him.

pages.text: None of this abuse stopped Robinson. He played well enough to move up to the Dodgers the next year. Wearing number 42, Jackie Robinson took the field on April 15, 1947, before a crowd of more than twenty-six thousand spectators. The Dodgers earned a victory that day, not only over the Boston Braves but also over prejudice against African Americans.
pages.brief: Show Jackie Robinson wearing number 42 taking the field for the Dodgers on April 15, 1947, before more than twenty-six thousand spectators. The abuse has not stopped him; he has moved up from the minors. Show the Dodgers earning a victory over the Boston Braves and over prejudice against African Americans.

pages.text: Another Great Steal Another Great Steal Robinson also went on to have a great career. He was chosen Rookie of the Year in 1947. In 1949, he was voted Most Valuable Player in the league. Robinson was a fast runner who led the league in stolen bases. He helped the Dodgers win six league championships and a World Series victory. In 1962, he became the first African American to enter the Baseball Hall of Fame.
pages.brief: Show Jackie Robinson in action as a fast runner stealing bases for the Dodgers. Include his Rookie of the Year award in 1947 and Most Valuable Player award in 1949, his league-leading stolen bases, six league championships, a World Series victory, and his 1962 entry into the Baseball Hall of Fame.

pages.text: His Number, His Day His Number, His Day.
pages.brief: Show Jackie Robinson being honored for his number and for a special day: a respectful portrait of Robinson in a Dodgers uniform, with his number 42 displayed prominently as the focus of the tribute and a calm, celebratory mood.

pages.text: Beyond Baseball After retiring from baseball in 1957, Robinson joined the coffee maker and fast-food chain Chock Full o’ Nuts. In doing so, he became the first black vice president of a U.S. national company. In 1964, he cofounded the Freedom National Bank, which grew to become one of the largest black-owned banks in the United States. Six years later, he launched a construction company. Robinson also became a civil rights leader who continued to work for equality for all people. He died in 1972 from heart problems and diabetes complications. Today in the United States, people of color have more opportunities in the world of sports than ever before. We all have Number 42 to thank for that.
pages.brief: Show Jackie Robinson after baseball as a business leader at Chock Full o’ Nuts, then cofounding Freedom National Bank and launching a construction company. Include him as a civil rights leader working for equality, and a final image of young athletes of color today in sports. Mark his death in 1972 from heart problems and diabetes complications.

books.title: Rainforests
books.art_why: Rainforests, their animals, and the Huli people exist today, so photographs are possible.

pages.text: Scarlet macaws fill the sky with color in Peru. A Place of Wonder Picture a forest so tall that the trees seem to touch the sky. Beneath these giants, a dense weave of leaves and branches shades the layers below. Squawking birds flash brilliant colors as monkeys scramble from branch to branch, filling the air with their howls. Snakes slither silently up tree trunks, hiding in wait for prey. Far below on the dark, damp forest floor, creatures scurry and creep through mushrooms, dead leaves, and fallen fruit. When nighttime arrives, larger animals will come out to hunt. Water is everywhere: it falls from the sky, drips from leaves, pools on the ground, and flows downhill into streams. Even the air is thick with moisture. All of nature celebrates the life-giving power of water and the abundant growth it supports. This is a rainforest—a place of astonishing beauty and wonder.
pages.brief: Scarlet macaws fill the sky with color above a tall Peruvian rainforest. Dense leaves and branches shade the layers below, where monkeys scramble and squawking birds flash bright colors. Snakes slither up tree trunks. On the dark, damp forest floor, creatures creep through mushrooms, dead leaves, and fallen fruit. Water drips, pools, and flows into streams.

pages.text: The Rainforest Biome Different types of environments cover Earth’s surface. These regions and the communities of plants and animals that live there are called biomes. Deserts, oceans, grasslands, and tundra are examples of biomes. So are rainforests. Many factors play a part in creating Earth’s biomes. Two important ones are latitude—how far a location is from the equator—and elevation, or height above sea level. Both help determine how warm or cool a place is. Climate, land, and water are also important building blocks of biomes, as are plants and animals. Rainforests are forests with very high rainfall. They receive more rain than any other biome and support by far the greatest diversity of plants and animals on Earth. Rainforests are found on every continent except Antarctica. There are two main types. More than twenty thousand kinds of orchids live in tropical rainforests. Flying frogs have webbed feet to help them glide from branch to branch.
pages.brief: An overview of Earth's biomes shows rainforests alongside deserts, oceans, grasslands, and tundra. In a lush rainforest, many orchids bloom and a flying frog glides from branch to branch with webbed feet. Rainforests receive more rain than any other biome and support great diversity.

pages.text: Earth’s Rainforest Regions Tropical rainforests are mainly located in the tropical zones, which are between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn. These zones are closest to the equator and receive the most direct sunlight. They also receive about the same amount of sunlight throughout the year. South America’s Amazon rainforest is the largest and best-known tropical rainforest. Others are found in Central America and parts of Africa, southern Asia, and Australia. Almost all rainforests are tropical rainforests. Temperate rainforests are mainly located along coasts in cool temperate regions farther from the equator. In North America, temperate rainforests stretch from Alaska to Oregon. They are also found along the coast of Chile, in Norway and the United Kingdom, and in parts of eastern Russia, Japan, Australia, and New Zealand.
pages.brief: A globe view shows tropical rainforests near the equator between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn, including the Amazon, Central America, Africa, southern Asia, and Australia. Farther from the equator, temperate rainforests stretch along coasts from Alaska to Oregon, Chile, Norway, the United Kingdom, eastern Russia, Japan, Australia, and New Zealand.

pages.text: Tropical Rainforests Climate and Soil Tropical rainforests are generally warm and humid year-round. As a rule, average temperatures range from about 20° to 30°C (68°–86°F), and humidity is often 80 percent or higher throughout the year. Yearly rainfall is at least 200 centimeters (80 in.) and can reach 1,000 centimeters (400 in.). Rainfall can be very heavy, as much as 5 centimeters (2 in.) in an hour. Most tropical rainforests lack distinct rainy and dry seasons. Soils in tropical rainforests are rarely rich. This is in part because the plants themselves contain so many nutrients that not much is left in the soil. Also, rainforest soil is often waterlogged because rainfall is almost always greater than the rate at which water evaporates. Water flows downhill into rivers and streams, carrying nutrients with it. The Importance of Rainforests During photosynthesis, plants produce oxygen as a waste product. Because the rate of photosynthesis is so high in rainforests, this biome produces most of Earth’s oxygen, which humans and other animals depend on for our survival. Rainforests also absorb carbon dioxide, which keeps this gas from entering Earth’s atmosphere and adding to global warming. These forests provide homes for enormous numbers of life-forms. The list of ways that rainforests benefit the environment goes on and on.
pages.brief: Warm, humid tropical rainforest air surrounds dense green plants as heavy rain falls. Water soaks the waterlogged soil and flows downhill into streams and rivers, carrying nutrients away. The lush plants grow rapidly in constant warmth and moisture, producing oxygen and absorbing carbon dioxide while supporting countless forms of life.

pages.text: Tropical rainforests have the highest biodiversity of any biome. Even though they cover only about 7 percent of Earth’s surface, they contain more than half of the planet’s plants and animals. This is a result of several factors. The almost-constant sunlight and warm temperatures support photosynthesis, which produces food for not only plants but also the animals they feed, either directly or indirectly. The availability of water, which all living things require, is another factor. In addition, tropical rainforests offer many and diverse kinds of food and shelter. This biome contains more than two-thirds of all known plant species, and new animal species are discovered every year. Lesulas live in Central Africa. They were unknown to scientists until 2007. Plants Plants in tropical rainforests grow in four layers. The emergent layer contains the tallest trees, which can grow to over 60 meters (200 ft.) in height. Because they rise above the other trees, they receive the most sun, rain, and wind. The heavy exposure to sunlight causes their water to evaporate. These trees have adaptations to survive in dry conditions, including small, waxy leaves.
pages.brief: Deep in a Central African rainforest, a lesula lives among dense plants beneath towering emergent trees more than sixty meters tall. These tallest trees rise above the others, receiving the most sun, rain, and wind. Their small, waxy leaves help them survive dry conditions, while the forest below supports extraordinary biodiversity.

pages.text: The canopy, roughly 18–45 meters (60–125 ft.) in height, is where most plants and animals live. Trees and vines grow so densely that they shade the layers below. Most flowers and fruit grow in the canopy. It also contains many epiphytes (EH-puh-fytes), or “air plants,” which live on other plants for support. Epiphytes get nutrients from rain and humidity in the air rather than from soil. In rainforests, they often grow on trees in order to reach sunlight. Tropical Rainforest Layers top of emergent layer top of canopy top of understory forest floor.
pages.brief: In the dense canopy, trees and vines weave together and shade the lower layers. Flowers and fruit grow among the branches. Epiphytes, or air plants, cling to trees for support, taking nutrients from rain and humid air rather than soil as they reach toward the sunlight.

pages.text: The understory receives much less sunlight than higher layers—only about 2 to 15 percent. Plants here have adaptations to survive in shade, including large, wide leaves to capture sunlight for photosynthesis. The understory also contains young trees as well as many climbing plants that seek sunlight. Mosses, algae, and fungi often grow on understory plants as well. The forest floor, or ground level, is dark and humid, receiving only about 2 percent of sunlight. The almost complete lack of sunlight prevents most plants from growing in this layer. It contains decomposing leaves and fallen trees, fruit, and branches. Decomposition supports rainforest food chains in important ways. Mosses, ferns, ginger, mushrooms, and fungi are also common here. Animals Animals vary widely from one tropical rainforest to another. However, certain adaptations are common among them. Many have adaptations for living in trees, including flying, climbing, leaping, and gliding. Communicating with loud calls is common since the dense trees block visibility. Bright colors help many birds spot each other. Other rainforest animals don’t want to be spotted; instead, they use camouflage to hide from predators.
pages.brief: In the shaded understory, young trees and climbing plants reach upward, their large, wide leaves capturing the little sunlight that filters down. Mosses, algae, and fungi coat plants. On the dark, humid forest floor, mushrooms and ferns grow among decomposing leaves, fallen trees, fruit, and branches.

pages.text: Because of the abundance of animals, competition for food is widespread. Some animals deal with this by having specialized diets or body parts. For example, a toucan’s huge, long bill allows it to reach fruit growing on branches too thin to support its weight. Many rainforest animals are active at night. This adaptation helps them avoid daytime heat and also reduces competition for food. Grasping and Gliding Some canopy animals have developed special adaptations to get across large spaces between branches. Especially in Central and South America, some have a grasping, or prehensile, tail that can be used like a fifth limb. For example, spider and howler monkeys use this body part when scrambling from branch to branch high above the ground. In Asia, some animals glide to cross gaps in the canopy. Flying squirrels, flying geckos, and several other animals have this adaptation. They don’t actually fly; instead, they soar from higher to lower branches using skin flaps around their body that catch air somewhat like a parachute. A flying squirrel glides from one tree to another at night.
pages.brief: A toucan stretches its huge, long bill to reach fruit on a thin branch. A spider monkey scrambles high above the ground, using its grasping tail like a fifth limb. At night, a flying squirrel glides from one tree to another, its skin flaps catching the air like a parachute.

pages.text: The algae growing on a sloth’s fur helps it blend in with green plants. Bats, butterflies, small monkeys, eagles, and other birds live in the emergent layer. The canopy is home to the most animals, including some that spend their entire life there. Sloths, toucans, and howler and spider monkeys are found in Central and South America. Orangutans live in Southeast Asia, and sugar gliders live in Australia and parts of Indonesia. Parrots live in all rainforest canopies. Frogs, salamanders, snakes, lizards, birds, and insects are found in the understory, and ground-dwelling animals live on the forest floor. Tapirs, deer, peccaries, boars, and capybaras live in the Amazon. Asian rainforests have elephants and tigers. Elephants are also found in African rainforests, as are gorillas and pygmy hippos. All rainforests except those in Australia have some kind of cat, such as tigers, jaguars, or leopards, and all but those in the Americas have crocodiles. Rainforests around the world have an abundance of insects, spiders, and earthworms.
pages.brief: High in the canopy, a sloth's fur is tinted green by algae, helping it blend with leaves. Toucans and howler monkeys share the branches. Below, frogs, snakes, and insects live in the understory, while tapirs and capybaras move on the forest floor.

pages.text: Temperate Rainforests Temperate rainforests receive less rain than tropical rainforests, but still quite a lot—150 to 500 centimeters (60–200 in.) yearly. Moisture from coastal fog adds another 18 to 30 centimeters (7–12 in.) of precipitation each year. Mild winters, cool summers, and rainfall throughout the year are typical, although summers tend to be drier. Plants grow in three layers instead of four, with no emergent layer. The tallest canopy trees grow to roughly 90 meters (300 ft.) tall. Temperate rainforests have far fewer species of trees and other plants than tropical rainforests. In the Northern Hemisphere, evergreens with needle-shaped leaves are common in the canopy. Mosses and deciduous shrubs—shrubs that drop their leaves in winter—grow in the understory. In the Southern Hemisphere, broadleaf evergreens grow in the canopy, and evergreen and deciduous shrubs and trees are found in the understory. Epiphytes are generally limited to ferns and mosses. Temperate rainforests have many animals living on the forest floor, where they are sheltered from rain and wind. Animals include tree frogs, squirrels, raccoons, deer, black bears, bobcats, wolves, mountain lions, and a variety of insects and spiders. Redwood trees and ferns grow in the temperate rainforest of Northern California. Some redwoods live up to two thousand years.
pages.brief: In a temperate rainforest in Northern California, towering redwood trees rise above ferns and mosses. Cool, moist air and coastal fog surround the forest. Squirrels, deer, black bears, bobcats, wolves, mountain lions, tree frogs, insects, and spiders find shelter on the forest floor.

pages.text: The Huli people of Papua New Guinea’s rainforests are known for their headgear and face painting. There are about ninety thousand Huli today. People in Rainforests Native peoples have lived in rainforests for thousands of years, and an estimated fifty million still live there. The changes caused by European settlers have had a significant impact on most traditional lifestyles, and some groups no longer exist. The largest number of remaining Native peoples live in the Amazon rainforest. In recent years, many people have moved to rainforests and cleared land of trees to start small farms and ranches. Logging and mining have also caused significant areas of forest to be cleared. Tropical rainforests provide a vast number of resources for modern life, including food, spices, wood, medicines, and minerals. Tourism in rainforests, especially in the Amazon, is very popular because of the diversity of wildlife.
pages.brief: Huli people of Papua New Guinea stand among rainforest plants, wearing distinctive headgear and face painting. Nearby, forest land has been cleared for a small farm and ranch, with cut trees and exposed ground. The scene reflects how logging, mining, farming, and ranching have changed areas of rainforest.

pages.text: A Celebration of Abundance Life exists almost everywhere on Earth— from Antarctica to the Sahara desert and from the ocean floor to Mount Everest. However, conditions in many places present challenges for living things. Those places may be cold for much or all of the year, or they may lack shelter or a steady water supply. Rainforests are different—nothing is lacking. They offer so much water, warmth, and shelter that life erupts in abundance. To get a sense of this biome’s biodiversity, think about this: more kinds of ants live on a single bush in the Amazon rainforest than in the entire United Kingdom. Rainforests are among Earth’s most precious jewels, where nature shines in all its glory. A cave opening frames a misty view of the tropical rainforest in Borneo, a large island in Southeast Asia.
pages.brief: A cave opening frames a misty view of a tropical rainforest in Borneo. Lush green plants fill the landscape, where water, warmth, and shelter support abundant life. On a single bush in the Amazon, many kinds of ants crawl among the leaves, illustrating the rainforest's extraordinary biodiversity.

books.title: Deserts
books.art_why: Deserts, their plants, animals, and people exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Spring wildflowers carpet the Mojave Desert in Southern California. Space and Stillness If you search online for descriptions of deserts, you’re likely to come across phrases like “empty wasteland” and “barren, desolate landscape.” Deserts have a reputation for being harsh, unpleasant places where life hangs by a thread and no one in their right mind would dare to go. If you talk to people who love deserts, however, you’ll hear a different story. To them, deserts are places of stillness and beauty where you can hear yourself think and see for miles in every direction. They’re also places with living things that have developed fascinating ways to survive where water is rare and precious.
pages.brief: Spring wildflowers carpet the Mojave Desert in Southern California, spreading color across open ground. The desert stretches wide and still, with distant horizons and room to see for miles. Small desert plants and animals live among the flowers, adapted to survive where water is rare and precious.

pages.text: The Desert Biome Different types of environments cover Earth’s surface. These regions and the communities of plants and animals that live there are called biomes. Grasslands, rainforests, and oceans are examples of biomes. So are deserts. Many factors play a part in creating Earth’s biomes. Two important ones are latitude—how far a location is from the equator—and elevation, or height above sea level. Both help determine how warm or cool a place is. Climate, land, and water are also important building blocks of biomes, as are plants and animals. People often think of deserts as hot, empty places with endless miles of sand. This description fits some deserts but not others. The defining trait of deserts is not heat but rather low rainfall. As a rule, deserts receive less than 25 centimeters (10 in.) of rainfall each year. The Sahara in northern Africa is the largest hot desert in the world. Its landscape is constantly reshaped by winds.
pages.brief: Wind reshapes the Sahara in northern Africa, the largest hot desert, moving sand across a vast landscape. Around it, different biomes such as grasslands, rainforests, and oceans cover Earth's surface. Latitude, elevation, climate, land, water, plants, and animals all help shape these environments, including deserts defined by low rainfall.

pages.text: Earth’s Desert Regions About one-fifth of Earth’s land is deserts. Every continent has deserts, including Antarctica, most of which is considered a cold desert. Cloudless skies for many days in a row are common in hot deserts. That’s because the humidity—the amount of water vapor in the air— is often too low for clouds to form. When they do, they may produce rain that evaporates before it reaches the ground. This kind of rain is called virga. Precipitation varies, depending on the type of desert. Some deserts may go a year or longer without any rain at all. Long dry spells can put deserts at risk for wildfires. In fact, wildfires are more common today than they were long ago. Global warming is causing droughts as well as higher temperatures in many desert regions.
pages.brief: A hot desert lies under a cloudless sky, while Antarctica appears as a vast cold desert of ice. Rain falls as virga and evaporates before reaching the ground. Dry vegetation and distant drought conditions suggest wildfire risk, with global warming bringing droughts and higher temperatures to many desert regions.

pages.text: A large haboob rolls across Mali, in West Africa. In cold deserts, much of the precipitation falls as snow rather than rain. Warmer deserts may have one rainy season or two. Sudden, violent rainstorms in some deserts can cause flash flooding. Thunderstorms often produce strong winds, and in hot deserts, these winds kick up a great deal of sand and dust. On occasion, the winds create haboobs—huge walls of sand and dust that may be nearly 3 kilometers (2 mi.) high. Wowser! • The hottest temperature in the world was recorded at Death Valley, in California, in 1913. The temperature was 57 degrees Celsius (134°F). • Daytime and nighttime temperatures in deserts can be very different because of the lack of humidity. (In wetter parts of the world, the humidity tends to hold in heat after sunset.) In Chihuahua, Mexico, daytime temperatures can reach 37°C (100°F), while nighttime temperatures on the same day can drop below freezing (0°C, or 32°F).
pages.brief: A huge haboob rolls across Mali, in West Africa, a towering wall of sand and dust nearly three kilometers high. The violent desert storm rises above the landscape. In other desert conditions, snow falls in cold deserts, and sudden rainstorms can cause flash flooding.

pages.text: Types of Deserts While Earth’s deserts have an amazing amount of variety, they can be grouped into four main types. Hot, Dry Deserts These deserts are the hottest type and also the best known. Although the weather is generally warm all year long, temperatures can reach extremes in summer—as high as 49 degrees Celsius (120°F). They can drop quickly after dark, especially in winter. Rainfall may be low year-round or occur in short bursts between long dry seasons. The largest hot, dry desert—the Sahara, in Africa—is almost as large as the continental United States. Other deserts of this type are located in southwestern North America, Central and South America, South Asia, and Australia. Semiarid Deserts Semiarid deserts have summers that are long and dry, though not as hot as those in hot, dry deserts. Winters are cold, with little rain or snow. In North America, Nevada’s Great Basin Desert is a semiarid desert. So is the Colorado Plateau, a large region that covers parts of Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico. Spain’s Tabernas Desert, which is Europe’s only true desert, is also classified as a semiarid desert.
pages.brief: Hot, dry deserts and semiarid deserts appear side by side. The Sahara stretches wide with extreme summer heat, while North America's Great Basin and Colorado Plateau show cooler, drier semiarid land. Spain's Tabernas Desert, Europe's only true desert, also appears among rocky, shrub-covered semiarid terrain.

pages.text: What’s a Rain Shadow Desert? rising air cools, clouds form, rain or snow falls dry air moves down and warms warm, wet air rain shadow Some deserts are dry because mountains block moisture from reaching them. Warm, wet air moves up one side of a mountain range. Clouds form, then drop rain and snow. When that air starts down the range’s other side, it warms again, and the clouds disappear. The result on the far side is a rain shadow. Coastal Deserts Coastal deserts are usually located along the western edges of continents. Cold ocean currents along the coast produce winter fog and often block sunlight. The weather in coastal deserts is very dry but not extremely hot. Summers are warm, and winters are cool. Average yearly rainfall is usually 8 to 13 centimeters (3–5 in.). The Atacama Desert (South America) and the Namib Desert (Africa) are both coastal deserts. Cold Deserts Cold deserts have long, cold winters with high snowfall. Summers are short, and the snow can stay frozen for years. Most of Antarctica is cold desert, as is the Gobi Desert (Asia), the Patagonian Desert (South America), and most of Greenland.
pages.brief: A mountain range blocks moisture: warm, wet air rises one side, clouds form and drop rain or snow, then dry air warms as it moves down the other side. Beyond the mountains lies a rain shadow. Coastal deserts with fog and cold deserts with long snowy winters appear in the wider desert landscape.

pages.text: Desert Plants Because deserts are so dry, very little liquid water is available for living things to use, but adaptations allow them to live in habitats with low precipitation. Desert plants have three main survival strategies. One group of plants—succulents— store water in their roots, stems, or leaves. Cactuses are succulents, and there are many others as well. Most succulents have thick, waxy skin that holds in water. They often have shallow roots that enable them to quickly absorb any rain that falls. A second group of desert plants drop their leaves and become dormant during the dry season, then quickly spring to life when the rains return. Some plants in this group, including mesquite trees, have a long taproot that reaches deep underground to find water. This plant, baby toes, is a succulent but not a cactus. It does not have spines.
pages.brief: Desert plants use different survival strategies. A cactus stores water in thick, waxy stems and has shallow roots to absorb rain quickly. A mesquite tree reaches deep underground with a long taproot. The baby toes succulent stores water too but has no spines, unlike a cactus.

pages.text: A third set of adaptations involves avoiding drought altogether. Plants in this group, including many desert wildflowers, mature quickly and complete their life cycle before the dry season begins. They devote their energy to producing seeds that germinate when the rains return. Photosynthesis in the Desert Plants produce their own food through a chemical process known as photosynthesis. This process involves taking in carbon dioxide gas through tiny holes called stomata, which are mainly located on the underside of leaves. Chlorophyll, a green pigment in the leaves, helps plants capture sunlight to make a simple sugar called glucose from carbon dioxide and water. Because photosynthesis requires sunlight, most plants conduct this process during the day. However, opening their stomata causes them to lose large amounts of water, which would be a problem for desert plants. Many desert plants conduct photosynthesis without losing much water. They keep their stomata closed during the day and open them at night, when the air is cooler and moister. They store carbon dioxide overnight and use it the next day to make food. Palo verde trees have a different way to conserve water. They drop their leaves during especially dry periods to avoid losing water. However, they can still make food because of the chlorophyll in their green bark. palo verde bark.
pages.brief: Many desert wildflowers mature quickly and complete their life cycle before the dry season, producing seeds that wait for rain. A palo verde tree conserves water by dropping its leaves during very dry periods, while its green bark still helps it make food in the desert sunlight.

pages.text: An African bullfrog hides beneath sand (left). A ground squirrel uses its tail to shield it from sunlight (right). Both live in Africa’s Kalahari Desert. Desert Animals The lack of water is also a challenge for animals, as are the high temperatures in many deserts.
