Few large mammals live in hot deserts compared to most other biomes because they don’t tolerate the heat and lack of water well. Many desert animals, including squirrels, avoid the heat and conserve water by staying in the shade during the hottest times of the day. They hide away in a burrow or under rocks or vegetation. Others, including owls and small Australian marsupials known as bilbies, are nocturnal, or active at night. Still others, such as rattlesnakes, are typically crepuscular—active at dawn and dusk. Some desert animals, including bats, migrate to other locations during the hottest or driest times of the year. Desert toads become dormant while waiting for rain or cooler temperatures to return.
pages.brief: In Africa's Kalahari Desert, an African bullfrog hides beneath the sand, while a ground squirrel uses its tail to shield itself from sunlight. Other desert animals escape the heat in shade, burrows, or under rocks and vegetation, and some become active at night or at dawn and dusk.

pages.text: Desert animals have other ways to stay cool as well. Coyotes pant, while owls flutter their throat. Jackrabbits and fennec foxes release body heat through their large ears. Bighorn sheep shed their winter coat in stages, with their belly and other shaded parts losing hair first to help body heat escape. Getting enough water is another challenge for desert animals. Many feed on succulents, nectar, or sap. Others, especially reptiles and birds, release waste that contains very little water. Some desert animals have very unusual adaptations that help them get water. For example, thorny devil lizards have grooves between their spikes that absorb collected dew and send it to their mouth. black-tailed jackrabbit thorny devil lizard.
pages.brief: Desert animals find ways to stay cool. A black-tailed jackrabbit releases body heat through its large ears, and a thorny devil lizard has grooves between its spikes that collect dew and carry it toward its mouth. A coyote pants, an owl flutters its throat, and a fennec fox uses its big ears.

pages.text: People in Deserts People have lived in deserts for many thousands of years. Today, roughly one billion people live in this biome—about one-seventh of Earth’s population. Like plants and nonhuman animals, people have had to adapt to find enough water to make their homes there. Traditionally, desert dwellers have been nomadic, moving with the seasons to find water and food. Protective clothing has shielded them from sunlight as well as sandstorms. In African and Asian deserts, camels, sheep, goats, and horses have often provided transportation as well as milk. The nomadic Tuareg people of the Sahara Desert are sometimes referred to as the “blue people.” Modern adaptations to desert life often involve bringing water in from elsewhere. Dams and irrigation have allowed millions of people to live in deserts. Residents of modern desert cities and towns consider air-conditioning essential. Deserts are popular destinations for tourists. Attractions include hiking, camping, and appreciating the stillness and natural beauty.
pages.brief: Tuareg people of the Sahara, sometimes called the blue people, wear protective clothing while traveling with camels. Desert dwellers move with the seasons to find water and food. Nearby, a modern desert town uses dams and irrigation, and tourists hike and camp among the still, beautiful landscape.

pages.text: In addition to animals, crepuscular describes other things related to twilight. Here, crepuscular rays shoot out from clouds during a Sonoran Desert sunset. So Much to See The plants, animals, and landscapes in deserts are all unique and fascinating—and there’s still more to appreciate. Because deserts have fewer tall trees than most other biomes, it’s easier to see the sky, which often puts on shows too dramatic to miss. Storm clouds can loom so large that they take on a life of their own. The sky sometimes fills with unusual sunrays so amazing that it’s hard to believe they’re real. Meteor showers and the huge arc of the Milky Way are also special nighttime treats. Although deserts have a reputation for being harsh places, in reality they’re treasures with wondrous gems just waiting to be discovered.
pages.brief: Crepuscular rays shoot out from clouds during a Sonoran Desert sunset, spreading across a wide sky above the desert. Storm clouds loom large, unusual sunrays fill the sky, and at night meteor showers and the huge arc of the Milky Way become special treats for anyone watching the open desert sky.

books.title: Oceans
books.art_why: Modern oceans, marine animals, and places exist today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: Waves crash on the Indian Ocean. A Vast, Hidden World The ocean is a vast and mysterious place. A quick glance from the deck of a ship might make you think you’re in the middle of nowhere. The endless water may seem lifeless on the surface, with nothing but dark, choppy waves stretching out in every direction. In truth, the ocean is filled with life, movement, and color. Marine organisms range in size from single-celled green algae to enormous colonies of seagrass and from microscopic viruses to blue whales—the largest animals ever known to have lived on Earth. The ocean is also home to mountain ranges, active volcanoes, huge plateaus, and deep trenches. This endlessly fascinating world still has much left for humans to explore. It is also one of Earth’s most important biomes, affecting everything from weather and climate to global food supplies.
pages.brief: From the deck of a ship, dark, choppy waves crash across the Indian Ocean and stretch to the horizon. Below the water, small green algae, seagrass, a blue whale, underwater mountains, active volcanoes, plateaus, and deep trenches show the ocean's hidden life and landforms.

pages.text: The Ocean Biome Different types of environments cover Earth’s surface. These regions and the communities of plants and animals that live there are called biomes. Deserts, rainforests, and rivers are examples of biomes. So are oceans. Many factors play a part in creating Earth’s biomes. For land biomes, two important factors are latitude—how far north or south of the equator a location is—and elevation, or height above sea level. Both help determine how warm or cool a place is. For water biomes, one of the most important factors is whether they contain salt water or fresh water. In this book, you’ll learn about the ocean biome, which covers about 70 percent of Earth’s surface and contains salt water. Earth’s Oceans.
pages.brief: A wide view of Earth's surface shows deserts, rainforests, rivers, and oceans side by side. A globe with a hot equator and cooler poles, and a mountain rising above sea level, shows how latitude and elevation affect climate. Salt water fills the ocean biome, which covers about 70 percent of the planet.

pages.text: Four or Five Oceans? Long ago, schoolchildren only learned about four oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, and Arctic. During that time, scientists debated whether there were four or five oceans. In 2000, the International Hydrographic Organization, which surveys and charts Earth’s oceans and seas, officially added the Southern Ocean to the list of oceans. It surrounds Antarctica and extends north to the latitude line at 60° south. Not all countries recognize the Southern Ocean, and some schoolchildren still learn that Earth has only four oceans. Oceans make up 97 percent of the planet’s water. They are the largest bodies of water on Earth. We often talk about oceans in the plural because we’ve named different sections of them. However, since all the oceans are connected, in fact there is only one. Smaller areas of the ocean that are partly surrounded by land are known as seas, gulfs, and bays. They also contain salt water. Oceans by Size Atlantic 24% Pacific 47% Indian 19% Southern 6% Arctic 4% The Pacific is so huge, it’s nearly as large as Earth’s other four oceans combined.
pages.brief: A globe shows the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic Oceans, with the Pacific nearly as large as the other four combined. Around Antarctica, the Southern Ocean reaches north to 60 degrees south. A child studies four oceans while a scientist points to the fifth.

pages.text: Water and Air Although Earth’s oceans all contain salt water, they differ in many other ways. At a basic level, regions of the ocean can be classified according to Earth’s three main climate zones: tropical, temperate, and polar. The tropical zones, which surround the equator, are the warmest, and the polar zones, which are near the poles, are the coldest. However, many other factors also play a part in ocean features. Water moves in currents, both on the ocean’s surface and deep below. Currents may carry warm water to cold regions or cold water to warm regions. Surface currents are caused by blowing wind as well as Earth’s rotation on its axis. Deep currents form as a result of differences in temperature and salinity, which is the amount of salt in the water. Wind is the most common cause of ocean waves. Waves may also form as a result of tides, which rise and fall each day. Tides are caused by the Moon’s gravity pulling on Earth. Because the Moon is so much closer to our planet than the Sun, its tidal effect on Earth is stronger.
pages.brief: A globe is split into warm tropical zones near the equator, temperate zones, and cold polar zones near the poles. Surface currents move warm and cold water, wind blows across the sea to make waves, and the Moon pulls on Earth to raise and lower tides.

pages.text: The temperature of the ocean also varies a great deal from the surface to the seafloor. Water is warmer near the surface partly because it’s warmed by the Sun. In addition, cold water sinks because it’s denser than warm water. It’s also under much more pressure. The ocean affects weather and climate by absorbing most of the Sun’s rays. It works much like a huge solar panel, especially in the tropical zones, and moves this heat around the world. Because of its enormous size, the ocean also helps drive the water cycle because of the amount of evaporation that takes place above it. This process sometimes creates huge storms. Climate Change and the Ocean The ocean absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, which helps lessen the effects of climate change. At the same time, the ocean is greatly affected by climate change. Rising temperatures and melting ice are altering weather patterns, ocean currents, coastal erosion, marine ecosystems, and more. Tropical cyclones, including hurricanes, are violent spinning storms that form over warm ocean water. They usually weaken as they move over land but can still cause a lot of damage.
pages.brief: Sunlight warms the ocean surface while cold, dense water sinks into the deep. The ocean absorbs the Sun's rays and moves heat around the world, driving evaporation, the water cycle, and huge storms. A tropical cyclone spins over warm ocean water, and melting ice and rising temperatures affect currents and coasts.

pages.text: Ocean Landforms Land along the edge of the ocean, called a coast or shoreline, may be sandy, rocky, or muddy. It lies next to shallow water located above slightly lower land called the continental shelf. Beyond this zone is the continental slope, a steep drop-off that leads down to the deep ocean. The seafloor is always changing because of the movement of tectonic plates in Earth’s crust, or rocky outer layer. Seafloor features include underwater volcanoes and seamounts as well as plateaus and plains. A notable feature of the seafloor is mid-ocean ridges, a system of mountain chains nearly 65,000 kilometers (40,390 mi.) long. This system formed and continues to change as a result of tectonic plates moving apart. Melted rock, called magma, fills in the space between the plates. The highest areas of the seafloor, which extend above the ocean’s surface, have formed volcanic islands such as Iceland and the Hawaiian Islands. Word Wise Word Wise Tectonic plates are huge pieces of Earth’s crust that move as hot, weak rock moves in the mantle, the layer underneath the crust. The movement of these plates causes earthquakes, volcanoes, and many other changes in Earth’s surface.
pages.brief: A coastline meets shallow water above the continental shelf, then drops steeply down the continental slope. On the seafloor, tectonic plates move apart along a long mid-ocean ridge, magma fills the gap, and underwater volcanoes, seamounts, plateaus, and plains rise. Volcanic islands such as Iceland and the Hawaiian Islands reach above the surface.

pages.text: The Ocean Floor continental shelf volcanic island continental slope seamount underwater volcano mid-ocean ridge trench seafloor magma Another feature of the seafloor is trenches, which are the deepest parts of the ocean. They form when two tectonic plates move toward each other and the lighter plate pushes the denser plate beneath it. When this happens, a steep, long V-shaped valley forms in the seafloor. Some of the largest earthquakes ever recorded have been caused by this process. It also causes volcanic islands to form. Japan’s islands as well as a group of islands off the coast of Alaska formed in this way. Most trenches are located in the Pacific Ocean. The deepest among them is the Mariana Trench, which is located south of Japan near the Mariana Islands. Trenches are completely dark and near freezing. Water pressure is over a thousand times greater than it is on the ocean’s surface.
pages.brief: A cutaway of the seafloor shows the continental shelf, a volcanic island, the continental slope, seamounts, an underwater volcano, a mid-ocean ridge, and a deep trench. Magma rises below. In the Pacific, the Mariana Trench lies south of Japan near the Mariana Islands, completely dark, near freezing, and under immense pressure.

pages.text: Zones and Organisms The ocean is divided vertically into zones by the amount of sunlight they receive. The surface receives the most sunlight, and darkness increases with greater depth. In addition to varying light, the zones have different temperatures, pressures, amounts of oxygen, and mineral nutrients. The sunlit, or surface, zone makes up only about 5 percent of the ocean’s depth. It receives enough sunlight for photosynthesis, the process by which plants and certain other organisms make their own food using sunlight, air, and water. Microscopic algae called phytoplankton, along with seagrass and giant kelp, another type of algae, are the ocean’s main photosynthesizers. They are crucial to all life on our planet because they produce at least half of Earth’s oxygen. Ocean Zones sunlit zone about 200 m (660 ft.) twilight zone about 1,000 m (3,300 ft.) midnight zone about 4,000 m (13,100 ft.) ocean floor as deep as 6,000 m (20,000 ft.)
pages.brief: The ocean is shown in vertical layers: a sunlit surface zone about 200 meters deep, a twilight zone near 1,000 meters, a midnight zone near 4,000 meters, and the ocean floor as deep as 6,000 meters. In the sunlit zone, phytoplankton, seagrass, and giant kelp use sunlight to make food and produce oxygen.

pages.text: Phytoplankton are also the foundation of many ocean food chains. They and other photosynthesizers provide food for a huge variety of animals, either directly or indirectly. These animals include sea jellies, crustaceans, fish, seabirds, sea turtles, and marine mammals such as seals and whales. Because of photosynthesis, this zone is home to about 90 percent of all ocean life. Coral reefs are also found in the sunlit zone. These huge undersea communities, which are made of the built- up skeletons of hard corals, support an incredible number of organisms. Algae living with the corals produce food for them as well as for reef fish and other animals. Most coral reefs are found in the sunlit zone because most corals depend on algae, which need sunlight for photosynthesis. The twilight zone is located beneath the sunlit zone. It receives some sunlight but not enough for photosynthesis, so it contains no plants or other photosynthetic organisms. The sunlight it receives isn’t enough to warm the water, which is always cold.
pages.brief: Tiny phytoplankton drift in sunlit water, the base of many ocean food chains. Sea jellies, crustaceans, fish, seabirds, sea turtles, seals, and whales feed on them directly or indirectly. Nearby, a coral reef built from hard coral skeletons supports reef fish and other animals, while algae living with the corals make food.

pages.text: Animals in the twilight zone include squid, octopuses, sperm whales, and certain kinds of fish. Creatures in and below this zone have adaptations for dealing with the increased darkness, cold, and pressure. Some glow, while others have no eyes and depend on senses besides vision. The midnight zone makes up about 90 percent of the ocean. It is completely dark and near freezing all the time. Sea cucumbers, gulper eels, and unusual fish are among the animals that make their homes here. We know very little about this zone because it is so hard to explore. Trenches are part of the midnight zone. Conditions in trenches are harsh, but a small number of organisms live here, too. Bacteria are the foundation of food chains. Instead of sunlight, they use hydrogen sulfide gas to produce energy. Glow-in-the-Dark Animals Some animals that live in the twilight and midnight zones have adapted to the dark by glowing. Some are bioluminescent; they make their own light by means of a chemical reaction in their body. Others are biofluorescent, which involves taking in blue light, changing it, and giving off different colors of light. This pyrosome flashes brightly in the water around Hawaii. It is bioluminescent.
pages.brief: In cold twilight water, squid, octopuses, sperm whales, and fish swim through increasing darkness. Some creatures glow, and others have no eyes. Deeper in the midnight zone, sea cucumbers, gulper eels, and unusual fish live in constant cold and dark. In trenches, bacteria use hydrogen sulfide gas for energy, and a bioluminescent pyrosome flashes near Hawaii.

pages.text: A fishing crew in Alaska loads their catch of silver salmon. People and Oceans Scientists study the ocean to learn about Earth’s landforms, weather, climate, animals, and much more. This biome is such a fascinating place that it would be easy to think its main value is to satisfy scientific curiosity. However, it also provides an enormous amount of food for people around the world—so much so that overfishing has become a serious problem. It also supplies ingredients for medicines used to treat cancers, ease pain, and help wounds heal. In addition, the ocean has allowed people to travel by water since ancient times. People also appreciate the ocean for the recreational opportunities it offers. These include scuba diving, snorkeling, surfing, boating, fishing, and whale watching as well as visiting distant islands.
pages.brief: A fishing crew in Alaska loads their catch of silver salmon onto a boat. Around them, the ocean provides food, ingredients for medicines, and routes for travel. People also enjoy scuba diving, snorkeling, surfing, boating, fishing, whale watching, and visiting distant islands.

pages.text: Treasures from a Hidden World The next time you wander along a beach examining seashells, stones, and bits of seaweed, take a moment to appreciate the ocean and the treasures it brings. Think about how deep it is and the organisms and landforms it contains. Where did each interesting thing that washed up onshore come from? What was its journey like? Most of us only get to experience a small part of the ocean. The sparkling surface of the water hides a world as fascinating and complex as any biome on land. From the sunny upper layer to the cold, dark depths of the ocean’s trenches, there will always be new and amazing things to discover. A sperm whale disappears into the Pacific Ocean near New Zealand.
pages.brief: A person wanders a beach examining seashells, stones, and bits of seaweed washed ashore. The sparkling surface stretches out toward deep water, hiding organisms and landforms below. Nearby in the Pacific Ocean near New Zealand, a sperm whale disappears beneath the waves.

books.title: Amazing Animal Adaptations
books.art_why: Real animals and habitats in the book can be photographed today.

pages.text: Amazing Animal Adaptations.
pages.brief: A wide natural-history collage evokes animal adaptation with a variety of generic creatures in land, water, and air habitats, emphasizing diverse body forms and survival features; no specific species, people, or events are shown, keeping the image open and thematic.

pages.text: A Penguin Surprise When you think of penguins, what image comes to mind? You probably imagine black- and-white birds sliding down snowy slopes and diving into icy waters, not sunning themselves on tropical islands near the equator! You might be surprised to learn that one kind of penguin inhabits just such a place. The Galapagos penguin lives on warm islands in the eastern Pacific Ocean. How does a species originally from Antarctica survive in such a climate? It changes over time, gradually developing physical and behavioral adaptations that suit the conditions. The Galapagos penguin is not the only species to do this. Most animal species exist today because of how they changed and adapted to their surroundings. Galapagos penguins are the only penguins found at the equator.
pages.brief: A Galapagos penguin stands on warm tropical island rock near the equator in the eastern Pacific Ocean, sunning itself rather than sliding on snow or diving in ice; the small black-and-white bird is shown in bright, mild island conditions.

pages.text: The monarch’s migration is legendary. For some, the journey to Mexico begins as far north as Canada. Survival Strategies The ability to adapt is key to any living thing’s survival: if it cannot thrive where it lives, it must change, go elsewhere, or die. There are two types of adaptations. One kind has to do with an animal’s behavior, or how it acts. For instance, animals that migrate from one place to another in search of better food and living conditions demonstrate a behavioral adaptation. Migration usually happens when seasons change. Monarch butterflies, for example, fly south to Mexico and other warm places when fall arrives in their northern summer homes; in the spring, they head north as temperatures rise.
pages.brief: Monarch butterflies fly south across a broad landscape toward warm places in Mexico as fall arrives, while others head north in spring as temperatures rise; the orange-and-black insects are shown migrating in large numbers over land.

pages.text: Hibernation is another kind of behavioral adaptation that occurs when seasons change. Instead of moving to a new place, some animals stay put and go into a state somewhat like sleep. True hibernators include frogs, ground squirrels, and bats; many animals once thought to hibernate, such as bears and skunks, actually enter a lighter state of sleep called torpor. Both groups of animals enter these states during cold winter months when food is scarce because they use less energy and need less food. When outside conditions improve in the spring, they become active again. A whiskered bat hibernates in a Netherlands limestone quarry (inset). A black bear mother sleeps with her cub inside their den in Minnesota (main). Bats are true hibernators, while bears enter a lighter state of sleep.
pages.brief: A whiskered bat hangs in a Netherlands limestone quarry, while a black bear mother sleeps with her cub inside a Minnesota den; the bat is shown in true hibernation and the bear in a lighter sleep during cold winter months.

pages.text: By contrast, structural adaptations are changes in body structure that make it easier for animals to live in their environment. These changes happen slowly over many generations. Chameleons, for example, developed skin that can change color, which helps them blend in with their surroundings and makes it hard for predators or prey to see them. Foxes have structural adaptations that help them use camouflage, too. The Arctic fox has a white coat, which makes it hard to see in the snow, while the desert fox has a tan coat, which blends in with the desert sand. Both foxes have other structural adaptations as well. The Arctic fox has much smaller ears than its cousin because foxes lose body heat through their ears. The Arctic fox lives in a cold environment, so it needs to hold in body heat. The desert fox, on the other hand, lives in a hot environment and needs to stay cool, so it has very large ears that help it shed heat.
pages.brief: A chameleon changes color to blend with its surroundings; nearby, an Arctic fox with a white coat and small ears stands in snow, while a desert fox with a tan coat and very large ears stands on sand, showing body structures suited to cold and hot places.

pages.text: Oddly Adaptable Some adaptations are odder than others. Take walking sharks. Found in waters near Australia and Indonesia, these small sharks have very strong front fins. At times, they use their muscular fins not to swim but rather to crawl across the ocean floor. Giraffes have a few odd adaptations of their own. Dig deep into a giraffe’s coat and you’ll end up holding your nose. That’s because giraffe fur works as a chemical defense. It is full of antibiotics and other smelly chemicals that keep parasites away. Giraffes also need very little sleep. Most giraffes get by on just two hours of shut-eye a day, and nearly all of that is while standing! Both behaviors help protect them from predators.
pages.brief: A small walking shark uses its strong front fins to crawl across the ocean floor near Australia and Indonesia, while a giraffe stands alert and barely sleeps; the shark’s muscular fins and the giraffe’s protective fur are shown in their natural habitats.

pages.text: A Slow Process Animal species don’t think about ways to change. Adaptation happens naturally over time. Early bears that entered a state of torpor survived cold winters. The bears that didn’t died. As a result, only the first group of bears was around to reproduce. Something similar happened with foxes. Arctic foxes with small ears survived, while those with large ears did not. The survivors mated, and, in time, all the foxes in that environment had small ears because that feature was passed down. Animal species evolve through a combination of behavioral and structural adaptations. The Galapagos penguin is a good example. Galapagos penguins found their way to the tropics by way of the Humboldt Current. This current carries cold water north from Antarctica and is rich in squid and fish like sardines. The penguins are right at home in the cold water. They must come on land to nest, however, and land in the tropics is much warmer than water. South America PACIFIC OCEAN.
pages.brief: Early bears shelter through a cold winter while small-eared foxes survive in a snowy environment; a Galapagos penguin swims in the cold, food-rich Humboldt Current near South America and comes ashore to nest in the tropics.

pages.text: Galapagos penguins have ways to cope with the heat. They pant to keep cool, and they stretch out their flippers to shade their feet and keep them from getting sunburned. The penguins build their nests in burrows between rocks, hidden from the Sun’s rays. While other penguins molt once a year, Galapagos penguins molt twice. Shedding their feathers helps them stay cool. These penguin behaviors and features developed over time. Penguins that lacked them died off. Prime nesting sites like this one are limited. In 2010, researchers built 120 shady penguin nest sites to help these endangered birds.
pages.brief: A Galapagos penguin stands on hot rocky land, panting and stretching its flippers to shade its feet; nearby, a nest burrow between rocks is hidden from the sun, and shady nesting sites show how the endangered birds cope with tropical heat.

pages.text: Odd Diets Diet is a behavioral adaptation. Some animal species have developed eating habits that help them survive. Kangaroo rats, for example, live in deserts with little water or rainfall, yet somehow survive without ever drinking water. They get the moisture they need from eating grass seeds and mesquite beans. A kangaroo rat hops in a manner similar to the much larger kangaroo, but the rat lives in North America. A parrot known as the scarlet macaw eats seeds, too, except these seeds contain a deadly poison. What may keep the macaw safe is its habit of also gnawing on rocks that contain clay. The clay absorbs the poison, which allows the birds to digest the seeds safely. Then again, new studies suggest the birds may be eating the clay in order to increase the salt in their diet. Either way, this instinctive behavior is a dietary adaptation that helps the birds survive. scarlet macaw.
pages.brief: A kangaroo rat hops across a North American desert and eats grass seeds and mesquite beans without drinking water; a scarlet macaw eats seeds and gnaws on clay-rich rocks, a dietary habit that may help the bird handle poison.

pages.text: Strange ocean creatures known as tube worms have their own way of dealing with poison. Tube worms live in total darkness at the bottom of the Pacific Ocean and cluster near hot vents that pump out dangerous gases from deep inside Earth. The gases would kill most life-forms, but tube worms survive and even thrive, thanks to their odd body structure. They lack body parts we would expect to see in animals, such as eyes and a stomach. They are basically bags of bacteria. The bacteria inside the tube worms use the gases as an energy source. Tube worms cluster near a warm gas vent in the North Pacific.
pages.brief: Tube worms cluster in total darkness at the bottom of the Pacific Ocean near hot vents that pump dangerous gases from inside Earth; the eyeless, stomachless creatures appear as pale bags of bacteria thriving around a warm gas vent in the North Pacific.

pages.text: Their Blood Runs Cold Subfreezing temperatures can kill an animal. Animals’ body cells are mostly made of water. When cells freeze, the water turns to ice and expands. The cells burst, which causes death. Animals have developed different ways to keep this from happening. When temperatures drop, some species migrate to warmer places, while others sleep in warm dens. Still others stay alive by “supercooling” their body fluids. Many insects produce chemicals that act as a kind of antifreeze. The chemicals keep ice crystals from growing, so body cells get supercool but never freeze. This adaptation helps cockroaches and caterpillars survive freezing temperatures for days. Alaska’s red flat bark beetle can supercool its body fluids to –50°C (–58°F). red flat bark beetle Wood frogs can survive for weeks at a time when temperatures drop as low as –14°C (7°F). Although ice does form within frogs’ bodies, it forms between cells rather than inside them. That way, cells are not at risk of bursting.
pages.brief: A red flat bark beetle from Alaska supercools its body fluids in freezing conditions, while a wood frog survives with ice forming between its cells rather than inside them; both animals are shown in cold surroundings, with the frog partly encased in ice.

pages.text: Other animals adapt by simply getting rid of the water in their body through a process called dehydration. Tiny insects known as Antarctic midges dry up, appear frozen, and seem to be dead. When they come in contact with water, however, they spring back to life. Only one mammal can supercool its body— the Arctic ground squirrel. This squirrel’s body temperature can drop as low as –3°C (26°F). Just how it does this is a mystery. It doesn’t make its own antifreeze, nor does it get rid of fluids. Yet somehow it has adapted to survive very low temperatures. wood frog An Arctic ground squirrel in Alaska finds a snack.
pages.brief: Tiny Antarctic midges appear dried, frozen, and dead until water touches them and they revive; nearby, an Arctic ground squirrel in Alaska finds a snack while its body temperature can drop below freezing, showing an unexplained way of surviving cold.

pages.text: Wondrous Water Bears The tiny water bear is not a bear at all. It’s a microscopic animal known as a tardigrade that has some pretty impressive adaptations. Water bears can withstand cold to –200°C (–328°F) and heat higher than 149°C (300°F). They can survive high levels of radiation, a dangerous form of energy, and pressure six times greater than that found at the bottom of the ocean. In many conditions, they survive by curling into a ball and entering a nearly lifeless state. They also produce many substances known as antioxidants, which keep vital organs intact. And they produce a protein that protects their cells from the effects of radiation. These adaptations make tardigrades nearly indestructible. Scientists think that tardigrades will outlast humans, thanks to their amazing adaptations!
pages.brief: A microscopic tardigrade, or water bear, is shown curled into a nearly lifeless ball; the tiny animal’s rounded body suggests its ability to withstand extreme cold, heat, radiation, and pressure in conditions where it can survive.

pages.text: Masters of Disguise Another structural adaptation is the ability to camouflage. Some animals are true masters of disguise, such as the leaf mantis. Parts of its body are the exact shape and color of dead leaves, a remarkable adaptation that makes it easy for this insect to hide and hunt on the forest floor without being seen. Like the mantis, the cuttlefish can masquerade as part of the landscape. It looks like a small squid. Its skin changes color and texture to match its surroundings almost perfectly. The cuttlefish has three skin layers and fleshy growths called papillae, which it uses to make itself look like bumpy coral or stone. This makes it practically invisible to prey and also keeps this effective hunter from being hunted itself! Adaptations are only helpful if they work, though. Changes to an animal’s habitat can turn an effective adaptation into a fatal flaw. This is what happened to an insect known as the peppered moth.
pages.brief: A leaf mantis shaped and colored like dead leaves hides on the forest floor, while a cuttlefish changes its skin color and texture to look like bumpy coral or stone; a peppered moth appears nearby, hinting at how habitat change can affect camouflage.

pages.text: Most early peppered moths had white wings with dark spots. The moths easily blended in with lichen-covered tree bark. Predators such as birds couldn’t see the moths. Some peppered moths, however, were only dark. Those moths were easy targets for birds and, as a result, there were many more white moths than dark ones. During the Industrial Revolution in the 1800s, pollution from factory smokestacks killed the lichen and turned the tree bark black. Now the dark peppered moths could blend in and hide. The white moths stood out against the dark bark. Birds could easily see them now. The number of white moths dropped, while the number of dark moths rose. When pollution controls took effect in the 1900s, the tree bark turned lighter again, and the moth populations shifted once more. Dark moths became rare once again. Even though the color variation may have been a fatal flaw for some individual moths, it allowed the species as a whole to survive in a changing environment. peppered moths.
pages.brief: White peppered moths with dark spots blend into lichen-covered tree bark, while dark moths stand out as easy targets; later, factory smokestacks blacken the bark during the Industrial Revolution, reversing which moths hide best, and lighter bark returns when pollution controls take effect.

pages.text: Life Finds a Way Adaptation is especially important in environments that are going through change. For most living things today, that change is climate change. Animals like the Galapagos penguin must once again adapt to conditions around them. As ocean waters warm and food supplies grow scarce, the penguins must change how, what, or where they eat. The same holds true for animals around the planet. Most will survive as long as they continue to adapt in response to their changing environment—if they have time to adapt. A Galapagos penguin feeds its chick. If the cool waters that supply their food warm permanently, the penguins may have to move.
pages.brief: A Galapagos penguin feeds its chick on a rocky shore as warming ocean waters and scarce food push the birds to change how, what, or where they eat; if the cool food-rich waters warm permanently, the penguins may have to move.

pages.text: A Race Against Time Many species are being pushed to adapt to climate change, but adaptation takes time. In their race against the clock, the outlook is better for some than others. Tawny owls come in different shades. With milder winters in recent decades, researchers in Finland have seen an increase in darker owls. Less snow means these owls blend in better and are more likely to survive and reproduce. Polar bears may have evolved from their brown bear ancestors as far back as six hundred thousand years ago. It took the species time to adapt to its conditions. Black skin, white fur, and fur-covered feet are adaptations that make the bears well-suited for Arctic survival. Now, loss of their sea ice habitat due to global warming poses a dire threat to polar bears. They were listed as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act in May 2008. polar bear American pikas are cute but tough. Because they live high on mountains, they have adapted to a cold climate. When exposed to warm temperatures, pikas can overheat and die. But since pikas live so high already, there is nowhere for them to go. Trapped at the top, they could be one of the first species to go extinct due to climate change. tawny owl pika.
pages.brief: A tawny owl in Finland shows a darker shade favored by milder winters with less snow; a polar bear with black skin, white fur, and fur-covered feet stands on shrinking sea ice, while an American pika sits high on a cold mountain with nowhere cooler to go.

books.title: National Parks
books.art_why: Drawn scenes suit broad wilderness views and the book's historical content.

pages.text: A Special Place Imagine finding a beautiful spot in the wilderness, no buildings or light posts around. As you pick your way across a slick log, you can hear cool water trickling in a stream below. The sun reflects off the red canyon walls while an eagle soars quietly overhead. Dry grasses rustle around the perfect hiding spot, and gazelles leap in the distance. Wild places like this are becoming rare as humans use more and more land for farming, housing, and resource harvesting. But thankfully, many nations of the world have preserved areas of wilderness as national parks. In national parks, you can still find special places in nature.
pages.brief: A person steps carefully across a slick log over a stream in a wild canyon. Red canyon walls catch the sunlight, an eagle glides overhead, dry grasses rustle, and gazelles leap in the distance. No buildings or light posts are visible.

pages.text: The Value of Parks Protected lands are important for many reasons. Many national parks protect a rich diversity of plants, animals, and natural landforms that might otherwise be changed by human development and overuse. In a protected area, native plants and animals can exist with minimal interference by humans. Endangered animals can survive without the threat of habitat destruction and hunting. While parks are designed mostly to benefit plants, animals, and natural landforms, they can also be beneficial for humans. National parks are beautiful spaces where people can relax and enjoy nature through hiking, backpacking, camping, and other activities.
pages.brief: A protected landscape shows rich plants, animals, and natural landforms living with minimal human interference. Endangered animals roam safely, while people hike, backpack, and camp on trails through the beautiful space, relaxing and enjoying nature.

pages.text: Troubled Beginnings While parks serve important purposes and are beautiful places to visit, many have troubled histories. National parks often exist on land that is or was homeland to Indigenous people. In order to create parks, governments often removed people (sometimes forcibly), separating them from land their families had lived on for generations. These forced displacements also often cut people off from their livelihoods, denying them land where they had hunted, grown crops, and fished for thousands of years. Do You Know? The Ancestral Puebloan people have lived in the area around the Grand Canyon for more than 13,000 years. There are eleven tribes of Indigenous people living in the area today. In the 1970s, governments started working with Indigenous communities to fix this history of inhuman treatment. Since then, many nations have been trying to reincorporate Indigenous knowledge into caring for the land. After all, Indigenous people once lived on and cared for land that is now protected.
pages.brief: Indigenous people stand near a canyon homeland their families have lived on for generations. Ancestral fields and hunting grounds stretch across the landscape. The scene suggests a difficult history of displacement and a present effort to care for the land again.

pages.text: Do You Know? Around the world, there are many types of sites that are protected by governments. Here are just a few of the designations you might see: National park National monument National forest Game preserve World Heritage Site National reserve Preservation area.
pages.brief: A drawing groups several protected places together: a national park, national monument, national forest, game preserve, World Heritage Site, national reserve, and preservation area. Each kind of site appears within a broader landscape of government-protected lands around the world.

pages.text: World-Famous Wonder: Serengeti National Park and Masai Mara Reserve Tanzania and Kenya— Films and photographs from the Serengeti (SARE-en-GET-ee) are some of the most famous images of Africa. Dry grasses rustle across broad landscapes colored brown, red, and orange by the African sun. Lions, gazelles, zebras, and antelopes lounge peacefully on the immense plains. The Masai people have called this land home for thousands of years. Serengeti National Park was established in 1951 by the British in Tanzania. The park’s creation forced many Masai to move away from their lands. They now have only a small part of the land that was once theirs. The Masai have always called the Serengeti Siringitu: “the place where the land goes on forever.”
pages.brief: Under a warm African sun, lions, gazelles, zebras, and antelopes rest on broad dry grasslands colored brown, red, and orange. Masai people appear near the plains where they have lived for thousands of years, with the vast Serengeti stretching far into the distance.

pages.text: The Serengeti, one of Earth’s oldest, largest savannas, or dry grasslands, is the last home of many famous African animals. Every year, hundreds of thousands of wildebeests and zebras migrate, moving across the plains, following seasonal rains. Amazing predators, including lions, crocodiles, cheetahs, and hyenas, follow them. Several of the Serengeti’s animals, including rhinos, cheetahs, and some antelopes, are severely endangered due to poaching and human-caused habitat loss. Without the park and its rangers to protect their habitat, these creatures would probably become extinct.
pages.brief: On a vast savanna, hundreds of wildebeests and zebras move across the plains in a seasonal migration. Lions, crocodiles, cheetahs, and hyenas follow them, while rhinos and antelopes graze nearby. Rangers watch over the protected habitat that keeps these animals from disappearing.

pages.text: A Country’s Proud Heritage: Santa Rosa National Park Costa Rica —Costa Rica, a tiny Central American country, includes many natural and cultural treasures. In Santa Rosa Park, many special features come together. Along the Pacific coastline, many endangered sea turtles gather by the thousands to nest. The oceans here are also great for surfing.
pages.brief: Along Costa Rica’s Pacific coastline, thousands of endangered sea turtles gather on the sand to nest. Offshore waves roll toward the beach, where surfers ride the water. The scene shows a small Central American country’s natural and cultural treasures coming together in Santa Rosa National Park.

pages.text: The inland portions of the park feature savannas and the largest area of dry tropical forest in Central America. This habitat supports howler monkeys, wild pigs, and over fifty species of bats that nest in the park’s many caves. Many scientists visit this rich natural landscape to study how the plants and animals of the forest and ocean interact. Two historical sites preserve the memory of important battles in Costa Rica’s struggle for independence from Spain. Visitors can tour these sites and enjoy hiking, camping, and surfing.
pages.brief: Inland from the coast, dry tropical forest and savanna spread across Santa Rosa. Howler monkeys and wild pigs move among trees, bats nest in caves, and scientists study how forest and ocean life interact. Nearby historical sites recall battles for independence, while visitors hike, camp, and surf.

pages.text: Park Among the People: Rock Creek Park Washington, D.C., U.S.A. —It’s easy to imagine national parks as expanses of wild territory. It’s not so easy to imagine a park inside a major city. Yet that’s just what Rock Creek Park is. It is a small, 1,700-acre area of preserved cultural and natural heritage, right in the center of the U.S. capital city. Established in 1890, this park provides city dwellers with a spot of nature. They can escape among the plants, animals, and rushing water of a forest. A theater hosts outdoor concerts and plays in the summer. The park is also filled with historical artifacts from the founding of the U.S. capital, the Civil War, and the displaced Piscataway people.
pages.brief: Inside Washington, D.C., Rock Creek Park offers city dwellers a forest escape with plants, animals, and rushing water. An outdoor theater hosts summer concerts and plays. Historical artifacts from the city’s founding, the Civil War, and the displaced Piscataway people are preserved in this small urban park.

pages.text: Other U.S. Urban Getaways 1 Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace National Historic Site, New York City 2 Gateway National Recreation Area, New York City 3 Jefferson National Expansion Memorial, St. Louis, Missouri 4 Golden Gate National Recreation Area, San Francisco, California.
pages.brief: A drawing shows four urban getaways across the United States: the Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace in New York City, Gateway National Recreation Area in New York City, Jefferson National Expansion Memorial in St. Louis, and Golden Gate National Recreation Area in San Francisco. City settings surround each protected place.

pages.text: A Whale of a Place: Saguenay–St. Lawrence National Marine Conservation Area of Canada Quebec, Canada —Mountains rise up from the shores of Saguenay Fjord (SAG-eh-nay fee- YORD), a narrow, but extremely deep, arm of the sea. From the east, the St. Lawrence Estuary flows into the fjord. An estuary is where freshwater from a river mixes with salt water from the ocean. In the fjord, waters of different temperatures and saltiness form layers, and each layer supports its own kind of wildlife. This unusual mix of water forms the whole park—it’s entirely underwater!
pages.brief: Mountains rise above the shores of a narrow, deep fjord in Quebec. Freshwater from the St. Lawrence Estuary flows into the salt water of the sea, forming layers of different temperature and saltiness. The protected marine area stretches entirely underwater, supporting distinct kinds of wildlife in each layer.

pages.text: The mix of freshwater and salt water in the fjord provides many nutrients that attract all sorts of sea creatures. Plankton, fish, birds, and mammals all call it home. Many species of whale, including minke, fin, pilot, humpback, and blue whales, come here during warmer months. The rare beluga, or white whale, lives here year-round. Seals, fish, and invertebrates such as crabs and shellfish are also abundant. So, how do you visit an underwater park? Many people choose to get close to whales and other animals by boat. The park offers whale watches and trips in kayaks—small, canoe- like boats. Visitors also can go scuba diving, hiking, and ice fishing.
pages.brief: In the fjord’s layered waters, plankton, fish, birds, and mammals thrive. Several whale species swim here in warmer months, while rare white belugas stay year-round. Seals, crabs, and shellfish are abundant. Above and below the surface, visitors watch whales from boats and kayaks, scuba dive, hike, and ice fish.

pages.text: Unique Spots Around the World Volcanoes National Park, Hawai’i, U.S.A. — This park boasts the world’s largest, most active volcano. Visitors watch red-hot, glowing lava roll in fiery streams from the volcano. Falling into the ocean, it sends up plumes of steam. This is the formation of the island, up close! Wilderness areas provide hiking and camping among Hawai’i’s unique landscapes and plants. Everglades National Park, Florida, U.S.A.—North America’s largest subtropical wilderness, this park sits on the homelands of Seminole, Taino, and Tequesta people. Fragile swamps, grasslands, and marshy coastline are preserved here. Rare mammals such as the Florida panther and the manatee also live here.
pages.brief: In Hawai’i, red-hot lava glows and pours in fiery streams from a volcano, sending steam up where it meets the ocean. In Florida’s Everglades, fragile swamps, grasslands, and marshy coastline shelter the rare Florida panther and manatee on Seminole, Taino, and Tequesta homelands.

pages.text: Sareks National Park, Sweden —Sweden was Europe’s first country to create national parks. This one, far north above the Arctic Circle, is Western Europe’s largest area of wilderness. It is filled with majestic mountains and glaciers. It is also the ancestral home of the Saami, or Lapp people, who herd reindeer. Tassili N’Ajjer National Park, Algeria (tah-SEE-LEE n-AH-jer)—Algeria, in Northern Africa, is situated in the fierce Sahara. The landscape wasn’t always desert, however, and past civilizations left behind more than 15,000 drawings and engravings in caves and on the sides of cliffs. The art documents the history of humans since 6000 bce!
pages.brief: In Sweden’s far north above the Arctic Circle, majestic mountains and glaciers fill Sarek National Park, ancestral home of the Saami reindeer herders. In Algeria’s Sahara, ancient drawings and engravings cover cave walls and cliff sides, documenting human history since 6000 BCE in what is now desert.

pages.text: Current and Future Challenges Even after a national park is established, preserved lands face many threats. In some countries, people use parklands for growing crops, grazing livestock, and gathering firewood to warm and feed hungry people. Wars and government instability, when political parties clash violently, can also damage these fragile environments. Because some preserved lands house natural resources like oil fields, mineral resources, or forests, some people believe these resources should be used to create economic growth. The boundaries of national parks are sometimes questioned and changed as people negotiate power over these natural resources.
pages.brief: Protected lands face many threats: people grow crops, graze livestock, and gather firewood inside parklands. Wars and government instability can damage fragile environments, while oil fields, minerals, and forests tempt some to use resources for economic growth. Boundaries are sometimes questioned and changed as people negotiate power over nature.

pages.text: The geysers in Yellowstone National Park attract millions of visitors each year. Even in a well-protected national park, too many visitors can cause plenty of problems, leaving behind litter, trampling trails, or polluting the air with snowmobile exhaust. It also can be difficult to experience wilderness while surrounded by people. National parks provide refuge for endangered wildlife. They protect millions of plant species, which give us oxygen and help lower the atmosphere’s temperature. As people continue to destroy natural ecosystems to build roads and buildings, it is more vital than ever to protect these beautiful places. If future generations are to enjoy these wild spaces, governments around the world need to work with Indigenous populations to preserve the land.
pages.brief: A Yellowstone geyser erupts before a crowd of visitors. Too many people can leave litter, trample trails, and pollute the air with snowmobile exhaust, making wilderness hard to experience. The scene also shows parks as refuge for endangered wildlife and plants, with governments and Indigenous populations working together to preserve the land.

books.title: Prehistoric Trade
books.art_why: Prehistoric peoples and artifacts predate photography.

pages.text: Introduction As soon as the bell rang, Robert stuffed that night’s homework into his backpack. He ran for the front steps of the school. Every day, Robert and his friends sat and played a trading card game. Robert, William, and Rudolfo liked to play, but sometimes they would just sit and trade cards. People play in a Yu-Gi-Oh! tournament. William often got good cards from his cousin in California, and Rudolfo got cool cards from his family’s shop downtown. Robert always liked to trade, but today was special. There was a new student in the class who had just moved from Japan, and Haruki liked to trade cards, too. Haruki wanted to trade cards with William, and had cool cards from Japan that William had never seen! All of Haruki’s cards were in Japanese, and no one at Robert’s school had them. Haruki traded cards to William that William had never played with, and William gave Haruki some cool cards in return. Haruki shared these English language cards with his friends in Japan.
pages.brief: At the school steps after the bell, Robert runs with his backpack, then sits with William and Rudolfo trading game cards. Haruki, a new student from Japan, trades Japanese cards with William and later shares English cards with friends in Japan.

pages.text: Long-Distance Trade Trade is an exchange of one thing for another. Trade can involve doing work in return for an object, or trading valuable items, just like William and Haruki traded game cards. If people didn’t trade, every family would have to grow its own food, sew its own clothes, and build its own house. Trade is a basic human activity that makes it possible to enjoy products from all over the world. Now, everyday objects can come from anywhere in the world. Things in your backpack might have been made in your hometown. They also might come from Canada, Mexico, Australia, China, France, or even Brazil! Stop & Think Where do the objects in your bedroom come from? Read the labels on your clothes or toys and look at a map. How far has your clothing traveled?
pages.brief: Two children swap game cards as an example of trade. Around them are everyday objects from a backpack and a world map suggesting Canada, Mexico, Australia, China, France, and Brazil, showing that useful items can travel from many distant places.

pages.text: Trade routes from 6300 BC — AD 1200 Asia Europe ATLANTIC OCEAN PACIFIC OCEAN PACIFIC OCEAN Africa INDIAN OCEAN Australia Prehistoric world trade routes These are just some examples of the routes ancient people used to trade goods, such as silk, gold, olive oil, gems and minerals, and more. KEY Antarctica sea routes land routes Ancient people, who lived thousands of years before us, also traded objects over long distances. In Europe, men would spend months crossing oceans and traveling up rivers to trade swords or hairpins. In North and South America, people lived and traded for thousands of years before meeting Europeans. Prehistoric North American trade is a perfect example of how people moved valuable objects thousands of miles to trade them for other special objects. (Prehistoric means it happened before those people made written records, such as books.)
pages.brief: A wide world map of Asia, Europe, Africa, Australia, and the Americas shows land and sea routes used by ancient traders. Small scenes show people crossing oceans and rivers to carry swords, hairpins, silk, gold, olive oil, gems, and minerals.

pages.text: How can we learn about prehistoric trade? One way is through oral tradition. Oral tradition is the set of stories that one generation tells to the next. Because many people like to add things to stories to make them more exciting or easier to understand, stories that are part of oral tradition change over the years. Another way to learn about prehistoric trade is through archaeology. Archaeology is the study of people through the things they leave behind. By looking at the remains of buildings, graves, and especially the trash people leave behind, we can learn about what people did. How can archaeology help figure out how prehistoric North American people traded? If an archaeologist finds a broken seashell in the trash of an ancient village in Colorado, she knows those people in Colorado traded with people who lived near an ocean. Archaeologists dig through buildings from about 1,000 years ago.
pages.brief: An elder tells traditional stories to listeners. Beside this, an archaeologist digs through buildings, graves, and trash about one thousand years old. In a Colorado village trash heap, she finds a broken seashell, evidence of trade with people near an ocean.

pages.text: Asia North America Nevada How might Japanese trading cards make the trip to Nevada? Japan PACIFIC OCEAN Think about William and his trading cards. If William’s family moved houses, and someone found a Japanese card in his old room, that person would know that, somehow, William was trading with Japan! If the person who found the card didn’t know about Haruki, she might think lots of different people traded the card, bringing it from Japan to William. But since it’s impossible to buy Japanese cards anywhere near William’s hometown, it must have come from Japan. People often travel farther for a rare and valuable commodity. A commodity is something that is traded, such as gold, seashells, or a trading card. Commodities that were traded in prehistoric North America include copper, shells, and animals. In prehistoric North America, people traveled long distances on foot or by boat. Because of this, trade commodities were usually light, valuable objects that would not spoil.
pages.brief: A map spans Japan, the Pacific Ocean, and Nevada as a Japanese trading card is imagined making the long trip. Nearby, light and valuable trade goods such as copper, shells, and animal items travel on foot or by boat.

pages.text: Objects made from the reddish metal called copper are found in many North American archaeological sites. An archaeological site is a place where people have left behind evidence of their lives, such as trash or parts of buildings. Objects found on these sites are called artifacts. An artifact is an object that has been shaped or changed by people. Whole copper artifacts have been found in graves in archaeological sites, and broken objects have been found in old garbage. Copper artifacts found in North America include fishhooks, knives, jewelry, and bells. Some of the copper used to make those artifacts was mined in the area around the Great Lakes, particularly around Lake Superior. In most of North America, it was hard for prehistoric people to make metal because metal is often mixed up in rock and that rock is only found in certain areas. Rock with metal in it is called ore. To get the metal out of the ore, people have to get it really hot. This is called smelting metal. Copper Gold and copper artifact from Peru, South America.
pages.brief: At an archaeological site, people study copper artifacts: fishhooks, knives, jewelry, and bells found in graves and old garbage. Copper was mined near the Great Lakes, especially Lake Superior; ore is heated to smelt metal. A gold and copper artifact from Peru appears.

pages.text: Native Copper Trade Lake Superior largest native copper deposits Bedford Mound a major prehistoric trading center areas where native copper artifacts would have been traded possible major trade route Near Lake Superior, there were very large deposits of native copper. Native copper is special because it is very pure copper that can be found in large chunks or as sheets in cracks of rocks. Native copper also does not need smelting. Hundreds of thousands of tons of native copper were mined in this area. Artifacts made from native copper have been found in areas on either side of the Mississippi River and far downstream.
pages.brief: A map around Lake Superior shows large native copper deposits, the Bedford Mound trading center, and routes spreading copper artifacts east and west of the Mississippi River and far downstream. Large chunks and sheets of pure native copper are mined from cracks in rock.

pages.text: We can tell that this copper was traded great distances in several ways. Many sites where archaeologists find copper artifacts have no natural copper nearby, so we know the copper must have come from far away. Also, by examining copper through a microscope, or examining small amounts of chemicals in the copper, we can tell native copper from smelted copper.
pages.brief: An archaeologist examines copper under a microscope and tests tiny amounts of chemicals, telling native copper from smelted copper. A map shows copper artifacts at sites with no natural copper nearby, proving the metal was traded from far away.

pages.text: A different example of long-distance copper trade involves copper bells. Copper bells found at sites in Arizona and New Mexico were made from smelted copper. Ancient people living in Mexico and Central America made copper bells. We know this because we have found tools used to smelt copper and make bells like these in Mexico and Central America, but not in Arizona or New Mexico. This is evidence that these copper bells were traded. Copper artifacts found in North America came from different places. What if William (from the beginning of this book) had trading cards in both Spanish and Japanese? The fact that they aren’t in English doesn’t mean they all came from Japan. Spanish cards might come from Mexico or Europe, while the Japanese cards would come from Japan. William has quite the collection! Stop & Think Designs on archaeological artifacts help us figure out where those artifacts come from. Do you have a T-shirt or sweatshirt with words or designs that tell people where you’ve been?
pages.brief: Copper bells from Arizona and New Mexico sit beside tools for smelting copper and making bells in Mexico and Central America, evidence of trade. Nearby, William holds Spanish and Japanese trading cards, showing that objects from different places can mix in one collection.

pages.text: Obsidian is a glassy volcanic rock. Many tools in prehistoric North America were made by chipping flakes off rock to make sharp edges. Obsidian is much better for making sharp edges than regular rock because it has been through a heating process. It can make sharper and harder blades than ordinary glass. Obsidian is found in places that had volcanic activity, and obsidian from different areas has different, tiny amounts of chemicals. We can guess where it came from by examining the chemicals in obsidian, just as we can with the chemicals in copper. Obsidian rock from Panum Crater in northeastern California Obsidian Obsidian sculpture.
pages.brief: At Panum Crater in northeastern California, glassy volcanic obsidian rock lies on the ground. Hands chip flakes from obsidian to make sharp, hard tools, better than ordinary glass. A smooth obsidian sculpture stands nearby as another use of the volcanic rock.

pages.text: People can learn about many objects, not just copper or obsidian, based on trace chemicals. For example, the type of paper used in William’s trading cards, or the kind of ink used to print his cards might reveal where a card comes from. Prehistoric North American people living in the Northwest could easily find obsidian. Obsidian came from areas such as Washington, Oregon, Northern California, and western Canada. Obsidian deposits are often in areas that have volcanoes. Many of the tallest mountains in the Northwest are volcanoes, such as Mt. Rainier near Seattle, Washington, and Mt. Saint Helens. When a volcano erupts and the conditions are right, lava that cools rapidly can form obsidian. Mount St. Helens before its 1980 eruption.
pages.brief: In the Northwest, people find obsidian near volcanoes such as Mt. Rainier and Mount St. Helens before its 1980 eruption. Lava cools rapidly to form obsidian. A scientist examines trace chemicals in obsidian, while trading cards suggest paper and ink can reveal origins.

pages.text: Obsidian Trade CANADA Mt. Rainier Obsidian Cliff Mt. St. Helens Bedford Mound Panum Crater areas of volcanic activity in the past 2,000 years PACIFIC OCEAN GULF OF MEXICO MEXICO Obsidian was traded all the way across North America, including the United States, Canada, and Mexico. Obsidian artifacts have been found in the United States throughout the Mississippi River Valley. The appearance and trace chemicals in these obsidian artifacts tell us that the obsidian came from northwestern North America.
pages.brief: A map from Canada through the United States to Mexico shows volcanic areas and obsidian trade reaching the Mississippi River Valley. Obsidian artifacts found there have appearances and trace chemicals that identify their source in northwestern North America, far from where they were found.

pages.text: Shells Shells from the ocean are beautiful and can be used for many purposes. Humans have used shells for jewelry, as small plates, and even as musical instruments. At archaeological sites near the ocean, huge piles of shells can be found in trash heaps. Often these piles are the garbage left over after eating the meat in the middle of shellfish. We know that seashells found in the Arizona desert or the upper Mississippi River Valley are not from food, because it would have taken too long to carry shellfish that far inland before it would have become rotten and dangerous to eat. An archaeologist examines seashells found in an ancient trash heap.
pages.brief: Ocean shells appear as jewelry, small plates, and musical instruments. Near the ocean, huge shell piles remain in trash heaps after shellfish meat was eaten. In the Arizona desert and upper Mississippi River Valley, seashells are not food remains, because shellfish would have spoiled on the long inland journey.

pages.text: How do we know that some shells found on archaeological sites were used for jewelry? Many of the shells have small holes, usually in the same place. By placing the shells on a string, they could have been made into a necklace. Also, some people wore jewelry when they were buried. Many people were buried with their valuable possessions. When an archaeological site includes ancient graves, archaeologists sometimes find objects in them that were traded great distances. In undisturbed graves, shells have been found in the pattern of a necklace. The string may be gone, but the shells are in the same place they would have been if there had been a string.
pages.brief: Shells with small holes in the same place are shown strung as a necklace. In an ancient grave, a person was buried with valuable possessions, and shells lie in the pattern of a necklace; the string is gone, but the shells stayed in place.

pages.text: Shells can be helpful in identifying trade connections. Some types of shellfish only live in certain areas. For example, if a type of shell from a shellfish that lived in the Gulf of Mexico is found in Colorado, we know that the people in Colorado traded with someone from near the Gulf of Mexico. Stop & Think Many grocery stores have a counter where seafood is sold. Where does the fish you eat come from? Read the labels or ask someone at the seafood counter where the store’s fish comes from.
pages.brief: A shellfish that lives only in the Gulf of Mexico is found in Colorado, showing that Colorado people traded with someone near the Gulf. An archaeologist compares shell types. At a grocery seafood counter, a shopper asks where the store's fish comes from.

pages.text: The bones of a dog uncovered in an ancient Israeli cemetery Birds and Animals All over the world, animals are a common trade item. When Europeans first came to North America, they brought horses. Horses can be used for transportation or to pull and carry things. After European contact, many animals became part of transatlantic trade. Valuable animals were transported across the Atlantic Ocean. Sometimes we find the bones of birds and other animals in archaeological sites. The bones of animals that live in the area, particularly those that are used as food, are common. For example, in eastern North America, deer bones are often found at sites where ancient people lived.
pages.brief: Bones of a dog lie in an ancient Israeli cemetery. Across the Atlantic, Europeans bring horses to North America, where horses carry and pull things. At an eastern North American site, deer bones are common among animal remains from local food.

pages.text: Copper, Shell, and Parrot Trade Four Corners area Ancient Puebloan culture area marine shells Chaco Canyon, a major prehistoric trading center marine shells copper and parrots MEXICO Sometimes we find the bones of exotic animals in an archaeological site. Exotic animals are those that come from a different place. An elephant is an exotic animal in North America, but normal in parts of Africa. Exotic animals are evidence of trade. For an elephant to come to a zoo in North America, it needs to be traded from a faraway place. Archaeological sites in the Southwest, such as Arizona, sometimes have bones from parrots. Parrots are exotic animals because they ordinarily only live in Central or South America. Archaeologists think these birds were valued for their colorful feathers. The remains of birds, such as parrots, being found thousands of miles north of where they usually live is evidence of long- distance trade.
pages.brief: A map of the Southwest shows the Four Corners area, the Ancient Puebloan culture area, Chaco Canyon trading center, marine shells, copper, and parrots from Mexico. At an Arizona site, parrot bones appear; these exotic birds were probably valued for their colorful feathers, evidence of long-distance trade.

pages.text: Conclusion In prehistoric North America, some people traveled thousands of miles to trade. Many times, traders used boats to travel along rivers or on the coast. For example, the Mississippi River was an important trade route that connected much of North America. Other times, people had to walk. Crossing mountain ranges, such as the Rocky or Appalachian Mountains, could take weeks of difficult walking. Today, it is easier to transport heavy trade goods long distances. Ships, trucks, trains, and planes are all used to carry trade goods among the countries of the world. Containers full of trade goods travel by barge.
pages.brief: Prehistoric traders travel by boat along rivers and the coast, including the Mississippi River, and walk for weeks across the Rocky or Appalachian Mountains. In the modern world, ships, trucks, trains, planes, and barges carry containers full of trade goods across countries.

pages.text: Trade doesn’t require a truck full of valuable objects such as televisions. Trade can occur when one person gives another person something in exchange for something else. Remember how William got his Japanese trading cards? Next time you take a trip, think about all the things you take with you. Afterward, think about the things you left behind. Did you exchange gifts with someone? Did you buy something you couldn’t get at home? That’s just what the prehistoric people of the world did. Peru Germany Holland Mexico.
pages.brief: A traveler with luggage thinks about gifts exchanged and something bought far from home. William's Japanese trading cards appear nearby. Two people make a simple exchange, showing trade without a truck full of televisions; prehistoric people did the same on journeys.
